“It is to distinguish what has come into existence from what has existed eternally.”

He thus explained that anyone who affirms Allah’s oneness must distinguish between the eternal Creator and His creation, which has come into existence, without confusing the two. These people say about those who know Allah what the Christians say about the Messiah and the Shia about their imams. Many proponents of indwelling and antinomianism criticize al-Junayd and other spiritual masters who know Allah and follow the Quran and Sunnah for rejecting indwelling and affirming divine commands and prohibitions. They believe that these masters have not perfected their knowledge of reality as they themselves and their fellow proponents of indwelling and antinomianism have.

(The fourth group consists of “the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars”: the foremost people of knowledge and religion, masters of learning and worship. They affirmed and believed in everything conveyed by the Quran and Sunnah, without distorting words from their proper meanings. They affirmed that Allah is above His heavens, over His Throne, distinct from His creation, and that His creation is distinct from Him. He is also with His servants generally through His knowledge, and with His prophets and His allies through victory, support, and sufficiency. He is also near and answers supplications. The verse concerning private conversation indicates that He knows them.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, You are the Companion on the journey;

---

## Page 1987

and the Guardian of the family.”

He is therefore with the traveller on his journey and with his family in their homeland. This does not entail that His essence is mingled with theirs, just as He says:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those who are with him.”

That is, they are with him in faith—not that his essence is within theirs; rather, they are his companions. His words:

“Those will be with the believers”

indicate their agreement with the believers in faith and their allegiance to them. Allah Most High knows His servants and is with them wherever they may be. His knowledge of them is necessarily entailed by His being with them.

Similarly, the woman said:

“My husband’s sword-strap is long; his ashes are abundant; his home is near the assembly place.”

All these descriptions are literal, and her purpose is to convey their implications: tall stature, generosity in providing abundant food, and a home close to where guests gather.

In the Quran:

“Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes indeed, and Our messengers are with them, recording.”

Affirming His seeing and hearing is intended to establish His knowledge of these things, and that He knows whether they are good or evil, so that He rewards good deeds and punishes evil deeds. Likewise, His power over creation is affirmed, as in His words:

“You cannot escape in the earth or in heaven.”

And His words:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think they can outstrip Us? How evil is their judgment!”

The purpose is to instil fear of the consequences necessarily following from evil deeds: punishment and retribution. Likewise, in many passages the Lord describes Himself as knowing His servants’ deeds in order to warn them, instil fear, and encourage them to seek what is good. He describes Himself in terms of power, hearing, seeing, and the recording of deeds. The meaning signified by the expression is intended, and the necessary implication of that meaning is also intended. Thus, what is intended is what is indicated

---

## Page 1988

by the expression in its original linguistic usage, both by direct signification and by necessary implication. The expression is therefore not used solely for the implication; rather, its underlying meaning, from which that implication follows, is also intended. This is literal usage.

As for “nearness,” He sometimes mentions it in the singular form, as in His words:

“And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near; I respond.”

And in the hadith:

“Be gentle with yourselves,”

until he said:

“Indeed, the One you call upon is nearer to each of you than the neck of his mount.”

At other times, He uses the plural form, as in His words:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

This is like His words: “We recite to you,” “We relate to you,” “It is for Us to collect it and recite it,” and “It is for Us to explain it.” The recitation here is when he hears it from Gabriel, and the explanation here is its explanation to those whom the Quran reaches.

The position of the early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and its later generations is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, heard the Quran from Gabriel, and Gabriel heard it from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for His saying, “We recite,” “We relate,” and similar expressions, this form is used in Arabic for a single person of great standing who has helpers who obey him. When his helpers do something at his command, he says, “We did it.” Thus a king says, “We conquered this land,” and “This army belongs to us,” and similar things.

Allah Most High’s words also fall into this category:

“Allah takes the souls.”

For He, glorified is He, takes them through His messengers, foremost among whom is the Angel of Death, as He says:

“Our messengers take his soul.”

“Say: ‘The Angel of Death takes your souls.’”

Likewise, the angels themselves draw near to the dying person. And His words:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

---

## Page 1989

For He, glorified and exalted is He, and His angels know the good and evil that a servant’s soul whispers to him, and the intention within his soul before he acts.

Thus, His words:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein”

refer to the nearness of the angels themselves and the nearness of Allah’s knowledge. The angels themselves are nearer to the servant’s heart than his jugular vein; thus, some of them may be nearer to certain parts of him than others are. Hence He says at the conclusion of the verse:

“When the two receivers receive.”

The word “when” is an adverb of time. He thus states that they are nearer to him than his jugular vein when the two receivers receive what he says. All of this, then, concerns the angels.

As for His words:

“Indeed, I am near,”

and:

“He is nearer to each of you than the neck of his mount,”

these occur only in the context of supplication. He did not state that He is near to His servants in every circumstance; rather, He mentioned this in certain circumstances, as in the hadith:

“The nearest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating,”

and similar texts.

And His words:

“Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by a cubit. Whoever draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by an armspan. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him at a run.”

One thing’s nearness to another necessarily entails the other’s nearness to it. Yet the second’s nearness may result from the first drawing near, and the second may also draw near through an action of its own.

(The first case is like someone approaching Mecca or the wall of the Kaaba: the closer he comes to it, the closer it becomes to him, without any action on its part.

---

## Page 1990

And the second case is like a person’s nearness to someone who himself draws near to him, as mentioned earlier in this “divine” report.

The servant’s drawing near to Allah, and Allah’s bringing him near, are affirmed in numerous texts, such as His words:

“Those whom they invoke seek a means of nearness to their Lord—which of them will be nearest.”

And other similar texts. This is the nearness of the Lord Himself to His servants, and it is like His descent to the lowest heaven. In an authentic hadith:

“Allah, exalted is He, draws near on the afternoon of ‘Arafah and boasts to the angels of the people gathered at ‘Arafah.”

All this nearness is particular to certain circumstances, rather than others. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah ever states that He Himself is near to all created beings in every circumstance. This establishes the falsity of the claim made by the proponents of divine indwelling: they took what was specific and qualified and made it universal and unqualified. Their brethren, the proponents of divine union, did likewise with such statements as:

“I become his hearing,”

and:

“He comes to them in a form other than His form,”

and the fact that Allah, exalted is He, said through His Prophet:

“Allah hears those who praise Him.”

All these texts are evidence against them.

Once this is clear, the person supplicating or prostrating directs his soul toward Allah, exalted is He. The soul has an ascent appropriate to it, and undoubtedly draws near to Allah according to the degree to which it frees itself from impurities. Allah, mighty and majestic, is thus near to it with a nearness that necessarily follows from its drawing near. There is also another nearness on His part, such as His drawing near on the afternoon of ‘Arafah and in the depths of the night; and when someone draws near to Him by a handspan, He draws near to that person by a cubit. In the latter part of the night, people’s hearts have a measure of turning toward Him, drawing near, and tenderness that is not found at any other

---

## Page 1991

time.

This accords with His descent to the lowest heaven and His words:

“Is there anyone supplicating? Is there anyone asking? Is there anyone repenting?”

As for this descent, is it like His drawing near on the afternoon of ‘Arafah, which does not occur for non-pilgrims in other lands, since no prescribed standing takes place there, nor any boasting before the angels? Similarly, the opening of the gates of Paradise, the closing of the gates of Hell, and the chaining of the devils when Ramadan begins are only for the Muslims who fast Ramadan, not for the disbelievers who do not acknowledge its sanctity. Likewise, His looking upon them on the day of Badr and His saying to them:

“Do whatever you wish,”

were particular to those people. Or is this descent general in scope? There is discussion concerning this, but this is not the place for it.

Discussion of this nearness is of the same kind as discussion of His descent every night, His drawing near on the afternoon of ‘Arafah, His speaking to Moses from the tree, and His words:

“Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it.”

Elsewhere, we have mentioned what the early generations said concerning such matters, including Hammād ibn Zayd, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and others: that He descends to the lowest heaven without the Throne becoming devoid of Him. We have explained that this is the correct view, although some who claim to follow the Sunnah think that the Throne becomes devoid of Him.

Abū al-Qāsim ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mandah wrote a work on this subject. He rejected as unsound the view of those who say that He descends without the Throne becoming devoid of Him, and judged weak what was reported on this matter from Ahmad ibn Hanbal

---

## Page 1992

in his epistle to Musaddad. He challenged the authenticity of this epistle, saying that it was falsely attributed to Ahmad. He also criticized its transmitter, Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barda‘ī, saying that he was unknown and was not known among Ahmad’s companions.

Another group withholds judgment, saying neither that the Throne becomes devoid of Him nor that it does not, and objecting to those who make either statement. Among them is the hadith scholar ‘Abd al-Ghanī al-Maqdisī. As for imagining that the heavens split apart and then close together again, this is among the greatest forms of ignorance, even though some men have fallen into it.

The correct view is that of the early generations: He descends without the Throne becoming devoid of Him. A servant’s soul remains in his body night and day until he dies. During sleep, it ascends and may prostrate beneath the Throne, although it has not departed from his body. Likewise, a servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating, even as his soul remains in his body. The laws governing souls differ from those governing bodies. What, then, of the angels—and what, then, of the Lord of the worlds?

Night occurs at different times: the third of the night arrives in the East before it does in the West. His descent, of which His Messenger informed us, is to the heaven above these people during the third of their night, and to the heaven above those people during the third of theirs. No affair distracts Him from another. Likewise, glory be to Him, hearing one thing does not distract Him from hearing another, nor do requests confound Him. Rather, glory be to Him, He will speak to His servants on the Day of Resurrection and call them to account, without attending to one distracting Him from another.

## Page 1993

And Ibn ‘Abbās was asked, “How will He speak to them all at the same time on the Day of Resurrection?” He replied, “Just as He provides for them all at the same time.”

In this world, Allah, glory be to Him, hears those who supplicate and answers those who ask, despite their different languages and varied needs. One of us may have sufficiently acute hearing to hear many people speaking, just as some Quran teachers listen to several people reciting. Yet this is limited to a small number close to him. He also feels within himself closeness, nearness, and an inclination toward some people rather than others, whether present or absent, and experiences varying degrees of that nearness and closeness. “The Lord Most High,” however, is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing: His hearing encompasses all voices, and His giving meets all needs.

Some people have mistakenly imagined that His nearness is like the movement of a human body: when it inclines in one direction, it turns away from the other. Yet a person experiences his soul acting differently from his body: he finds his soul drawing near to the souls of many people, without its nearness to one diverting it from nearness to another.

“In short,” the Lord’s nearness to the hearts of the believers, and their hearts’ nearness to Him, is a well-known matter, not something obscure. Their hearts ascend to Him in proportion to the faith, knowledge, remembrance, reverent fear, and trust in Him that they contain. This is agreed upon by all people, unlike the nearness

mean that He took control, possessed dominion, and subdued, and that He is everywhere. They denied that He is above His Throne, as the people of truth affirm, and interpreted rising over the Throne as referring to power. If matters were as they claimed, there would be no distinction between the Throne and the seventh earth, for Allah has power over all things.”

Further on, he said (they spoke at length on this matter):

“All the imams, in the East and the West, have agreed upon believing in the Quran and the hadiths transmitted by trustworthy narrators from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning the attributes of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, without interpretation, description, or likening Him to creation. Whoever today interprets any of this has departed from the way of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and has separated from the community. They neither described nor interpreted; rather, they affirmed what is in the Book and the Sunnah, then remained silent. Whoever adopts Jahm’s position has separated from the community, for he has described Him as a nonentity.”

## Page 2004

Section

The interpretation of istawā (“rose over”) as istawlā (“took control”) is refuted on several grounds:

First: None of the early Muslims, whether the Companions or their successors, gave this explanation. It is not authentically reported from any of them in the books transmitting their statements. Rather, the first to advance it were some of the Jahmiyyah and Mu‘tazilah, as Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī mentioned in his books al-Maqālāt and al-Ibānah.

Second: The meaning of this word is well known. Thus, when Rabī‘ah ibn Abī ‘Abd al-Rahmān and Mālik ibn Anas were asked about His words,

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne,”

they said: “Rising is known, its manner is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation.”

This does not mean that rising is known in the language but not in the verse—for the question concerns the rising mentioned in the verse, as people rise.

Third: If its meaning is known in the language in which the Quran was revealed, then its meaning is known in the Quran.

---

## Page 2005

Fourth: If the meaning of rising in the verse were not known, there would have been no need to say, “Its manner is unknown.” For denying knowledge of its manner presupposes knowledge of its basic meaning. Likewise, we say that we acknowledge Allah and believe in Him, yet do not know how He is.

Fifth: Taking control—whether understood as power, subjugation, or something similar—extends to all created things, just as Lordship does. Although the Throne is the greatest created thing, attributing Lordship over it does not exclude Lordship over anything else, as in His words:

“Say, ‘Who is Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Great Throne?’”

The same applies to the supplication recited in distress. Thus, if istawā (“rose over”) meant istawlā (“took control”)—which applies to all existing things—it would be permissible, alongside its attribution to the Throne, to say: “He rose over heaven, over hawā (inclination), the seas and the earth, and above it and beneath it, and the like,” since He rose over the Throne.

Yet Muslims agree that one says, “He rose over the Throne,” but does not say, “He rose over these things,” even though one may say that He holds control over the Throne and these things. It is therefore clear that the meaning of istawā is specific to the Throne, rather than extending generally to all things.

Sixth: He stated that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He also stated that His Throne was upon the water before their creation. This is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Allah was, and there was nothing other than Him. His Throne was upon the water, and He recorded everything in the Record, then created the heavens and the earth.”

Since the Throne had already been created before that, it is known that He has always held control over it

---

## Page 2006

before and after. Universal control therefore cannot be the control described here, which is confined to a particular time as well as to the Throne.

(Seventh: It has not been established that istawā (“rose over”) means istawlā (“took control”) in Arabic. Those who maintain this rely chiefly on the well-known verse:

“Then Bishr rose over Iraq,
Without sword or bloodshed.”

No authentic transmission has established that this is genuine Arabic poetry. Several leading authorities on Arabic rejected it, saying that it was a fabricated verse unknown in the language. It is well known that anyone citing a hadith of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as evidence would need to establish its authenticity. How, then, can one cite a verse of poetry whose chain of transmission is unknown and which leading authorities on Arabic have challenged?

A report from al-Khalīl is cited, as related by Abū al-Muzaffar in his book al-Ifsāh (Elucidation): “Al-Khalīl was asked, ‘Have you found istawā used in Arabic to mean istawlā?’ He replied, ‘This is unknown to the Arabs and is not permissible in their language.’” Al-Khalīl was, as is well known, a leading authority on Arabic. Thus, interpreting the word in a sense unknown in the language is invalid.

Eighth: It is reported that a number of authorities on Arabic said that istawā cannot mean istawlā except when referring to someone who was powerless and then prevailed. Yet nothing is beyond the power of Allah, glorified be He, and the Throne never contends with Him. It therefore cannot mean “took control.”

Once this is clear, the poet’s words:

“Then Bishr rose over Iraq”

---

## Page 2007

is a figurative expression. The wording may not be understood in that sense unless a contextual indication shows that it is intended. This applies all the more to a word with multiple meanings. It is well known that nothing in the discourse indicates that taking control is what He intended by the verse.

“Furthermore,” authorities on Arabic have said that istawā cannot mean istawlā except where there is rivalry and a struggle for dominance: when one contender overcomes the other, it is said that he has taken control. No one has contested the Throne with Allah. Thus, even if its use in this more specific sense were established, while its conveying the broader sense remained disputed, it would not have to be interpreted in that sense merely because some authorities on Arabic said so, when they themselves disagree about it. Yet these people have claimed that, in Arabic, it means “took control” without qualification. The word istiwā occurs in several places in the Quran, as in His words:

“you and those with you have boarded the ship”

“and it came to rest on Mount Jūdī”

“so that you may settle yourselves upon their backs”

And in the hadith of Adī:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came with his mount. When he placed his foot in the stirrup, he said, ‘In the name of Allah.’ Once he was seated on its back, he said, ‘Praise be to Allah.’”

(Ninth: Even if it were established that this usage belongs to the Arabic language, it would not necessarily belong to the language of the pure Arabs. Even if some of the pure Arabs used it, it would not necessarily belong to the language and speech of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Even if it belonged to his language, it would bear the meaning known from the Quran and Sunnah. That is the intended meaning, and no other meaning may be intended.

(Tenth: Interpreting it in this sense would lead to an objectionable implication from which some of the leading scholars must be deemed free

## Page 2008

of it; still less the Companions, and still less Allah and His Messenger. ‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne’

## Page 2009

anything contrary to what is firmly established in the minds of ordinary people is a Jahmī.”

Anyone seeking greater clarity regarding this principle should examine some aspects of cosmography—namely, encompassing and sphericity. Encompassing must be discussed for this to be understood.

## Page 2010

Section

Know that they have agreed that the earth is spherical. It lies within water that surrounds most of it, since dry land constitutes slightly more than one-sixth of it. The water, too, curves around the earth on every side. The distance between the water above the earth and heaven is like the distance between us and heaven overhead. Beneath the earth’s surface lies only its interior, and the ultimate point downward is the center.

Thus, we have only two clearly defined directions: up and down. Directions vary according to a person’s position. The earth’s upper side is its surface on every side. Its lower region lies beneath its surface, and the ultimate central point is what is called the resting place of heavy bodies. Movement from the surface of the earth and water toward the center, from any direction, is descent; movement from the center toward the surface is ascent.

Since the lowest heaven is above the earth and surrounds it, the second heaven is spherical, as are the remaining heavens. The Kursī (Footstool) is above all the celestial spheres, and the Throne is above the Kursī. The celestial spheres and everything within them, compared with the Kursī, are like a ring in a vast wilderness; all of them together, compared with the Throne, are like a ring in a vast wilderness.

The celestial spheres are round, as established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. The word falak (celestial sphere) itself denotes roundness. Hence Allah’s words:

“And each floats in an orbit.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “In a circle like a spindle whorl.”

The same usage appears in the expression tafallaka thady al-jāriya, said when a young woman’s breast becomes rounded. Scholars of cosmography and mathematical calculation agree on this.

## Page 2011

As for the “Throne,” it is dome-shaped, as indicated by the report in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd from Jubayr ibn Mut‘im, who said:

“A Bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him, and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, people are exhausted and their dependants are hungry.’ He related the hadith up to the point where the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Allah is upon His Throne, and His Throne is above His heavens and His earth like this.’” He gestured with his finger to indicate the shape of a dome.

It has not been established that it is a celestial sphere that is round in every respect. Rather, it has been established that it is above the celestial spheres and that it has legs, as reported in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Sa‘īd, who said:

“A Jewish man whose face had been slapped came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Muhammad, one of your Companions slapped my face.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Summon him,’ and they summoned him.

“He asked, ‘Why did you slap his face?’

“The man replied, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I was passing through the marketplace when he was saying, “By Him who chose Moses above all mankind!” I said, “You wicked man! Even above Muhammad?” Then anger seized me, and I slapped him.’

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Do not give preference to one prophet over another. People will fall unconscious on the Day of Resurrection, and I will be the first to regain consciousness. Then I will find Moses holding one of the legs of the Throne. I do not know whether he regained consciousness before me or was recompensed for his swoon at Mount Sinai.’”

Concerning its “elevation,” the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When you ask Allah, ask Him for Firdaws, for it is the middle and highest part of Paradise. Above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise spring forth.”

These hadiths thus make clear that the Throne is the highest of all created things and the roof over them, that it is dome-shaped, and that it has

---

## Page 2012

legs. Whatever the case, it is above them, whether it encompasses the celestial spheres or otherwise. One must therefore understand that the upper and lower worlds are exceedingly small in relation to the Creator—glorified and exalted is He—as He, Most High, says:

“They have not given Allah His due,”

and the rest of the verse.

A Great Principle Affirming His Being Above Creation

This is necessarily affirmed by clear reason and sound human nature. The argument is as follows:

Allah existed, and nothing existed with Him. Then He created the world. There are only three possibilities: either He created it within Himself and it then became separate from Him—which is impossible, for Allah is exalted above contact with impurities or anything else—or He created it outside Himself and then entered it—which is also impossible, for He is exalted above indwelling His creation. No Muslim disputes the impossibility of these two alternatives. Or He created it outside His noble Self and did not indwell it. This is the truth: no other possibility is admissible, and nothing else befits Allah.

This principle was among the arguments Imam Ahmad used against the Jahmiyyah during the ordeal. In al-Maqālāt (The Doctrines), al-Ashʿarī recorded the position of Muhammad ibn Kullāb, whom he followed: reason establishes that Allah is above the world, while His rising over the Throne is known through revelation and the reports of the messengers. They were sent to perfect people’s innate nature, and there is no altering the innate nature bestowed by Allah. The revealed law affirms this, contrary to the misguided philosophers and others, who have inverted the realities. End of quotation.

then severed his aorta.”

## Page 2017

## Page 2019

## Page 2020

The reply is:

Most of the differences concerning the Quran reliably reported from the Companions—and indeed from the leading Successors—fall into several categories:

- (The first is that each expresses the meaning of a name in wording different from that used by the other. The referent is one and the same, yet each name conveys a meaning that the other does not, while both are true. This is like referring to Allah Most High by His most beautiful names, to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by his names, and to the glorious Quran by its names. Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever name you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.’”

Thus, when one says, “the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, the Sovereign, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace,” these are all names of one and the same Being, glorified and exalted is He, although each name denotes an attribute of Allah Most High that the other does not.

An example of “this interpretation” is what scholars have said in explaining “the straight path.” One says it is Islam; another says it is the Quran, meaning following the Quran; another says it is the Sunnah and the community; another says it is the path of servitude to Allah; and another says it is obedience to Allah and His Messenger. It is well known that the straight path can be described by all these attributes and called by all these names. Each scholar, however, directed his audience to an attribute by which the path could be recognized and from the knowledge of which they could benefit.

---

## Page 2021

The second category is that each of them, when explaining a “term,” mentions some of its categories or individual instances as examples for the listener, rather than as an exhaustive account. It is as though a non-Arabic speaker asked the meaning of the word “bread,” and was shown a loaf and told, “This is it.” That loaf is an example of bread, pointing to the general category, not exclusively to that particular loaf.

An example is what has been reported from them concerning the words of Allah Most High:

“Among them are those who wrong themselves, among them are those who are moderate, and among them are those who are foremost in good deeds.”

The comprehensive explanation is that “one who wrongs himself” is someone who falls short by neglecting something commanded or doing something forbidden. The “moderate” person fulfils his obligations and refrains from what is forbidden. The one “foremost in good deeds” holds the rank of one brought near to Allah, drawing closer to Him through voluntary acts after fulfilling the obligatory ones, until the True One loves him. Each commentator then mentions a particular instance of this.

Thus, if one says that “the wrongdoer” is someone who delays prayer beyond its prescribed time, the “moderate” person is someone who prays within its prescribed time, and the one “foremost” is someone who prays at the beginning of its time whenever praying early is preferable;

and another says that “one who wrongs himself” is the miser who neither maintains ties of kinship nor pays the zakat due on his wealth, the “moderate” person fulfils his obligations regarding zakat, maintaining ties of kinship, hospitality to guests, and giving assistance when calamity strikes, and the one “foremost” performs recommended deeds after fulfilling his obligations, just as

---

## Page 2022

the greatest affirmer of truth did when he brought all his wealth, while taking nothing from anyone;

and another says that “one who wrongs himself” is someone who abstains from food but not from sins, the “moderate” person abstains from both food and sins, and the one “foremost” abstains from everything that does not bring him nearer to Allah Most High—or offers similar explanations—then these statements are not mutually exclusive. Rather, each commentator has mentioned a category encompassed by the verse.

(The third category: one commentator mentions an “occasion” for the revelation of a verse, while another mentions a different “occasion” that does not contradict the first. The verse may have been revealed on account of both occasions together, or it may have been revealed twice: once for this occasion and once for the other.

As for matters in which authentic reports establish that the early generations held mutually contradictory views, these are few compared with the matters on which they did not differ. Similarly, their disagreements over certain matters of the Sunnah—such as some questions concerning prayer, zakat, fasting, Hajj, inheritance shares, divorce, and the like—do not preclude these practices from having their foundation in the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or their broad outlines from having been conveyed from him through mass transmission.

It has become clear that Allah Most High sent down to him the Book and wisdom, and commanded the wives of His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to remember what is recited in their homes “of Allah’s revelations and wisdom.”

## Page 2023

And more than one of the early generations said that “wisdom” is the Sunnah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, I have been given the Book and something like it along with it.”

We must therefore follow whatever is established from his Sunnah, whether it is said to be in the Quran, though we have not understood it, or is said not to be in the Quran. Likewise, we must follow the earliest forerunners and those who followed them in righteousness in whatever they agreed upon, whether it is said to have been explicitly stated in the Sunnah, though no report of it has reached us, or to be something they inferred and derived from the Book and the Sunnah through their scholarly reasoning.

## Page 2024

Section

Now that this is clear, the obligation to affirm that Allah Most High is on high, and related matters, becomes evident in several ways.

First: the Quran, the widely transmitted reports of the Sunnah—whether mass-transmitted or otherwise—and the statements of the earliest forerunners, the Successors, and the rest of the first three generations are replete with affirmations that Allah Most High is above His Throne. They convey this through various kinds of evidence, descriptions, and expressions. Sometimes He states that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He mentions rising over the Throne in seven places.

Sometimes He speaks of things ascending, rising, and being raised to Him, as in His words:

“Rather, Allah raised him to Himself.”

“I will take you and raise you to Myself.”

“The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him.”

And His words:

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it.”

Sometimes He speaks of their coming down from Him or from His presence, as in His words:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.”

“Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.”

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

---

## Page 2025

And sometimes He declares that He is “the Most High, the Highest,” as in His words, Most High:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Highest.”

And His words:

“And He is the Most High, the Most Great.”

Sometimes He states that He is “in heaven,” as in His words, Most High:

“Do you feel secure that He who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you, and then it would sway?”

“Or do you feel secure that He who is in heaven will not send against you a storm of stones?”

He thus mentions heaven, not the earth, without qualifying this by reference to His divinity or anything else, as He does in His words, Most High:

“It is He who is God in heaven and God on earth.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And He is Allah in the heavens and on earth.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Will you not trust me, when I am the trusted one of Him who is in heaven?”

He also said to the slave woman, “Where is Allah?” She replied, “In heaven.” He said, “Free her, for she is a believer.”

Sometimes He describes some of His creation, but not others, as being “in His presence,” as in His words, Most High:

“To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth.”

He also describes those in His presence as obedient, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who are in the presence of your Lord are not too proud to worship Him; they glorify Him and prostrate to Him.”

If being in His presence meant something general, such as being subject to His power and will, or the like, then every created being would be in His presence. No one would be too proud to worship Him; rather, everyone would glorify Him and prostrate to Him. Yet He, Most High, has said:

“Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled.”

And He

---

## Page 2026

—glory be to Him—described the angels in these terms as a rebuttal to the disbelievers who are too proud to worship Him. Examples of this in the Quran cannot be counted without considerable effort. As for the hadiths and reports from the “Companions and Successors,” none but Allah Most High can count them.

There are only two possibilities: either what these texts jointly affirm—that Allah Himself is above His creation—is the truth, or its opposite is the truth, for the truth cannot lie outside two contradictory alternatives. Either He Himself is above creation, or He is not above creation—as the Jahmiyyah say.

Sometimes they say, “He is neither above them nor within them, neither inside the world nor outside it, neither separate from it nor co-located with it.” At other times they say, “He is in every place in His very essence.” Both positions reject the affirmation that He Himself is above His creation.

Thus, the truth must lie either in affirming this or in denying it. If denying it is the truth, then it is well known that the Quran has never conveyed this denial—neither explicitly nor through its apparent meaning. Nor has the Messenger, nor any of the Companions, the Successors, or the leading scholars of the Muslims, whether the imams of the four schools or anyone else. No one can transmit from any one of them a denial of this or a statement to that effect.

As for the affirmations transmitted from them, they are too numerous to count or enumerate.

---

## Page 2027

If, then, the truth lies in denial rather than affirmation, while the Book, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus indicate only affirmation and make no mention whatsoever of denial, it necessarily follows that the Messenger and the believers did not speak the truth on this matter. Rather, they spoke words indicating—either explicitly or through their apparent meaning—misguidance and error, contrary to guidance and truth. It is well known that whoever believes this about “the Messenger and the believers” has the fullest share in the warning contained in the words of the Most High:

“Whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will leave him to what he has chosen and cast him into Hell. What an evil destination!”

For if someone says, “These texts were intended to mean something contrary to what is understood from them, or contrary to what they indicate; or they were not intended to affirm that Allah Himself is above His creation, but only His exalted status and the like”—as we have discussed at length elsewhere—the reply to him is:

He should, then, have explained to people the truth in which they must believe (inwardly and outwardly); indeed, he should also have explained what would show them that these words were not intended to convey their understood meaning and implications. For the most that can be supposed is that he spoke figuratively rather than literally, intending an inner meaning contrary to the apparent meaning.

All rational people agree that when someone addressing others to make something clear uses figurative language, he must accompany his words with an indication that the figurative meaning is intended. Thus, if the Messenger—who conveyed and explained the message, making clear to people what had been sent down to them—knew that the intended meaning of these words was contrary to their understood meaning and implications, then it was

---

## Page 2028

incumbent upon him to accompany his address with something that would turn their minds away from the meaning he did not intend—especially if that meaning was false and impermissible to believe concerning Allah. For he was obliged to forbid them from holding impermissible beliefs concerning Allah whenever there was reason to fear that they might do so, even if he had not addressed them in terms indicating such beliefs. What, then, if his very words led them to the belief that the deniers declare false?

Thus, if nothing in the Book, the Sunnah, or the statements of any of the early generations and the imams agrees at all with the deniers’ position, and they instead consistently speak only in terms of affirmation, then it is impossible that they intended anything other than affirmation, or that denial was what they believed and relied upon, when they never once expressed or disclosed it. Rather, they openly expressed only what contradicted and opposed it. This is a clear argument from which no one can escape. Yet the Jahmī speculative theologians have one response here, and the Jahmī philosophers another.

As for “the philosophers and the Qarmatians,” they say that the messengers addressed people with something contrary to the truth and outwardly presented the opposite of what they inwardly believed. They sometimes even say that the messengers lied for the welfare of the common people, since their welfare could only be secured by publicly teaching affirmation, even though it was false in reality.

Besides its blatant heresy and manifest unbelief, this position is internally contradictory. For they may be told: If matters were as you claim, and the messengers were like your leaders,

---

## Page 2029

then the messengers’ closest followers would have known this, and they would have made their own closest followers aware of the matter. Denial would thus have been the doctrine of the community’s elite—those most accomplished in intellect, knowledge, and understanding. Yet the opposite is true. Whoever examines the statements of “the early generations and the imams” will find that those whom the community regards as its most knowledgeable members—such as Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Salmān al-Fārisī, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Abū al-Dardāʾ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, and others like them—were the strongest of all people in affirmation.

The same holds for the foremost of the Successors: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and his peers, al-Hasan al-Basrī and his peers, ʿAlī ibn al-Husayn and his peers, and the companions of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās, who were among the most eminent Successors.

Indeed, the reports transmitted from these figures concerning affirmation include matters that many people shrink from affirming. It was in this light that Yahyā ibn ʿAmmār and his companion, Shaykh al-Islām Abū Ismāʿīl al-Ansārī, interpreted the report:

“There is knowledge that is, as it were, concealed, known only to those who possess knowledge of Allah. When they mention it, none reject it except those who are heedless concerning Allah.”

They understood this as referring to the reports concerning affirmation, for affirmation is established in what is transmitted from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the earliest believers, and those who followed them in righteousness. Denial, by contrast, is not found in their teachings, so the report cannot be understood as referring to it. The hadith scholars have collected so much material transmitted from the early generations concerning affirmation that none can enumerate

---

## Page 2030

their number except the Lord of the heavens. No one has been able to produce a single statement from them supporting denial, unless it be among the conflicting reports transmitted by those least familiar with their words.

Some of these people cling to “ambiguous statements” they have heard, some false and some true. One example is what they relate from ʿUmar, that he said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Abū Bakr would converse, and I was like an East African between them.”

This is false by the consensus of scholars versed in transmitted reports. Even supposing it were true, its meaning is unspecified. If those who affirm maintain that the two were discussing affirmation, since this accords with what has been transmitted from them, their interpretation would be more justified than the deniers’ claim that they were discussing denial.

The same applies to the hadith concerning Abū Hurayra’s bags, in which he said:

“I learned from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, two bags’ worth of knowledge. One I have spread among you; as for the other, were I to spread it, you would cut this throat.”

This hadith is authentic, but its meaning is unspecified. An explanation has, however, been transmitted: the other bag contained reports of great battles and tribulations. Even supposing it contained something concerning the divine attributes, nothing in it indicates denial. Rather, the reliably preserved hadiths of Abū Hurayra—such as those concerning “His coming on the Day of Resurrection,” “descent,” “laughter,” and similar matters—all support affirmation. Not a single statement resembling the deniers’ doctrine has been transmitted from Abū Hurayra.

As for the “Jahmī speculative theologians,” they say that reason is the indication that diverts them from what the discourse signifies, and that he therefore deemed rational evidence consonant with the deniers’ doctrine sufficient.

---

## Page 2031

They are therefore told, first: If his words bring them nothing but misguidance, while they derive guidance only from their own reason, then the Messenger would have provided them with the means of misguidance, but not the means of guidance, leaving them to rely on themselves for guidance. Their position thus entails that being left in the state of pre-Islamic ignorance would have been better for them than this message, which brought them no benefit but instead harmed them.

Second, they are told: The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained affirmation, which is more evident to reason than the deniers’ position. He mentioned, for example, Allah’s creation, power, will, knowledge, and similar matters, which are known through reason far more clearly than the Jahmīs’ negations. He said nothing that contradicts this affirmation. How, then, could he leave them to rely on reason alone for negation, which is more obscure and subtle, when his words did not indicate it, but indicated its very opposite? Whoever attributes this to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will have Allah to call him to account for what he says.

There are three possibilities: either he speaks words of guidance, speaks words of misguidance, or remains silent about both. It is well known that remaining silent about both is better than saying what leads people astray. Here, reason recognizes that he did not remain silent about affirmation; rather, he explained it, and what revelation conveyed agreed with reason. Thus, concerning what reason negates, he ought to have explicitly negated it, just as he explicitly affirmed what reason affirms. If he did not do so, remaining silent about it would have been safer for the Muslim community.

But if he spoke about it in terms indicating affirmation, while intending them to believe only in negation because their unaided reason would make it known to them, then attributing this to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is among the gravest forms of heresy and hypocrisy.

---

## Page 2032

Third, they are told: Who has conceded to you that reason agrees with the position of the deniers? Rather, sound reason agrees only with what the Messenger affirmed. There is no contradiction whatsoever between sound reason and authentic revelation. We have discussed this at length elsewhere, explaining that the supposedly rational arguments they advance against what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought are nothing but ignorance and misguidance, which their later followers blindly inherited from their predecessors. They called these rational insights, whereas they are merely products of ignorance. When any of them is asked to substantiate the claims of the leaders of misguidance through reason, he falls back on nothing but blind adherence to them. Thus, they disbelieve in revelation and contradict reason out of blind adherence to those whom they imagine to be versed in rational matters.

Their relationship with their misguided leaders is like that of Pharaoh’s people with him. Allah Most High says:

“He made fools of his people, and they obeyed him.”

And He, Most High, says of him:

“He and his troops behaved arrogantly in the land without right, thinking that they would not be returned to Us.”

“So We seized him and his troops and cast them into the sea. See, then, what was the end of the wrongdoers!”

“We made them leaders inviting to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.”

“We caused a curse to pursue them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.”

Pharaoh is the leader of the deniers. Hence, the leading exponents of negation have explicitly acknowledged that they hold his position, as the advocates of union among the Jahmī deniers openly declare. For he denied that Allah is above, accused Moses of lying about this, and denied that Allah spoke to Moses. Allah Most High says:

“Pharaoh said, ‘O Hāmān, build me a lofty tower so that I may reach the pathways—the pathways of the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses, though I certainly think he is a liar.’”

---

## Page 2033

And Allah Most High has related that Pharaoh denied “the Maker” with his tongue, saying:

“What is the Lord of all worlds?”

He sought to ascend so that he might look upon the God of Moses. Had Moses not told him that his God was above, he would not have sought to do so, for Pharaoh himself did not acknowledge Him. Had Moses not told him this, neither Pharaoh nor Moses would have affirmed that Allah is above. Pharaoh would therefore have had no reason to seek to look upon Him, nor would this have served his intended deception of his people by claiming that he had ascended to the God of Moses. Ascending to Him would have been no different from descending into wells and rivers, which would have been easier for him, without his having to undertake the construction of the lofty tower.

“When our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was taken up on the night of the Night Journey, he found Adam, peace be upon him, in the first heaven; John and Jesus in the second; Joseph in the third; Idrīs in the fourth; and Aaron in the fifth. Then he found Moses and Abraham. He then ascended to his Lord, who enjoined fifty prayers upon him. He then returned to Moses, who said to him, ‘Return to your Lord and ask Him to lighten the burden for your community, for your community cannot bear that.’ He said, ‘So I returned to my Lord and asked Him to lighten the burden for my community.’ He related that he went back to Moses and then returned to his Lord several times.”

Thus Moses spoke the truth in saying that his Lord is above the heavens, whereas Pharaoh accused Moses of lying about this. The “Jahmī deniers” agree with Pharaoh’s people, the leaders of misguidance, while the “adherents of the Sunnah and affirmation” agree with the family of Abraham, the leaders of guidance. Allah Most High says:

“We granted him Isaac, and Jacob as an additional gift, and made them all righteous.”

“And We made them leaders who guided

by Our command, and We inspired them to do good deeds, establish prayer, and give zakat; and they were devoted worshippers of Us.” Moses and Muhammad belong to the family of Abraham; indeed, they are its foremost members. May Allah’s blessings be upon them all.

The second argument:

To explain why affirmation and Allah’s being above the heavens must be acknowledged, we may say: It is well known that Allah Most High has perfected the religion and completed His favour; that Allah has sent down the Book as an explanation of all things; that knowing what is rightfully affirmed of Allah and what He is exalted above is among the most momentous matters of religion and its greatest foundations; and that explaining this in detail takes precedence over everything else.

How, then, could the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, have left this subject unexplained, without setting it out in detail or teaching his community what to say concerning it? How could the religion have been perfected, and they have been left upon the clear, radiant path, while they did not know how to understand their Lord: through what the deniers say, or through the statements of those who uphold affirmation?

(The third argument)

We may say: Anyone with even the slightest love of knowledge or worship must reflect upon this subject and seek the truth concerning it, striving to distinguish error from what is right. It is therefore inconceivable that the Companions and the Successors should all have disregarded this matter, neither asking about it nor longing to understand it, with their hearts not seeking the truth, even as they turned their hearts towards Him night and day and called upon Him humbly and fearfully, with hope and dread. Hearts are naturally disposed to seek knowledge of this matter and to know the truth concerning it; they yearn for it more than they yearn for many other things. And firm resolve, coupled with ability, must bring about

what is sought; and they were able to question the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and to question one another.

They had asked him about matters less momentous than this. They asked him, “Will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?” and he answered them. Abū Razīn also asked him, “Does our Lord laugh?” He replied, “Yes.” Abū Razīn said, “We shall not lack goodness from a Lord who laughs.”

Then, when they asked him about (seeing Him), he said, “You will see your Lord as you see the sun and the moon.” Thus, he compared the act of seeing to the act of seeing, not the One seen to the objects seen. The deniers do not say that He will be seen as the sun and the moon are seen. Rather, their actual position is that He cannot be seen at all. Those among them who say that He will be seen, outwardly agreeing with those who uphold affirmation while concealing their disagreement, interpret seeing as an increase in knowledge; it would therefore not be like seeing the sun and the moon.

The point here is that they would inevitably ask him about their Lord whom they worshipped, and, if they asked him, he would necessarily answer them. It is known beyond doubt that what the Jahmī deniers say has not been transmitted by anyone who conveyed his teachings. Rather, they transmitted from him what accords with the position of those who uphold affirmation.

(The fourth argument is as follows:

Either Allah loves for us to believe the position of the deniers, or to believe the position of those who uphold affirmation, or to believe neither.

If what He requires of us is to believe the position of the deniers—namely, that He is neither within the world nor outside it, and that there is not above

## Page 2036

the heavens any Lord, nor upon the Throne any God; that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was not taken up to Allah, but only to the heavens, not to Allah; that the angels do not ascend to Allah, but to His dominion; that nothing descends from Allah and nothing ascends to Him; and other such claims. They may express this in newly introduced formulations marked by ambiguity, obscurity, and misleading implications, such as saying, “He does not occupy space, nor is He a body or a substance, nor is He in a direction or a place.” Ordinary people understand these and similar expressions as declaring the Lord Most High free of imperfections. Yet what they intend by them is that there is no Lord above the heavens, no God upon the Throne to be worshipped, and that the Messenger was not taken up to Allah.

And (the point is that if Allah loves for us to believe this negation, then the Companions and the Successors, who were better than us, would have believed it, and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have believed it too. Moreover, statements affirming what Allah loves and approves, and what brings one nearer to Him, must necessarily be evident in his teachings and those of the believers—especially given His words, mighty and majestic is He:

This is all the more so since the Jahmiyyah make this the foundation of religion. To them, it is “monotheism,” which only a wretched person would oppose. And the philosophers and the Mu'tazilah

## Page 2037

and their followers call the doctrine of those who negate the divine attributes “monotheism.” The author of al-Murshidah called his followers the monotheists, since, in their view, the doctrine of negation is “monotheism.” If that were so, it would necessarily follow that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, must explain it. Yet it is known beyond doubt that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions did not teach the doctrine of negation. Thus, it is known that this doctrine is neither obligatory nor recommended; indeed, it is known that it is not part of the “monotheism” that Allah Most High prescribed for His servants. If, on the other hand, He loves for us to follow the doctrine of affirmation—which is what we have been commanded to do—then this too must be explained to us.

It is well known that the Quran and Sunnah affirm “Allah’s being above His creation and His attributes” far more extensively than they establish ablution, dry ablution, fasting, the prohibition of marriage to women within the forbidden degrees, the prohibition of unclean foods, and other such “religious ordinances.” Thus, according to those who affirm the divine attributes, the religion is complete; the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed and explained it; and monotheism is well known and widely transmitted from the early generations. The Quran and Sunnah corroborate one another; the early generations are the best of this community, and their path is the best of paths. The Quran is entirely true: it contains nothing misleading, nor does it point to unbelief or anything impossible. Rather, it is healing, guidance, and light. All these are implications they accept and conclusions they endorse. Their position is therefore consistent, not contradictory, and acceptable, not to be rejected.

## Page 2038

But if what Allah loves from us is that we neither affirm nor deny, but remain in mere ignorance and in layers of darkness, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, or truthfulness from lies; rather, that we stand between those who affirm and those who negate, doubtful and bewildered—“Wavering between the two, belonging neither to these nor to those”—neither believing nor disbelieving, then it necessarily follows that Allah loves for us to have no knowledge of what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, no knowledge of the perfect attributes that befit Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, and no knowledge by which to distinguish truth from falsehood; and that He loves bewilderment and doubt from us.

Yet it is well known that Allah does not love ignorance, doubt, bewilderment, or misguidance. Rather, He loves religion, knowledge, and certainty. He has condemned “bewilderment” in His words, Exalted is He:

“Say: Shall we invoke besides Allah that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like someone whom the devils have lured away in the land, bewildered, while he has companions calling him to guidance, ‘Come to us’? “And to establish prayer and fear Him. It is to Him that you will be gathered.”

Allah Most High has commanded us to say:

“Guide us to the straight path,”

“The path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray.”

In Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, it is narrated from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

would say when he rose at night to pray:

Thus he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asks his Lord to guide him to the truth concerning which people have differed. How, then, could Allah love the absence of guidance in disputed matters?

Allah Most High said to him:

As for the saying some people attribute to him:

“Increase me in bewilderment concerning You,”

it is a fabrication, according to the unanimous agreement of those versed in his hadith, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, this is the request of someone who is bewildered and has asked for still greater bewilderment. No one who is bewildered may ask and pray for greater bewilderment; rather, he should ask for guidance and knowledge. How much more so in the case of the one who guides creation out of misguidance? Such words are only reported from certain shaykhs who are not to be followed in such matters—if the report from such a person is authentic.

The position of those who suspend judgment—neither affirming nor denying, and objecting to any categorical acceptance of either position—entails several consequences.

First: whoever adopts this position must object to those who negate, for they have introduced expressions and meanings with no basis in the Quran or the Sunnah. As for those who affirm, if they confine themselves to the scriptural texts, he has no right to object to them. And these

---

## Page 2040

people who suspend judgment inwardly agree with those who negate, or acquiesce in their position, while opposing only those who affirm. Thus, it is clear that they have acquiesced in the position of the people of innovation and opposed the people of the Sunnah.

Second: Not knowing the meanings of the Quran and hadith is not something Allah and His Messenger love. This position is therefore false.

Third: Muslims agree that doubt and bewilderment are not praiseworthy in themselves. At most, someone who has no knowledge warranting either negation or affirmation should remain silent. But when someone knows the truth through evidence consistent with the explanation of His Messenger, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, the doubting, bewildered person who suspends judgment has no right to object to this knowledgeable person, who possesses certainty and insight, follows the Messenger, and understands both transmitted evidence and rational arguments.

Fourth: All the early generations denounced the negating Jahmiyyah, upheld affirmation, and stated it explicitly. Their statements affirming and denouncing those who negate are too numerous to record here. The statements of renowned imams—such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, Hammād ibn Zayd, Hammād ibn Salamah, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū ‘Ubayd, and the leading scholars among the followers of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad—are extant in such abundance that no one can enumerate them.

Mālik’s answer on this matter explicitly affirms it. The questioner said to him: “O Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne’—how did He rise over it?”

Mālik replied: “Rising over

---

## Page 2041

is known, but its manner is unknown.” In another wording: “His rising over the Throne is known—or intelligible—but its manner is not comprehensible. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation.”

He thus stated, may Allah be pleased with him, that rising over the Throne itself is known, while its manner is unknown. This is precisely the position of those who affirm. As for “those who negate,” they affirm no rising over the Throne whose manner could be unknown. Rather, this doubting speaker and others like him hold that rising over the Throne is unknown, not known. If rising over the Throne were unknown, there would be no need to say that its manner is unknown—especially if rising over the Throne were denied altogether, since what is denied and nonexistent has no manner that could be described as known or unknown. Mālik’s words explicitly affirm rising over the Throne, that it is known, and that it has a manner. That manner, however, is unknown to us; we do not know it.

For this reason, he declared the questioner who asked him about this manner an innovator. For a question can only concern something known to us, whereas we do not know the manner of His rising over the Throne. Not everything that is known and has a manner necessarily has a manner known to us.

This is further clarified by the fact that Mālikī scholars and others transmitted that Mālik said: “Allah is in heaven, and His knowledge is everywhere.” Indeed, Makkī, the preacher of Cordoba, included this in the Book of Quranic Commentary that he compiled from Mālik’s statements. It was also transmitted by Abū ‘Amr al-Talamankī, Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, Ibn Abī Zayd in The Abridgment, and several others. Countless others besides these also transmitted it from Mālik, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, his son ‘Abd Allāh, al-Athram, al-Khallāl, al-Ājurrī, Ibn Battah, and groups

---

of other writers on the Sunnah. Had Mālik been among those who withhold judgment or those who negate, this affirmation would not have been transmitted from him.

## Page 2056

Nu'aym ibn Hammād al-Khuzā'ī said:

“Whoever likens Allah to His creation has disbelieved, and whoever denies what Allah has described Himself with has disbelieved. What Allah and His Messenger have described Him with does not constitute likening Him to creation.”

The way of the early generations stands between two doctrines, offering guidance between two errors: affirming the attributes while denying any likeness to created beings. Thus, His saying, Most High:

“There is nothing like Him,”

refutes those who liken Allah to creation and assert resemblance between them. His saying:

“And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing,”

refutes those who deny and negate His attributes. The one who likens Him to creation is dim-sighted, while the one who negates His attributes is blind: the former worships an idol, and the latter worships nothingness.

All those who affirm the attributes agree that Allah truly lives, truly knows, truly has power, truly hears, truly sees, truly wills, and truly speaks. Even the Mu'tazilīs, who deny the attributes, say that Allah truly speaks, just as they say—along with all other Muslims—that Allah truly knows and truly has power. Indeed, some of them, such as Abū al-'Abbās al-Nāshi', held that these names apply literally to Allah and figuratively to creation.

The majority of the Mu'tazilīs, however, together with the scholastic theologians who affirm the attributes—the Ash'arī-Kullābīs, Karrāmīs, Sālimīs, the followers of the four imams among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, Shāfi'īs, and Hanbalīs, the people of hadith, and the Sufis—say that these names apply literally to the Creator, glorified and exalted be He, even though they also apply literally to His creation. They also say that He possesses real knowledge, real power, real hearing, and real sight.

Allah Most High of His most beautiful names and attributes. Rather, this amounts to denying the Creator and likening Him to nonexistent things. Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr said:

“Ahl al-Sunnah unanimously affirm all the attributes mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah, believe in them, and understand them literally rather than figuratively. However, they do not specify how any of these attributes are, nor do they define them in circumscribed terms. What Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr reports here concerning the Mu‘tazilah and others like them applies to some of the attributes they deny. As for the names and attributes they affirm, such as the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, and the One who speaks, they say that these apply literally.

Whoever denies that any of these names and attributes applies literally does so only because he does not understand what “literal” means, or because of his disbelief and denial of what rightfully belongs to the Lord of all worlds. He may suppose that applying these terms entails that the created being resembles the Creator. He should therefore be told: This is false. Allah truly exists, and the servant truly exists, yet the two are not alike. Allah Most High has a real essence, and the servant has a real essence, yet His essence is not like the essences of created beings. Likewise, He truly has knowledge, hearing, and sight, and the servant truly has knowledge, hearing, and sight; yet it is not the case that

---

## Page 2059

his knowledge, hearing, and sight are like Allah’s knowledge, hearing, and sight. Allah truly speaks, and the servant truly speaks; yet the Creator’s speech is not like the speech of created beings. Allah Most High truly rose over His Throne, and the servant truly settles aboard a ship; yet the Creator’s rising is not like the settling of created beings. For Allah depends on nothing and needs nothing; rather, He is entirely free of need for anything. Allah Most High sustains the Throne and its bearers by His power, and He holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease to be.

Whoever supposes that the imams’ statement, “Allah is truly established over His Throne,” entails that His being established is like the servant’s settling upon ships and livestock must likewise hold that their statement, “Allah truly has knowledge, hearing, sight, and speech,” entails that His knowledge, hearing, sight, and speech are like those of created beings.
