Likewise, it suffices to refute a sophist by saying: “What you deny consists of self-evident propositions; their denial cannot therefore be accepted on the strength of the specious inferential arguments you present.”

The second, detailed response is to demonstrate the unsoundness of the arguments offered by those who deny the attributes to establish the possibility of what they claim.

Those who affirm the attributes say:

The arguments you have presented to establish the existence of a being neither within the world nor outside it are the arguments of a sophist. As for the humanity shared by human beings and other such “universals,” these cannot be said to exist outside the mind while being neither within the world nor outside it. They are things established in the mind and in conception. If they are said to exist in external reality, they must be either an entity subsisting in its own right or an attribute subsisting in an entity. Undoubtedly, they do not exist in external reality as unrestricted universals, subject to the unrestrictedness with which they are conceived. Rather, they exist in external reality only as particular, individual instances.

---

## Page 2153

As for the assertion, “Examination extracts the intelligible from the sensible”: if this means something intelligible that exists in the mind, then what exists in the mind is not the very thing that exists in external reality. If, however, it means that a sensible object existing in external reality contains something intelligible that is not in the mind, this is false. A particular human being contains only what is particular: this individual’s body, soul, and attributes. All of this is particular, determinate, and individual—not universal or unrestricted.

What he mentions in conjunction with affirming mutually separate beings—intellects and souls—that are neither within the world nor outside it constitutes no proof. Rather, this very argument, along with others, refutes them just as it refutes their counterparts. Indeed, their position is more manifestly unsound and less defensible than the positions of those who deny the attributes and Allah’s being above creation. How, then, can a position be supported by something weaker and further removed from the truth? It is well known that rational people generally, whether adherents of religious traditions or otherwise, reject this claim of theirs.

As for his assertion that, in maintaining this, they were not advancing a position whose falsity is self-evident, that is not the case. Rather, those who affirm the attributes and maintain that two existing beings must either be separate from one another or co-located say that these people’s claims to the contrary are self-evidently false. Indeed, even the leading speculative theologians who deny that Allah is above creation claim to know self-evidently that a contingent being is either a body or something subsisting in a body. As for the entities posited by these would-be philosophers

---

## Page 2154

that are contingent, neither bodies nor accidents subsisting in bodies—such as intellect, soul, prime matter, and form, which they claim are intelligible substances existing outside the mind, neither bodies nor accidents of bodies—the leading “speculative thinkers” maintain that the falsity of this is self-evident. This has been stated by Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī and other leading figures in speculative reasoning and theology.

Those who failed to recognize this, such as al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others like them, disputed weakly with the philosophers. They did not establish the unsoundness of their fundamental principles as did the leading speculative thinkers who were greater than they. These men yielded to the philosophers, disputing weakly and failing to expose the unsoundness of their fundamental principles, accepting false premises by which the philosophers led them away from certain truths. This contrasts with leading speculative thinkers such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Haysam al-Karrāmī, and Abū al-Wafā’ ‘Alī ibn ‘Aqīl.

Before these were figures such as Abū ‘Alī al-Jubbā’ī, his son Abū Hāshim, Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, and al-Hasan ibn Yahyā al-Nawbakhtī.

Before these were figures such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn Karrām, Ibn Kullāb, Ja‘far ibn Mubashshir, Ja‘far ibn Harb, Abū Ishāq al-Nazzām, Abū al-Hudhayl al-‘Allāf, ‘Amr ibn Bahr al-Jāhiz, Hishām al-Jawālīqī, Hishām ibn al-Hakam, Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Najjār, Dirār ibn ‘Amr al-Kūfī, and Abū ‘Īsā Muhammad ibn ‘Īsā

---

## Page 2155

Burghūth, and Hafs al-Fard, along with other leading figures in speculative reasoning and theology whose number Allah alone knows. These men debated the philosophers more effectively than the former group did. They and others do not concede to the philosophers the possibility of a contingent being that is neither a body nor something subsisting in a body. Indeed, their leading authorities have explicitly declared the invalidity of this “third category” to be self-evident.

Indeed, Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb, the leading authority of those who affirm the divine attributes—such as Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mujāhid, and others—demonstrated that existing things must be either separate from or co-located with another, and that the claim that something exists which is neither separate from nor co-located with another is self-evidently false. His demonstration was comparable to, and even more forceful than, those thinkers’ demonstration that contingent beings are confined to bodies and their accidents.

Some groups of speculative thinkers have maintained that nothing exists except a body or something subsisting in a body—when “body” is understood in its technical rather than its linguistic sense. This is firmly rooted in the innate understanding of ordinary people. It is also the position of many philosophers, or most of them.

Likewise, the great imams, such as Imam Ahmad in his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Makkī in his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, and others, explained that the claim made by those who negate the attributes—that there is a third category, neither separate from nor co-located with another—is manifestly false according to sound reason. This is among the evident propositions that rational people recognize through their own reason.

Affirming or denying the term “body” is an innovation; none of the early generations or the imams spoke in such terms, just as they did not affirm

---

## Page 2156

the term “spatial occupancy,” nor deny it, nor affirm or deny the term “direction.” Rather, they affirmed the attributes conveyed by the Book and the Sunnah and denied any likeness to created beings. Whoever examines people’s statements on this subject will find that most of those renowned for reason and knowledge explicitly state that affirming the existence of a being neither co-located with nor separate from another, and similar claims, is known by clear reason, with necessary certainty, to be [unsound or false] (*).

As for the third argument, he says:

“Reason divides what is known into that which is separate, that which is co-located, and that which is neither separate nor co-located,” and similarly with other divisions.

The reply is:

The familiar division into the necessary, the contingent, and that which is neither necessary nor contingent; into the eternal, the originated, and that which is neither eternal nor originated; into that which subsists in itself, that which subsists in another, and that which subsists neither in itself nor in another—and similar divisions—are mental suppositions. It is well known that such suppositions do not establish that these things are possible in external reality. Not every category or supposition posited by the mind is possible or actually exists outside it. Rather, the mind divides whatever occurs to it into the necessary, the impossible, and the contingent, and into the existent and the nonexistent. The mind thus entertains whatever occurs to it, and it is well known that this includes impossibilities that cannot exist outside the mind.

As for his statement:

“The division into the separate and the co-located is not known to be false, just as the proposition that one is half of two is not known to be false.”

We say:

It is not a requirement of self-evident propositions that

> **Footnotes:**
> (*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 47):
> The text between square brackets was omitted, reversing the meaning.

---

## Page 2157

their constituent concepts be clear to everyone; rather, the requirement is that, once those concepts are grasped, reason should assent to the propositions with certainty. The conception of one as half of two is clear to everyone; hence the assent that follows it is more evident than in other cases. This is also why its clarity to the mind differs from that of the proposition that fifty-five and a quarter and an eighth is half of one hundred and ten and a half and a quarter, although both are self-evident. There are many comparable examples.

The meaning of “separate” and “co-located” is not immediately clear, since these terms are ambiguous, as explained earlier. Yet once their meaning is explained to rational people, they affirm with certainty that there is no “third category.” Likewise, since the meanings of the eternal and the originated, the necessary and the contingent, substance and accident, and similar terms are not clear in themselves to rational people generally, they do not affirm with certainty that whatever exists must fall within one of the two categories. Once the meaning is explained to them, however, they affirm this with certainty.

Thus, if rational people are told, “There are two self-subsisting beings, one of which is neither outside and separate from the other, nor inside it; neither distant, nor near it, nor far from it; neither above it nor below it; neither to its right nor to its left; neither in front of it nor behind it. Nor can one conceive of either pointing to the other, going to it, drawing near to it, becoming distant from it, moving towards it or away from it, turning towards it or turning away from it, veiling itself from it or revealing itself to it, appearing before its eyes or concealing itself from it”—or are presented with similar notions asserted by those who advocate negation—they know with necessary certainty that the existence of two such beings is impossible.

---

## Page 2158

As for the objector’s statement:

“This can only be conceived in the case of a body occupying space. If something is posited that is neither a body nor occupies space, it falls outside these two categories, and the division into them is no longer exhaustive.”

The response is as follows:

First, the terms “body,” “space,” and “direction” are ambiguous and imprecise. They are conventional technical terms that may convey various meanings. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah affirms or denies these terms, nor has any affirmation or denial of them whatsoever been transmitted from the early generations of this community or its imams. An objection framed in these terms is therefore not an objection based on scriptural evidence—whether from the Quran, the Sunnah, or consensus. Indeed, it is not even based on a report from a Companion, a Successor, or any imam of the Muslims. Rather, the leading imams denounced those who spoke in such terms and counted them among the practitioners of false, innovated speculative theology. They made stern statements about them, well known from the imams, such as the statement of al-Shāfi‘ī, may Allah have mercy on him:

“My judgment concerning the practitioners of speculative theology is that they should be beaten with palm branches and sandals and paraded among the tribes and clans, while it is proclaimed: ‘This is the recompense of whoever abandons the Quran and the Sunnah and turns to speculative theology.’”

In short, it is well known that terms are of two kinds. The first is a term found in the Quran, the Sunnah, or consensus. What such a term entails must be affirmed, whether or not we understand its meaning, because the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, speaks nothing but the truth, and the Muslim community does not unanimously agree upon misguidance.

---

## Page 2159

The second kind is a term for which no scriptural evidence has been given, such as these terms disputed by the practitioners of speculative theology and philosophy. One says, “He occupies space,” while another says, “He does not occupy space.” One says, “He is in a direction,” while another says, “He is not in a direction.” One says, “He is a body or a substance,” while another says, “He is neither a body nor a substance.”

No one is obliged to affirm or deny anything using these terms until the person using them is asked to clarify his meaning. If he makes clear that he is affirming something true, one affirms it; if he affirms something false, one rejects it. If he denies something false, one denies it; if he denies something true, one does not deny it. Many of these people combine truth and falsehood in these terms, both in affirmation and in negation.

If someone says that He is in a direction, meaning that He is contained and confined within some created thing—whatever it may be—this affirmation is not accepted. This is the position of those who uphold divine indwelling. But if he says that He is separate from created things and above them, this affirmation is not disputed. Indeed, it is the opposite of the position of those who uphold divine indwelling.

If someone says that He is not in a direction, meaning that He is neither separate from the world nor above it, this negation is not accepted.

Likewise, the term “occupying space” may mean that something existent surrounds the thing described, as in the words of the Most High:

“Or joining another group.”

It may also mean that something has withdrawn from and become separate from something else. Thus, if someone says that Allah occupies space

---

## Page 2160

in the first sense, his claim is not accepted. But if he means that Allah is separate from created things, the meaning is accepted, even if the expression itself is not used.

Once this is clear, if someone says, “This division is self-evidently known,” and is told, “This is only conceivable of something that occupies space or has a direction,” this does not undermine what is self-evidently known. Rather, he replies: “Either this is a necessary consequence or it is not. If it is not, the objection falls away. If it is, then a necessary consequence of a self-evident truth is itself true.” For when self-evident propositions entail certain consequences, this establishes the truth of those consequences. One cannot argue that those propositions are false by denying their consequences, because that denial rests on inference, and inferential reasoning cannot undermine self-evident knowledge.

As for his statement, “If an existent is posited that neither occupies space nor is in a direction, this division is valid in its case,” the reply is: its validity on this assumption does not entail its validity in reality unless the assumption itself holds true in reality. Yet this division rules out that assumption’s holding true in reality. If the division is self-evidently known, it necessarily follows that this assumption is false. An attempt to establish this assumption through inferential reasoning is therefore unacceptable, because it entails undermining self-evident knowledge through inference. If there is no way to establish this assumption, the division is not undermined by its being invalid on the supposition that the assumption holds true. For this amounts to the division being invalid on the supposition that something holds true which has not been established and cannot be established.

---

## Page 2161

And even if it were assumed that this supposition could be established, this would constitute a counterargument, not a challenge to any of the premises. A counterargument requires a proof of its own, and we shall discuss that later.

If the objector were to say, “I challenge the validity of the division and make this the basis of my challenge,” this would not be valid. The reply is that a challenge must concern a premise for which no proof has been offered. Yet the proponent has shown that the division is self-evidently valid, so it cannot validly be challenged. If, however, the objector establishes the possibility of an existent that is neither within the world nor outside it, he is presenting an argument for the opposite of his opponent’s position. He would then be usurping the proponent’s role, for such usurpation consists in challenging a premise by establishing the opposite of the conclusion to be proved.

In effect, he is saying: “If the proponent’s proof were sound, my position would be invalid. But my position is not invalid, for such-and-such reasons.” This is usurping the proponent’s role and is therefore not accepted.

The same applies here: if he challenges the division by establishing this supposition, that supposition is itself his position. For he claims that there is an existent to which this division does not apply, and this is precisely the point at issue. If he argues for its possibility, he is usurping the proponent’s role, and this is not accepted from him. Thus, it is clear that the proof is complete.

This objection therefore amounts to saying: “If an existent is posited that is neither eternal nor originated, then the division of existents into originated and eternal is invalid. And if an existent is posited that is neither necessary nor contingent, neither subsisting in itself nor subsisting in another, then the division of existents into the necessary, the contingent, that which subsists in itself, and that which subsists in another is invalid.” And it is well known that a division which is known

---

## Page 2162

by necessity is not invalidated by supposing its negation or something that entails its negation. Rather, a division is invalidated only by establishing something that contradicts it. If that alleged contradiction can be known only through reasoning, it cannot validly contradict it. It is thus clear that this amounts to opposing necessary knowledge with inferential knowledge, and is therefore neither acceptable nor true.

At this point, people offer four responses:

One is the position of those who say: “This division is rationally intelligible without qualification. As for this supposition, I do not discuss whether it is established or refuted, because that would mean challenging necessary truths through inferential arguments. This is unacceptable and is comparable to the arguments of the sophists. When we know something by necessity and someone challenges it through reasoning and disputation, we are not obliged to give a detailed response resolving the counterargument. It is enough for us to know that it is unsound because it contradicts necessary knowledge, and whatever contradicts necessary knowledge is unsound.” This is how many hadith scholars, jurists, speculative theologians, and others respond to such objections.

Someone taking this position says:

“I do not say that He occupies space or that He does not, nor that He is in a direction or that He is not. Rather, I know that He is separate from the world, and that it is impossible for Him to be neither separate from it nor within it.”

This is like the statement of the Qarmatian esotericist:

“I do not say that He is existent or nonexistent, knowing or ignorant, capable or incapable, because these are attributes of bodies. Bodies are divided into the living and the dead, the knowing and the ignorant, the capable and the incapable, and the existent and the nonexistent. Thus, if

---

## Page 2163

we posit something that is not a body, it would be neither knowing nor ignorant, neither capable nor incapable, and neither living nor dead.” This statement of the Qarmatian is equivalent to the statement of these Jahmiyyah that He is neither within the world nor outside it. The positions of Jahm and the Qarmatians are of the same kind, as the writers on sectarian doctrines have reported concerning both groups: neither “He is a thing” nor “He is not a thing” should be said. Whoever denies of Him these opposites, one of each pair of which must apply to anything that exists, [cannot] conclusively refute the Qarmatians. This is why their arguments against the Qarmatians were weak, as explained at length elsewhere.

The second response is that of someone who says:

“Rather, I say that He does not occupy space and is not in a direction, while also saying that He is separate from the world.”

This is the position of those who say that He is above the world but is neither a body nor a substance, nor does He occupy space. This is maintained by some among the Kullābiyyah, Ashʿariyyah, and Karrāmiyyah, and by those who agree with them among the jurists following the four imams, the scholars of hadith, and the Sufis.

If they are told, “To affirm something separate that does not occupy space contradicts necessary reason,” they reply:

“To affirm an existent that is neither within the world nor separate from it is even more obviously untenable according to necessary reason. If reason’s judgment is accepted, your position is unsound, and the point at issue—that He is separate from the world—is thereby established. If reason’s judgment is rejected, your argument against our position—that He is above the world, separate from it, and neither a body nor a substance—falls apart. And if there is no argument establishing the falsity of

---

## Page 2164

His being above the world, this cannot legitimately be denied. Moreover, the revealed texts, together with the innate disposition, indicate this. On this premise, therefore, He must be separate from the world.”

This is a “sound analysis,” to which attention has also been drawn earlier. These negationists treat reason as authoritative when it supports them, but not when it counts against them. They argue against their opponents on the basis of self-evident propositions, yet oppose them concerning propositions that are even more self-evident. Every objection they raise can be turned against their own position. For example, they say, “This is a judgment of imagination and fancy, not of reason.” This very objection can be raised against their argument here. They may be told:

“Your denial of the existence of a being separate from the world, who is neither a body nor occupies space, is a judgment of imagination and fancy, not of reason.”

Let the discerning reader reflect carefully on this point.

(The third response:

The position of someone who accepts that He occupies space, is in a direction, or is a body, and says: “There is no evidence for denying any of these things, and the arguments advanced by those who deny them are unsound.” They agree that the denial of these things is not known self-evidently; rather, they claim to establish it through discursive reasoning. Yet those who deny these things have not agreed upon a single proof. Instead, each challenges the proof of the other.

As for the philosophers who deny these things on the basis of denying the attributes, the negationists among the speculative theologians—together with other rational thinkers and proponents of affirmation—challenge their proofs with the well-known objections that demonstrate their unsoundness. The speculative theologians who deny these things, together with other rational thinkers and proponents of affirmation, also challenge the proofs of the negationist philosophers: namely, the argument based on the temporal origination of whatever has accidents and acts subsisting in it.

---

## Page 2165

The arguments of the proponents of affirmation establishing the unsoundness of the negationists’ proofs, together with the ambiguous statements, subtle discussions, and rational inquiries involved in these matters, are discussed at length elsewhere.

(The fourth response:

The response of those who seek clarification. They say: The terms “occupying space,” “direction,” “substance,” and the like are ambiguous expressions with no basis in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger. Nor did any of the early generations of the Muslim community or its imams use them concerning Allah Most High, whether in denial or affirmation. Thus, unqualified denial or affirmation of these terms is undoubtedly not the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, nor is there any evidence from revelation supporting it. Rather, unqualified statements on either side are innovations introduced by the speculative theologians who delve into these matters. When we engage them in rational inquiry, we therefore ask them to clarify what they mean by these terms.

If someone who affirms them says, “By His occupying space, being a body, and being in a direction, I mean that He is inside created things, that created things contain Him, that He resembles them, that what is possible for them is possible for Him, or something similar,” then this is false. His being separate from the world does not entail His occupying space, being in a direction, or being a body in this sense.

If, on the other hand, someone who denies these things says: “Whatever is above the world is in a direction, occupies space, and is a body, and that is impossible.”

---

## Page 2166

he is told:

Denying that He is separate from the world is false, and whatever entails a falsehood is itself false. Thus, if denying the meanings designated by these expressions entails denying His separateness, then denying those meanings is false. The aforementioned arguments for denying their meanings, understood in this sense, are therefore invalid.

The proponent of affirmation says: Denying His separateness from the world and His being above His creation is false. Indeed, these denials entail rejecting as false what the Messenger affirmed concerning his Lord and reported about Him, which is also disbelief. Yet not everyone who utters disbelief becomes a disbeliever: the proof establishing his disbelief must first be established against him. Once that proof has been established against him, he then becomes a disbeliever. Indeed, denying these matters entails declaring the Messenger a disbeliever on account of what he affirmed concerning his Lord and reported about Him. In reality, it even amounts to denying the Maker and negating Him.

Although denying these things entails disbelief in this respect, many groups among the believers have denied them. An implication of a position is not itself the position of its adherent unless he accepts that implication. Many people deny or affirm certain expressions—indeed, they deny or affirm certain meanings—and this entails things that constitute disbelief, without their knowing that these implications follow. Rather, they contradict themselves. How frequently people contradict themselves, especially in this matter! Contradiction is not disbelief.

The versifier says:

I was told that whoever says this is both misled and misleading. This is true, for he has misled others through his statement and has himself been misled by others. Not everyone who misleads others is a disbeliever. I also maintained that the statement of anyone who says this entails negation; thus, disbelief lies latent

---

## Page 2167

in his statement. What lies latent in something need not be manifest in it. Were disbelief manifest in his statement, its speaker would necessarily have to be declared a disbeliever. But when it is latent and hidden, someone who does not understand the true nature of the disbelief it contains does not thereby become a disbeliever, even though the statement contains and entails disbelief.

As for the term “corporealism,” it is an ambiguous expression with no basis in revelation. Affirming or denying it therefore requires clarification and evidence, as explained previously.

If someone who affirms it says, “What is meant is that He is above the world and separate from it,” he is told, “This meaning is correct.” If someone who denies it says, “What is meant is that created things neither encompass Him nor resemble Him,” he is told, “This meaning is correct.” There is no contradiction between your two statements: He is above the world and separate from it, while created things neither confine nor encompass Him. He has no need of the Throne or anything else, although He is above created things and separate from them. He does not resemble them, nor can what is possible for them be possible for Him. These meanings expressed by those who deny and those who affirm are correct and acceptable; those other meanings expressed by them are rejected. Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

Furthermore, the answer given by those who affirm to the eternalists—namely, that acts which He wills and has the power to perform subsist in Him, glorified be He, and that through these He creates things separate from Himself—accords with the accounts transmitted from the Messengers, may Allah’s blessings be upon them. Allah has stated that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. And before His rising

---

## Page 2168

over the Throne:

“He turned toward the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly.’ They said, ‘We come willingly.’”

This and similar passages concern the beginning of creation. As for its re-creation, He, exalted is He, says:

“They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves. On the Day of Resurrection, the whole earth will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand. Glorified and exalted is He above what they associate with Him!”

It is authentically reported in the Sahīh collection from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will grasp the earth and roll up the heaven in His right hand. Then He will say, ‘I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Umar reports:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited this verse on the pulpit, then said, ‘Allah will roll up the heavens in His right hand and grasp the earth in His other hand. Then He will say: “I am the King; I am the Most Holy; I am the Source of Peace; I am the Giver of Security; I am the Guardian; I am the Almighty; I am the Compeller; I am the Supreme. I am the One who brought the world into being when it was nothing; I am the One who will restore it.”’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, began closing and opening his hands. The pulpit was shaking beneath him so much that I found myself saying, ‘Will it collapse beneath the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’”

Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The seven heavens, the seven earths, and everything within them are, in the Hand of the Most Merciful, no more than a mustard seed in the palm of one of you.”

It is also related that he said:

“He tosses them as a child tosses a ball.”

This shows that the celestial spheres are as nothing compared with the power of Allah, exalted is He, even as He, glorified and exalted is He, rolls up the heaven and grasps the earth.

---

## Page 2169

The two Sahīh collections also relate from Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“A Jewish man said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will hold the heaven on one finger, the earth on one finger, the trees and soil on one finger, the mountains on one finger, and all creatures on one finger.’

“He said: The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, laughed in amazement and in affirmation of the rabbi’s statement. Then he recited the verse beginning, ‘They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves.’”

Here is clear evidence from the acts of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, that refutes the specious arguments of the philosophizers.

‘Possessor of the ways of ascent.’

‘The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him.’

And He, exalted is He, said:

‘He is the Subduer, above His servants.’

And He, exalted is He, said:

‘He is the Most High, the Magnificent.’

He said: This, then, is Allah’s declaration that He is in heaven. We find that everything in a lower position is spoken of with disapproval. He, exalted be His praise, says:

‘Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire.’

And He, exalted is He, said:

‘Those who disbelieve will say, “Our Lord, show us the two who led us astray from among the jinn and mankind, so that we may put them beneath our feet and make them among the lowest.”’

We said to them: Do you not know that Iblīs has his place and the devils have theirs? Allah would never be together with Iblīs in one and the same place. Rather, the meaning of His words, mighty and majestic is He:

‘And He is Allah in the heavens and on earth’

is that He is the God of those in the heavens and the God of those on earth. He is Allah, above the Throne, and His knowledge encompasses everything beneath the Throne. No place is devoid of Allah’s knowledge, nor is Allah’s knowledge in one place rather than another. This is expressed in His words:

‘So that you may know that Allah has power over all things, and that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.’

He also offered the following illustration: If a man held a clear glass cup containing something clear, his sight would encompass the cup without

---

## Page 2172

the man being inside the cup. Allah—to whom belongs the highest description—encompasses all His creation without being in any part of His creation.

Here is another illustration: If a man built a house with all its facilities, then closed its door and left, he would still know how many rooms his house contained and how spacious each room was, without being inside the house. Likewise, Allah, mighty and majestic—to whom belongs the highest description—encompasses everything He has created and knows what it is and how it is, without being in anything He has created.

As for the Jahmiyyah’s interpretation of Allah’s words, mighty and majestic:

“There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth,”

they said, “Allah, mighty and majestic, is with us and within us.”

We said, “Why have you quoted only part of His statement? Allah says:

‘Do you not see that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth? There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth, nor among five but He is their sixth, nor among fewer or more than that but He is with them’—meaning, through His knowledge of them—‘wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah knows all things.’”

Thus, He began the statement with His knowledge and ended it with His knowledge.

The Jahmī is also asked, “If Allah is with us in the majesty of His very Self, does Allah forgive you concerning what is between Him and His creation?” If he says yes, he has thereby maintained that Allah, exalted is He, is distinct from His creation and that His creation is beneath Him. If he says no, he has disbelieved.

He said: “If you wish to know that the Jahmī is lying about Allah when he claims that He is everywhere and is not in one place rather than another, say to him, ‘Did Allah not exist when nothing else existed?’”

---

## Page 2173

He will say, “Yes.”

Then say to him, “When He created things, did He create them within Himself or outside Himself?” He must then adopt one of “three positions”:

First, if he claims that Allah created creation within Himself, he has disbelieved by claiming that He created the jinn, human beings and devils within Himself.

If he says, “He created them outside Himself, then entered into them,” this too is disbelief, since he claims that He entered a filthy, unclean and foul place.

If he says, “He created them outside Himself and did not then enter into them,” he has abandoned his position entirely. This is the position of the people of the Sunnah.

Imam Ahmad has thus explained what is known through sound reason and the self-evident dictates of the natural disposition: He must have created creation either within Himself or outside Himself. If He created it outside Himself, then either He subsequently indwelt it or He has always remained distinct from it. Thus, he mentioned the three possibilities.

He also said in the course of his discussion:

“When the proof was established against the Jahmī concerning his claim about Allah—that He is with His creation in everything, without being in contact with anything or distinct from it—we said, ‘If He is not distinct from it, is He not in contact with it?’

“He said, ‘No.’

“We said, ‘How, then, can He be in something without being

## Page 2176

The reply is:

As for your question, “How did He rise over the Throne?”—the question “how” does not apply to Allah Most High. He has told us that He

“rose over the Throne,”

but He has not told us how He rose over it. Since He did not tell them how that was, and their eyes did not see Him in this world so that they could describe Him according to what they had seen, and since they were forbidden to say about Him what they did not know, they believed His account of His rising over the Throne and entrusted the knowledge of how He rose over it to Allah Most High.

But you, O Jahmī, must say that Allah Most High is bounded and encompassed by places, since you claim that He is in places. For one cannot conceive of anything being in a place without that place encompassing it. Thus the Arabs say, “So-and-so is in the house,” and “The water is in the well”: the house encompasses that person, and the well encompasses the water.

An even more abhorrent consequence follows from your position, for you have said something more appalling than what the Christians asserted. They said, “Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is in Jesus,” and Jesus is the body of a single human being. They disbelieved by saying this, and they were told, “You have not revered Allah, since you have placed Him in Mary’s womb.”

Yet you say that He is in every place—in the wombs of all women, in the body of Jesus, and in the bodies of all people.

You must also say that He is inside dogs and pigs, for these are places, and according to you He is in every place. Exalted is Allah, far above that!

He said: When I exposed the repugnance of his position, he said, “I say that Allah is in every place, but not as a thing

---

## Page 2177

in a thing, nor as a thing upon a thing, nor as a thing outside a thing, nor separate from a thing.”

He said:

He should be told: “Your position rests on inference and rational understanding, yet by inference and rational understanding you have demonstrated that you worship nothing. For if He were something to which inference and rational understanding applied, He would have to be either within a thing or outside it. Since, according to you, He is not a thing, it is impossible for that thing to be within another thing or outside it. By my life, you have described something obscure that has no existence. This is your religion, and negation is the foundation of your doctrine.”

Thus, ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Makkī has explained that inference and rational understanding necessarily establish that whatever is neither within a thing nor outside it is nothing, and that this is the description of something nonexistent, having no existence. Here, inference means rational proofs, while rational understanding means self-evident knowledge.

Likewise, Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb—the leading authority of the theologians who affirm the divine attributes, such as al-Qalānisī, al-Ash‘arī, and his followers—made a similar statement, recorded by Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak in his compilation of al-Ash‘arī’s statements. Ibn Fūrak cited Ibn Kullāb as saying:

“The assertion of someone who says, ‘He is neither within the world nor outside it,’ falls outside the bounds of rational inquiry and revelation. He has thereby negated Him completely. For if he were told, ‘Describe Him as nonexistent,’ he could say no more than this. He has rejected what Allah has explicitly stated and made a claim in this matter that neither revealed texts nor reason allow. He claims that this is pure monotheism. In their view, pure negation is pure affirmation, and they consider themselves exponents of rational inference.”

He said:

If they say, ‘He is below and He is above,’ they should be told: ‘Then above is below, and below is above.’”

## Page 2181

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

What does our master and shaykh—Shaykh al-Islām and an example for all people, may Allah support him and be pleased with him—say concerning two men who disputed the hadith of the descent, one affirming it and the other denying it?

The one who affirmed it said, “Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains.”

The one who denied it asked, “How does He descend?”

The one who affirmed it replied, “He descends, without specifying how.”

The one who denied it asked, “Does the Throne become vacant of Him or not?”

The one who affirmed it replied, “This is an innovated statement and an invented opinion.”

The one who denied it said, “That does not answer my question; rather, it evades the answer.”

The one who affirmed it told him, “That is your answer.”

The one who denied it said, “It is only His command and His mercy that descend.”

The one who affirmed it replied, “His command and His mercy descend at every hour, whereas the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, specified the last third of the night as the time of the descent.”

The one who denied it said, “The night is not of equal length in all lands. For in some lands the night may last

---

## Page 2182

Thus, the length of the night varies according to regions and lands. In some lands, night and day may be equal, while in others the night may extend over most of the twenty-four hours, leaving only a short period of daylight. It follows from this that a third of the night must always be occurring, and that the Lord must always be descending to heaven.”

We ask that you dispel these doubts and difficulties and refute the people of misguidance.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The first speaker, who quoted the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was correct in what he said. His statement has been widely transmitted in the Sunnah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and those versed in the Sunnah and hadith have unanimously affirmed its truth and received it with acceptance.

Whoever says what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said speaks truthfully and correctly, even if he does not know the full reality of the meanings it contains. This is like someone who recites the Quran without understanding its meanings. Indeed, the truest speech is Allah’s speech, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke these words and others like them openly and conveyed them to the entire community. He did not reserve them for some people rather than others, nor did he conceal them from anyone. The Companions and the Successors would mention them, relate them, and convey them

---

## Page 2183

and narrate them in private and public gatherings. They are also contained in the Islamic books read in private and public gatherings, such as the Sahīhs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, Mālik’s Muwatta’, Imām Ahmad’s Musnad, the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, and al-Nasā’ī, and other such books of the Muslims.

However, whoever understands this hadith and others like it to imply something from which Allah must be declared free—such as likening Him to the attributes of created beings or attributing to Him an imperfection incompatible with the perfection that rightfully belongs to Him—has erred. If he expresses this understanding openly, he must be prevented from doing so. If he claims that the hadith indicates and entails such a meaning, he has likewise erred.

For describing Him, glorified and exalted is He, in this hadith as descending is like describing Him with His other attributes: His rising toward heaven while it was smoke; His having created the heavens and the earth in six days, then risen over the Throne; and His coming, as in His words, exalted is He:

And other such actions by which

---

## Page 2185

The position of the early generations of this Ummah and its leading scholars is to describe Him as He has described Himself and as His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has described Him, in both negation and affirmation.

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has denied that He is like created beings. He, exalted is He, says:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, the One.’”

“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

“He neither begets nor is born.”

“Nor is there any equivalent to Him.”

Thus, He has made clear that none is His equal. He, exalted is He, also says:

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

He thereby denies that He has any equal. He, exalted is He, says:

“So do not set up rivals to Allah.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“So do not draw comparisons with Allah.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

What He has declared about Himself—that He is above having any equal, peer, likeness or rival, or having comparisons drawn with Him—makes clear that nothing is like Him in His attributes or His actions. For sameness in attributes and actions entails sameness in essence. Two different essences cannot have identical attributes and actions, since identical attributes and actions necessarily entail identical essences. An attribute depends upon that which possesses it, and an action likewise depends upon its agent; indeed, an action is itself something by which the agent is described.

Thus, if two attributes are identical, the two beings possessing them are identical. Indeed, the degree of similarity and difference between attributes corresponds to that between the beings possessing them. Take two human beings, for example: although they belong to a single species, their sizes and attributes differ according to the differences between their individual essences, and resemble one another according to the resemblance between those essences.

Likewise, if it is said that a human being and a horse resemble one another in that the former is an animal and the latter

---

## Page 2186

is an animal, and differ in that the former is rational and the latter neighs, and in other respects, then the similarity and difference between their attributes correspond to those between their essences.

This is because an essence stripped of attributes exists only in the mind. The mind conceives of an essence stripped of attributes and of an absolute existence that is not individuated. As for things that actually exist, there can be neither an essence stripped of every attribute nor an absolute existence that is neither individuated nor particularized.

When someone who affirms the divine attributes says, “I affirm Allah’s attributes as additional to His essence,” what this really means is that we affirm them as additional to what the deniers have affirmed of the essence. For the deniers believed in the existence of an essence stripped of attributes, so those who affirm the attributes said: “We affirm attributes in addition to what these people have affirmed.” As for the actually existing essence itself, it is inconceivable that it could exist without any attributes whatsoever.

Rather, this is like someone saying: “I affirm a human being who is neither an animal nor rational, who neither subsists in himself nor in anything else, and who has neither power nor life, neither motion nor rest,” or something similar. Or it is like saying: “I affirm a palm tree that has neither stem nor trunk nor fibre nor anything else of that kind.” Such a person affirms something that has no reality outside the mind and cannot be rationally conceived.

For this reason, the early generations and leading scholars called those who deny the attributes “negators,” because the true import of their position is to negate the very essence of Allah, exalted is He—even though they themselves may not realize that their position necessarily entails such negation. Rather, they describe Him in two contradictory ways, saying: “He exists, is eternal, and necessarily exists”; then they deny

---

## Page 2187

the necessary implications of His existence. Their position thus amounts to saying: “He exists but does not exist; He is real but not real; He is a creator but not a creator.” They deny both sides of a contradiction concerning Him, either explicitly denying both or refraining from affirming either. For this reason, their most thoroughgoing exponents—the Qarmatians—deny both sides of a contradiction concerning Him. They do not say that He exists or does not exist, that He is living or not living, or that He is knowing or not knowing.

They say: “Describing Him in affirmative terms likens Him to existing things, while describing Him in negative terms likens Him to nonexistent things.” Their excessive rejection of any likeness thus led them to describe Him in terms of utter negation. Yet they did not escape what they sought to avoid. Rather, by the logic of their own position, they must have likened Him to that which is impossible, which is baser than what exists and what does not exist but could. Thus, while claiming to avoid likening Him to existing and nonexistent things, they described Him with the attributes of impossible things, which cannot exist—unlike nonexistent things whose existence is possible. Likening Him to impossible things is worse than likening Him to existing things and nonexistent things whose existence is possible.

What these heretics sought to avoid is not, in fact, objectionable. For if He is called real, existent, self-subsisting, living, knowing, compassionate, and merciful, and a created being is described by these same terms, it does not follow at all that He is like that created being. Were that true, every existing thing would be like every other existing thing, and every nonexistent thing would be like every other nonexistent thing. Likewise, everything of which an attribute is denied would be like everything else of which that same attribute is denied.

---

## Page 2188

Thus, if one says, “Blackness exists,” then, according to their position, we have made everything that exists like blackness. And if we say, “Whiteness does not exist,” we have made everything nonexistent like whiteness. Clearly, this is utterly absurd, and this alone suffices to disgrace the party of heresy.

If no such consequence follows concerning blackness—which undoubtedly has its counterparts—then, when it is said of the Creator of the world that He exists and is not nonexistent, is living and does not die, and is the Self-Subsisting Sustainer whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes, how could it follow that He is like every existing, nonexistent, living, and subsisting thing; or like everything of which nonexistence is denied, everything of which the attribute of nonexistence is denied, and everything of which death and sleep are denied, such as the inhabitants of Paradise, who neither sleep nor die?

The reason is that these general, univocal terms—which grammarians call generic nouns—are used in one of two ways. This holds whether their meanings apply equally to their respective subjects or vary in degree, as with blackness and the like; and whether they are called “graded” terms, with graded terms regarded as a kind of univocal term.

They may be used in an “unrestricted and general” sense, as when it is said: “What exists is divided into necessary and contingent, eternal and originated, creator and created; and knowledge is divided into eternal and originated knowledge.” Alternatively, they may be used in a “specific and determinate” sense, as when one speaks of Zayd’s and Amr’s existence, Zayd’s and Amr’s knowledge, or Zayd’s and Amr’s essence.

When used in a specific and determinate sense, they denote what is peculiar to the entity named; they do not denote anything in external reality that it shares with another. For what is peculiar to the entity named is not shared between it and anything else.

---

## Page 2189

Thus, when one speaks of Zayd’s knowledge, descent, rising, and the like, these expressions denote only the knowledge, descent, rising, and other attributes peculiar to Zayd; they do not denote anything that another shares with him. Yet we know that Zayd is comparable to Amr, and that his knowledge, descent, and rising are comparable to Amr’s. We know this through analogy, reason, and comparison, not through what the wording itself denotes. If this holds for the attributes of a created being, it holds all the more for the Creator.

Thus, when one speaks of Allah’s knowledge, speech, descent, rising, existence, life, and the like, these expressions, with still greater reason, do not denote anything that any created being shares with Him. Nor do they indicate that another is like Him in these respects, as was established in the case of Zayd and Amr. In that case, we knew their likeness through comparison and analogy, because Zayd is like Amr. Here, however, we know that Allah has no likeness, equal, or rival. We must therefore not understand these expressions to mean that His knowledge is like another’s knowledge, His speech like another’s speech, His rising like another’s rising, His descent like another’s descent, or His life like another’s life.

For this reason, the position of the early generations and the imams was to affirm the attributes while denying that they are like the attributes of created beings. Allah Most High possesses attributes of perfection without any deficiency. He is utterly free of attributes of deficiency, and none is like Him in His attributes of perfection.

These two meanings together encompass His transcendence, and both are indicated by His words, Most High:

“Say: He is Allah, the One.”

“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

The name al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge) encompasses the attributes of perfection, while the name al-Ahad (the One) encompasses the denial of any likeness to Him, as has been explained at length in the commentary on this surah.

---

## Page 2190

Thus, what is said of His attributes is like what is said of His essence. Nothing is like Allah Most High, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions. What is understood, however, is that the relation of an attribute to its possessor is like the relation of the corresponding attribute to its possessor. Allah’s knowledge, speech, descent, and rising are appropriate to His essence and befit it, just as a servant’s attributes are appropriate to his essence and befit it. The relation of His attributes to His essence is like the relation of the servant’s attributes to his essence.

For this reason, some have said:

“If someone asks you, ‘How does He descend? How did He rise? How does He know, speak, decree, and create?’ say to him, ‘What is He like in Himself?’ If he says, ‘I do not know what His essence is like,’ say to him, ‘Nor do I know what His attributes are like, for knowing what an attribute is like depends upon knowing what its possessor is like.’”

This applies when these names and attributes are used with a specific, determinate reference—which is how they occur in the Quran and Sunnah. But when they are used in an unqualified, general sense—as in the statements of speculative thinkers, “What exists is divided into the eternal and the originated,” and “Knowledge is divided into eternal and originated knowledge,” and similar statements—this is what the unqualified, general expression denotes, and knowledge is an unqualified, general concept. Concepts are unqualified and general only in the mind, not in concrete reality. Thus, an existent with unqualified or general existence is found only in the mind; anything unqualified or general is found only in the mind; and an unqualified, general human being or animal is found only in the mind. Existing things themselves, by contrast, are always determinate, particular, and distinct from others.

Let the discerning reader reflect carefully on this crucial distinction, for many speculative thinkers have stumbled here while delving

---

## Page 2191

into the nature of things, until they came to suppose that these general, unqualified, universal concepts exist as such in external reality. They supposed that if we say, “Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exists, lives, and knows, and the servant exists, lives, and knows,” this necessarily entails something existing in external reality that the Lord and the servant share, with that very same thing present in both the servant and the Lord—indeed, in every existing thing. The Lord must also have something distinguishing Him from creation, so He would consist of two parts:

The first belongs to every creature: the common element shared by Him and all other existing things.

The second is exclusive to Him: that which distinguishes Him from all other existing things. Yet whatever they identify as exclusive to Him entails the same difficulty.

Thus, when they say, “He is distinguished by His essence, His reality, His quiddity,” or something similar, this amounts to saying that He is distinguished by His existence. For “essence,” “reality,” and “quiddity” can be used both without qualification and with a determinate reference, exactly like the term “existence.”

This issue has bewildered groups of leading speculative thinkers, to the point that some have said that “existence” and other such terms are used purely equivocally. They attributed this view to everyone who denies states—and these constitute the general body of those who affirm the divine attributes. Their account thus amounts to attributing the following position to the general body of Muslims and to speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes—such as Ibn Kullāb, al-Ash'arī, Ibn Karrām, and others, and even to such exacting Mu'tazilī scholars as Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī and others: the term “existent,” and other terms applied both to Allah and to created beings, are used purely equivocally, without any general meaning shared by the two referents. This would be like the word mushtarī, used for both a purchaser and the planet Jupiter, or the name Suhayl, applied both to a star and to a man.

---

## Page 2192

Yet this attribution gravely misrepresents those to whom they ascribe it. These scholars agree that such terms are general and univocal—taking univocity in its broad sense, which includes graded predication—and admit of division and classification into types. This is possible only with univocal terms, as when we say: “Existents are divided into the eternal and the originated, and into the necessary and the contingent.”

Indeed, the very people who report this view, such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Rāzī and other later thinkers, combine in their writings the claim that these terms are purely equivocal with this division of them. Yet they themselves maintain that division applies only to univocal terms, which share both wording and meaning, not to terms that share wording alone. These include what they call graded terms. Division cannot apply to terms whose referents share no general meaning.

Such is the contradiction of these men, who rank among the later thinkers most renowned for rational inquiry and rigorous investigation in philosophy and speculative theology. In this attribution and their investigation of so fundamental a principle, they have fallen into an error into which even the least discerning ordinary person would not fall. This stems from the unsound principles they received from certain logicians—principles that stray from guidance and sound judgment. They supposed that unqualified universals exist in external reality as parts of particular things, and that this entails each particular being composed of that shared universal and whatever is exclusive to it. On this view, they were thus committed to holding that the Lord Most High, whose existence is necessary, is composed of shared existence and whatever is exclusive to Him, whether necessity, existence, or quiddity. Yet it is well known among logicians that universals are universal only in minds, not in external entities.

---

## Page 2193

Anyone whom Allah Most High guides knows that existent things share nothing that actually exists within them. Rather, each existent is distinct in itself and in its attributes and actions. When we say, “This human being is alive and speaks,” or “is a rational animal,” or the like, his animality or rationality, or his speech and life, are not shared between him and anyone else. Rather, he has what is particular to him, and another has what is particular to that other. They resemble one another to the extent that their animality, rationality, and other attributes resemble one another.

If someone says that a human being is composed of that by which he shares something with others—animality—and that by which he is distinguished—rationality—then, if he means a mental composition, the claim is correct. For when we conceive a rational animal in our minds, animality is one part of this mental meaning and rationality its other part; and the animal component has more counterparts than the rational component. When we conceive what is designated by “animal” and what is designated by “rational,” the former encompasses human beings and others, whereas the latter is specific to human beings. Thus, the claim of composition in these mental meanings is correct. Yet this provides no fixed criterion. Rather, it depends on what a person conceives, whether that conception is true or false.

If by the part internal to a quiddity one means what enters into this conception; by its part external to it but necessarily accompanying its existence, what this expression signifies by inclusion and necessary implication; and by the whole quiddity, what it signifies by correspondence—then this is correct. But this does not entail that

---

## Page 2194

realities existing outside the mind are composed of particular and general attributes, nor that some of their inseparable attributes are internal to their reality and essential to it, while others are external to their reality and accidental to it, as the proponents of Greek logic claim. This is one of the matters in which they went astray, and their error led astray those groups of speculative thinkers who followed them in it. They were also blindly followed in this by those who neither understood the true meaning and implications of their position nor conceived it fully.

If by composition they mean that a human being possesses life and rationality—with one attribute having counterparts in other animals and the other being specific to human beings—then this is a sound meaning. But if they mean that his animality is shared between him and others, they are mistaken. The animality of each animal is like the rationality of each rational being: each is particular to the subject in which it inheres.

Likewise, if by composition they mean that there is an existent described as an animal distinct from the existent described as rational or as neighing, and that a human being is composed of this existent and that existent, and a horse is composed of this existent and that existent, then they are mistaken. Rather, nothing exists here except this human being, described as a rational animal, and this horse, described as a neighing animal. The same applies to all other animals and existent things.

Thus, if someone’s statement, “A human being is composed of this and that,” is intended to mean that there is something

---

## Page 2195

composite, with two distinct parts of which it is composed, then he speaks out of ignorance. Rather, it is one thing possessing two attributes: it exists only with its two attributes, and its two attributes exist only in it.

The following meaning, however, is correct: a human being is truly described as an animal and as rational, and is an essence that necessarily entails its attributes. The thing described cannot exist without its inseparable attribute. But this is not composition in external reality.

Nor is there in external reality an inseparable essential attribute, another accidental attribute inseparable from the quiddity, and yet another inseparable from its existence. Rather, there is only the particular existent, whose attributes fall into two categories: inseparable and incidental. It cannot exist without any one of its inseparable attributes. Thus, none of these attributes is inseparable from the essence existing in external reality yet not inseparable from that essence, being instead inseparable from the externally existing thing—as some logicians suppose.

Their fundamental error is that they confused what is conceived in the mind with what exists in concrete reality. The mind conceives a triangle before it exists externally, and they supposed that quiddity is distinct from existence. This is correct if quiddity is understood as what the mind conceives.

But to suppose that a triangle in external reality has a quiddity established externally that is distinct from the thing existing externally is a manifest error. Once this is understood concerning the attributes of a created being, the Creator is even further removed from what these people call composition.

---

## Page 2196

Thus, when it is said that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, is living, knowing and powerful, He is being described as the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful. When it is said that He exists and is necessary in Himself, He, glorified be He, is being described as possessing existence and necessity. There is therefore no actually existing thing shared between Him and anything else. Nor is He composed of two parts, or of constitutive attributes that form parts of His existence, or anything similar among the alleged forms of composition that are impossible even in a created being—and still more emphatically impossible in the Creator.

However, the term “composition” is ambiguous. These people include within it a thing’s possession of its inseparable attributes, although this is not what is ordinarily understood by “composition.” They have introduced their own technical usage of this term, without precedent among the authorities on the language or any group of scholars. They have made “composition” encompass “five kinds”:

First: composition from existence and quiddity, because they suppose that the external existence of every contingent being is distinct from its quiddity. Whenever the “internal part of quiddity” is understood as what enters into this conception, and its “external concomitant” as what this conception necessarily entails, these are the two meanings signified by the expression.

Second: composition from genus and differentia, as when they say that a human being is composed of animality and rationality. They may also include composition from a general meaning and a specific meaning, calling it composition from a genus and a differentia, or from a specific property and a common accident.

Third: composition from essence and attributes, as in that which is designated as living, knowing and capable

---

## Page 2197

and the composition of a body from its sensible parts, according to those who say that it is composed of indivisible atoms (1), or its composition from two intelligible components, according to those who say that it is composed of matter and form.

As for the “first” and “second” kinds of composition, the majority of rational thinkers dispute their existence in external reality, saying that no composition of this sort exists there. The “fourth” and “fifth” kinds are the subject of a well-known dispute among rational thinkers: some affirm one of these two kinds of composition in a body, while others say that it is composed in neither way.

As for the “fourth,” the great majority of rational thinkers agree with them in affirming it; I know of no one who disputes it in substance (*). However, a group of speculative thinkers, such as ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Kaysān al-Asamm and others, are reported to have denied accidents: they did not affirm accidents as something additional to the body, and denied that motion was something additional to the body. Most thinkers disagreed with them on this.

This—and Allah knows best—is a verbal dispute: does the term “body” encompass the body together with its accidents, or are accidents additional to what the term “body” designates? Otherwise, no rational person denies the existence of taste, colour, smell, motion, and other attributes inhering in the things they qualify.

>

> 
> Both were mentioned above, but they were not distinguished from one another. The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—mentioned these types in several places in his books and treatises, including his statement in al-Safadiyya, 1:105: ‘Fourth: composition in quantity, namely, the composition of a body from its constituent parts: either from indivisible atoms, which is sensible composition, or from matter and form, which is intelligible composition. These two types are the fourth and fifth.’
> 
> Second: His statement, ‘As for the “fourth,” the great majority of scholars agree with them in affirming it…,’ may contain a copyist’s error. The correct reading is ‘third,’ namely, composition from ‘essence’ and ‘attributes,’ which is the subject of the ensuing discussion.
