---

## Page 2198

This resembles the dispute over whether attributes are additional to the essence. For whoever means by “essence” the “bare essence,” the attributes are additional to it. But for whoever means the “essence qualified by attributes,” the attributes are not separate from the essence qualified by its inseparable attributes.

These people then claimed that they deny these types of composition. As for the “four types,” whoever holds that they are absent from created beings must hold that they are all the more absent from the Creator. As for the “fourth type,” if the dispute concerns whether attributes are additional to the essence, then it is a verbal dispute. But if someone disputes the actual existence of these attributes, denies that Allah has knowledge, power, and will, and regards one attribute as identical with another, and the attribute as identical with the one it qualifies, then the falsity of his position becomes evident once it is fully understood.

Once it is known that He—glorified be He—is Living, All-Knowing, and All-Powerful, and that what it means for Him to be Living differs from what it means for Him to be All-Knowing, and that what it means for Him to be All-Knowing differs from what it means for Him to be All-Powerful, this is precisely the affirmation of the attributes. If someone says that what it means for Him to be All-Knowing is the same as what it means for Him to possess will, to be All-Powerful, and to be Living, this is a wilful denial of the obvious. The same applies if he claims that these meanings are identical with the meaning of the essence qualified by them.

But if he acknowledges that these qualities belong to Allah and says, “I deny that Allah depends on entities or qualities through which He becomes living, knowing, and powerful,” then his dispute is with those who affirm “states”

---

## Page 2199

such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Abū Ya‘lā, and others who say: “He possesses knowledge and the state of being knowing, and His state of being knowing is a meaning additional to His knowledge.” This is the position of some who affirm the attributes, but the majority of them reject it, saying instead: “Knowledge and being knowing have the same meaning.”

There are “three matters” concerning the attributes:

The first is describing Him as Living, All-Knowing, and All-Powerful. There is agreement on affirming this, and it is termed predication.

The second is that these are meanings subsisting in His essence. This, too, is affirmed by those who affirm the attributes: the early generations, the imams, and those affiliated with the Sunnah across the various groups.

The third is states, namely, the states of being knowing and being powerful. There is disagreement concerning these among both those who affirm the attributes and those who deny them. Abū Hāshim and his followers affirm states but not attributes; al-Qādī Abū Bakr and his followers affirm both states and attributes; and most of the Jahmiyyah and Mu‘tazilah deny both states and attributes.

As for the great majority of the “people of the Sunnah,” they affirm the attributes but not states. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

---

## Page 2200

The purpose here is to discuss composition, both as a term and as a concept, and to show that these people use it in a technical sense at odds with that of most rational people, and that they are compelled to acknowledge the reality of what they deny. Yet they say, “This is commonality, and commonality is resemblance.” They also say, “These are parts, and this is composition from these parts.” Nevertheless, they cannot deny what they have called commonality and resemblance, nor can they deny these things that they have called parts, composition, and division. For they say, “He is the one who apprehends, the object of apprehension, and intellect itself; the object of pleasure, pleasure itself, and the one who takes pleasure; the lover, the beloved, and love itself.”

They may also say, “He is knowing, powerful, and willing,” and then say, “Knowledge is power, and power is will,” thus identifying each attribute with the other. They also say, “Knowledge is the knower”—and may say, “It is the object known”—thus identifying the attribute with the one possessing it, or with created things.

These are the statements of their leading authorities, and they are utterly unsound in the light of plain reason. They are compelled to acknowledge what they call resemblance and composition, while claiming to deny resemblance, composition, and division. Let the discerning reader reflect on their falsehood, inconsistency, bewilderment, and misguidance. This is why they ultimately end up either affirming both of two contradictories or denying both.

Moreover, they deny of Allah what He has affirmed of Himself and what His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has affirmed of Him, claiming that this entails resemblance and composition. They apply these labels to those who affirm the attributes, yet it is they themselves whom their own principles bind to these things, with no way to escape them.

They are thus as the saying goes:
“She accused me of her own disease, then slipped away.”

---

## Page 2201

They did not intend this contradiction; rather, they were led into it by their unsound rules of logic, in which they claimed that things possessing attributes are composed of their attributes, and that shared universals exist in their concrete instances. Those unsound rules of logic—which they made into laws whose observance supposedly prevents the mind from going astray in its thinking—led them into this very error and contradiction. Yet some of these laws are undoubtedly sound, which further demonstrates their inconsistency and ignorance. For they have established among their logical laws that a universal is that whose conception does not preclude its being shared, unlike a particular.

They have also established that universals are universal only in minds, not in concrete reality, and that the absolute, taken on condition of its absoluteness, exists only in the mind. These are sound laws. Yet they then claim, as the foremost of their later thinkers claimed, that the Necessary Existent is absolute existence, on condition that it be free of every positive determination.

Or, as one group among them says, He is absolute existence, on condition that it be free of every positive and negative determination. This is the position maintained by some of the heretical esotericists who affiliate themselves with Shiism or Sufism.

Or a third group says that He is absolute existence without any condition, as some among them put it. They agree that the absolute, on condition that it be free of all determinations involving existence and nonexistence

---

## Page 2202

does not exist in concrete reality.

The absolute, on condition that it be free of every positive determination, is even less capable of existing. For what is conditioned by the negation of both existence and nonexistence stands in the same relation to both, whereas what is conditioned by the negation of existence pertains exclusively to nonexistence, not existence. As for the absolute without any condition, it exists as absolute only in minds.

When it is said, “It exists in concrete reality,” this means that it exists there with determinations, not that it exists there as absolute. The latter is false, even though a group claims it. Whoever fully grasps this will recognize the falsity of their position. This is self-evidently true. Yet this sound principle did not benefit them in establishing the existence of the Lord. Instead, they made Him absolute, either on condition that He be free of both contradictories, or of all positive determinations, or without any condition. Such an absolute can be conceived only in minds. Their unsound principles led them into this contradiction and nonsense.

They seek to avoid affirming any likeness whatsoever, yet they say, “Existence is divided into necessary and contingent.” Thus, the two share in what is denoted by “existence.” The same applies to the terms “quiddity,” “reality,” and “essence.”

Whatever is said to be divided into necessary and contingent, the subject of that division is shared by its divisions. These divisions therefore share a general, universal meaning encompassing that in which they resemble one another. This is a likeness that they themselves affirm, although they claim to deny everything that could be called likeness, to the point of denying the names. Thus, the extremists among the Jahmiyyah and the esotericists would not even call Him a “thing,” seeking to avoid this.

---

## Page 2203

Whatever they affirm, the same consequence follows. Otherwise, it would follow that the existence of the Necessary Existent is not contingent, eternal, and originated, and that whatever is originated and contingent must have an eternal cause. It is necessarily known that among existing things are those that are originated and contingent, and that whatever is originated and contingent must have an eternal cause that exists necessarily in itself. The existence of both kinds is therefore a necessary, inescapable fact.

The truth of the matter is that the term “absolute” may mean something universal, the conception of whose meaning does not preclude its being shared by multiple things. Nothing existing in concrete reality, whether self-subsisting or an attribute of something else, can exist in this manner—let alone the Lord of the worlds, the One, the Self-Sufficient.

The term “absolute” may also mean that which is divested of positive attributes, or of both positive and negative attributes; and the absolute without the condition of absoluteness. If this is conceived as something determinate and particular rather than universal, its existence in concrete reality is even more impossible than that of absolute universals conditioned by their universality. For those universals have particulars existing in concrete reality, to which the universals correspond. By contrast, something divested of any positive or negative attribute cannot be realized in concrete reality, whether as a universal or as a particular. The same applies to something divested of positive attributes; indeed, this is even more impossible than the former.

And if this shares with all other existing things what is denoted by “existence,” and is distinguished from them only by negative determinations, whereas they are distinguished from it by positive determinations,

---

## Page 2204

then every contingent existent would be more perfect than this which they claim is the Necessary Existent. For universal existence is shared by it and them; it is distinguished from them only by an absence, whereas they are distinguished from it by something existent. Thus, what distinguishes them from it is more perfect than what distinguishes it from them, since existence is more perfect than nonexistence.

If, however, it is said that it is existence without qualification, then this is universal and natural existence, applicable to every existent. This is universal only in the mind; in external reality, it exists only as something particular.

Some people say that this universal is a part of particular existents. If the first view is correct, it follows either that the Necessary Existent does not exist in external reality, or that the Necessary Existent and the contingent existent are one and the same entity, as some proponents of the oneness of existence maintain. If the second view is correct, it follows that its existence is a part of every existent; the Necessary Existent would thus be a part of the existence of contingent things.

Sound reason plainly recognizes that a part of something cannot be the creator of that thing in its entirety. Indeed, it cannot even create itself, let alone create that of which it is a part, since the whole is greater than the part. If it cannot create the part, its inability to create the whole is all the more evident.

Thus, they have gained no benefit from sound logic in knowing Allah, while false logic has led them into the utmost falsehood and ignorance concerning Allah.

“Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

And “Allah is the Protector of

those who believe. He brings them out of darkness into light. As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are false gods, who bring them out of light into darkness.”

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose to pray at night, he would say, as Muslim reported in his Sahīh:

“O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differed. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth concerning which people have differed. Indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.”

---

## Page 2206

Section

To complete the discussion of this subject, you should understand that we can know what lies beyond our experience only through knowing what we have experienced. We know things through our outward or inward senses, and this knowledge concerns particular, specific things. Then, through reason, we infer what lies beyond our experience from what we have experienced, leaving general, universal propositions in our minds. Thus, when something beyond our experience is described to us, we understand what we are told only through our knowledge of what we have experienced. Had we not experienced within ourselves hunger and thirst, satiety and the quenching of thirst, love and hatred, pleasure and pain, contentment and displeasure, we would not understand the reality of these things when they are described to us and we are told that others experience them.

Likewise, had we not known life, power, knowledge, and speech in the realm of our experience, we would not understand what we are told when something beyond our experience is described in these terms. Similarly, had we never experienced anything that exists, we would not know of the existence of anything beyond our experience. There must therefore be a shared element between what we have experienced and what lies beyond our experience: this is what a univocal term denotes. Through this agreement, commonality, similarity, and correspondence, we understand what lies beyond our experience and affirm its reality. This is the distinctive function of reason. Without it, we would know only what we perceive through our senses; we would know neither general truths nor things beyond our outward and inward senses. Hence, whoever has never perceived a thing or anything comparable to it cannot know its reality.

---

## Page 2207

Furthermore, Allah Most High has told us of the bliss and punishment He has promised us in the Hereafter, and of its food, drink, spouses, furnishings, and other things. Were we not familiar with things resembling these in this world, we would not understand what He has promised us. Yet we know that those realities are not like these. Indeed, Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “Nothing of what is in Paradise is found in this world except the names.” According to one view, this explains His words:

“And it is given to them in likeness.”

Thus, the things that exist in this world and those that exist in the Hereafter resemble one another, correspond, and share certain features. Through this, we understand what is meant and come to love and desire it, or to hate it and recoil from it. Yet between them lie differences and disparities in excellence whose extent cannot be measured in this world. This belongs to the ta’wīl—the ultimate reality—that we do not know, but Allah Most High knows.

Hence, the statement, “None but Allah knows the ta’wīl of the ambiguous passages,” is true, as is the statement, “Those firmly grounded in knowledge know their ta’wīl.” Both statements have been transmitted from the early generations: the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness.

Those who said that they know their ta’wīl meant that they know their explanation and meaning. Otherwise, could a Muslim permissibly say that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not know the meaning of the verses and hadiths he uttered and conveyed, but instead spoke words whose meanings he did not know? Those who said that they do not know their ta’wīl meant the actual manner of being, knowledge of which is the exclusive prerogative of

---

## Page 2208

Allah.

This is why the early generations, including Rabīʿah, Mālik ibn Anas, and others, would say: “Rising over is known, but its manner is unknown.” This was also the position of the rest of the early generations, including Ibn al-Mājishūn, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others, and it applies to the other attributes as well. The meaning of rising over is thus known: this is the ta’wīl—the explanation—known to those firmly grounded in knowledge. Its actual manner, however, is the ta’wīl unknown to the children of Adam and all others, which none knows except Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Likewise, regarding what He has promised in Paradise, His servants understand the meaning of what Allah has told them. As for its actual manner, He Most High has said:

“No soul knows what delights have been hidden for them as a reward for what they used to do.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived.’”

Thus, we know the explanation and meaning of what Allah has told us about the attributes of created things, and we understand the words addressed to us. We know what honey, meat, milk, silk, gold, and silver mean, and we distinguish between the things these names denote. As for their true realities as they actually are, we cannot know them, nor do we know when the Hour will come. No angel brought near to Allah and no prophet sent by Him knows the full details of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has prepared for His servants. Rather, this belongs to the ta’wīl that none knows except Allah, blessed and exalted is He. If this is the case with these two created realities, then the distinction between the Creator and creation is greater still;

---

## Page 2209

for Allah’s distinction from His creation, His greatness, majesty, and superiority, far exceed any difference between one created thing and another.

If the attributes of that created thing, despite their resemblance to those of this created thing, differ in excellence and nature to an extent that we neither know nor can know in this world—rather, this belongs to the ta’wīl known only to Allah, blessed and exalted is He—then all the more must the attributes of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, differ from those of creation in nature and excellence to an extent known only to Allah, blessed and exalted is He. This must likewise belong to the ta’wīl that not everyone knows: some of it is known to those firmly grounded in knowledge, some to the prophets and angels, and some to Allah alone.

As it is reported that Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Quranic explanation is of four kinds: explanation that the Arabs know from their own language; explanation of which no one is excused for being ignorant; explanation known to the scholars; and explanation known only to Allah. Whoever claims knowledge of this last kind is a liar.”

In the speech of the early generations, the term “ta’wīl” means only explanation or the concrete reality to which something ultimately refers, as in His Most High’s words:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes…”

And so on in the verse.

As for using ta’wīl to mean turning an expression from its more likely meaning to a less likely meaning on the basis of accompanying evidence, subsequent evidence, or evidence without further qualification, this is the terminology of

---

## Page 2210

some later scholars; none of the early generations ever used the word ta’wīl in this sense.

Then, when this usage became widespread among later scholars, they began to suppose that this was the ta’wīl meant in His Most High’s words:

“No one knows its interpretation except Allah.”

One group then said, “No one knows it except Allah,” while another said, “Rather, those firmly grounded in knowledge know it.” Both groups are mistaken, for this has no reality; rather, it is false, and Allah knows that it is unfounded and that He did not intend it. Such are the interpretations of the Qarmatian esotericists, the Jahmiyyah, and other proponents of heresy and religious innovation. These interpretations are false, and Allah did not intend them by His words. What He did not intend, we cannot say He knows to be His intended meaning, for this would be a lie against Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Those firmly grounded in knowledge do not speak falsely about Allah, blessed and exalted is He, even though we know from what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has told us about Himself—indeed, also through rational consideration of the fact that to Allah belongs the highest description—that Allah is described by attributes of perfection. He possesses life, knowledge, and power, and these are attributes of perfection. The Creator is more entitled to them than the created being. It is therefore impossible for the created being to possess attributes of perfection that the Creator does not possess.

Were it not that these names and attributes signify a shared, universal meaning, involving sufficient correspondence, agreement, and resemblance for these meanings to be understood and affirmed of Allah, we would have known nothing of Allah, nor would our hearts have contained any faith in Him, knowledge, recognition, or love

---

## Page 2211

or any desire to worship Him, supplicate to Him, ask of Him, love Him, or magnify Him. All these things require knowledge, and knowledge is possible only by affirming “those meanings,” which contain the correspondence and agreement through which we have acquired whatever knowledge we possess of what lies beyond our observation.

Whoever understands these noble truths and these great, beneficial principles will gain knowledge, recognition, sound understanding, affirmation of Allah’s oneness, and faith, while doubts, misguidance, and bewilderment will be dispelled from him. This will make him, in this field, among the finest of those whom Allah has favored—not those who have incurred His anger, nor those who have gone astray—and among the foremost people of knowledge and faith. It will become clear to him that what is said concerning some of the “attributes of Allah” applies equally to the rest, and that what is said concerning His attributes is like what is said concerning “His essence.” Whoever affirms one attribute conveyed by the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while denying another, even though both share the very feature on which he bases his denial, is inconsistent.

Thus, whoever denies descent and rising above, or pleasure and anger, or knowledge and power, or the name “the All-Knowing” or “the All-Powerful,” or the designation “the Existing One,” seeking, as he claims, to avoid a resemblance involving composition and corporeality, faces an analogous objection regarding what he affirms to the objection he levels against others regarding what he himself denies and they affirm.

Every argument used to deny descent, rising above, pleasure, and anger can be matched by his opponent with an analogous argument denying will, hearing, sight, power, and knowledge.

Every argument he uses to deny power, knowledge, hearing, and sight can be matched by his opponent with an analogous argument denying the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, and the All-Seeing.

And every argument he uses to deny these names can be used by his opponent to deny the Existing One and the Necessary Existent.

---

## Page 2212

It is self-evident that there must be a beginningless being whose existence is necessary in itself and whose nonexistence is impossible. For whatever exists is either contingent and originated, or necessary and beginningless. What is contingent and originated can exist only through a necessary, beginningless being. Thus, if the arguments used to deny the established attributes entail denying the necessary, beginningless being, and denying that being entails denying existence altogether, it follows that whoever denies any established attribute through such an argument advances a position that necessarily entails denying the existence of what we plainly observe.

For example, someone may say: “Descent, rising above, and the like are attributes of bodies, for descent and rising above can only be conceived of in a composite body. Allah, glorified be He, is far above these necessary consequences, so He must also be declared free of that which entails them.” Or he may say: “These occur in time, and temporal occurrences can subsist only in a composite body.” Likewise, he may say: “Pleasure, anger, joy, love, and the like are attributes of bodies.”

He is then told: “The same applies to will, hearing, sight, knowledge, and power: they too are attributes of bodies. For just as we can conceive of nothing that descends, rises above, becomes angry, or is pleased except a body, we can conceive of nothing that hears, sees, wills, knows, or decrees except a body.”

If he says: “His hearing is not like our hearing, His sight is not like our sight, and His will is not like our will; the same applies to His knowledge and power,” he is told: “Likewise, His pleasure is not like our pleasure, His anger is not like our anger, His joy is not like our joy, and His descent and rising above are not like our descent and rising above.”

---

## Page 2213

If he then says: “In the observable world, anger can only be conceived of as the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of revenge, and descent can only be conceived of as movement from one place to another. Such movement requires vacating one space and occupying another. Thus, if He were to descend, no Lord would remain above the Throne.”

The reply is:

Nor, in the observable world, can will be conceived of except as the heart’s inclination to obtain what one needs and benefits from—things for which one depends upon others—and to ward off what harms one. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has said concerning His holy Self in His divine hadith:

“O My servants, you will never be able to benefit Me, nor will you ever be able to harm Me.”

Thus, He is far above the only kind of will conceivable in the observable world. Likewise, hearing can only be conceived of in the observable world as sound entering the ear canal, which can occur only in something with an internal cavity. Allah, glorified be He, is One and al-Samad, far above anything of that kind. Indeed, the same applies to sight and speech: in the observable world, they can only be conceived of as residing in something with an internal cavity. Allah, glorified be He, is One and al-Samad, far above that.

Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Hasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and many of the early generations said: “Al-Samad is He who has no internal cavity.” Others said: “He is the Master whose mastery is perfect.” Both statements are true, for the Arabic word al-Samad encompasses both meanings. In Arabic, al-samad means “the master”; it also means al-musammad (solid), and al-musammad means al-musmat (without an internal cavity). Both usages are well established in Arabic.

---

## Page 2214

For this reason, Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: “Angels have no internal cavities, whereas human beings do.”

This also provides another proof. For if the angels—who were created from light, as established in Sahīh Muslim on the authority of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Angels were created from light, jinn were created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you”—

if, then, they are created from light, neither eat nor drink, and have no internal cavities as human beings do, yet speak, hear, see, ascend and descend, as established by authentic texts, while their attributes and actions nevertheless do not resemble human attributes and actions, then the Creator, exalted is He, differs from His creatures far more than angels differ from human beings. For both angels and human beings are created, and one creature is closer to resembling another creature than to resembling the Creator, glorified and exalted be He.

Likewise, the human soul hears, sees, speaks, descends and ascends, as established by authentic texts and clear rational evidence. Nevertheless, its attributes and actions are not like those of the body.

If, then, one may not say that the soul’s attributes and actions are like the attributes of the body—the physical frame—even though the soul is joined to it and together they constitute the human being, and if the human soul is not like the physical body, how can it be permissible to liken the Lord, blessed and exalted be He, His attributes and His actions to the body, its attributes and its actions?!

If the one who negates these attributes wishes to remain consistent with his own principle and says: “I maintain that He has no speech subsisting in Him; rather,

His speech is created,” he should be told: “Then the same implication applies to hearing and sight, for the Basran Mu‘tazilah affirm perception.”

If he goes further in negating the divine attributes and says: “I do not follow the Mu‘tazilah, but rather the pure Jahmiyyah and the esotericists among the philosophers and the Qarmatians. For it has been said that Jahm affirmed His being an agent and powerful, because, according to him, a human being is neither powerful nor an agent; thus, in his view, this involves no likening of Allah to creation.”

Once he reaches this point, he must adopt the position of one of their groups and say:

---

## Page 2216

“I ascribe to Him neither existence nor nonexistence. I call Him neither existent nor nonexistent—or neither existent nor not existent. Rather, I refrain from either of these contradictories, making neither a denial nor an affirmation.”

Or he may say:

“I never describe Him in affirmative terms, but only in negative terms. Thus, I do not say that He is existent; rather, I say that He is not nonexistent.”

Or it may be said:

“Rather, He is nonexistent.”

The division is exhaustive. Either he describes Him in affirmative terms, in which case the same implications of likening Him to creation and ascribing corporeality to Him that he imposed upon others also apply to him; or he says: “I do not describe Him by affirming existence, but by denying nonexistence. Thus, I do not say that He is existent, but that He is not nonexistent.” Or he commits himself to absolute negation and says:

“Nothing exists necessarily.”

If he adopts the first position and says, “I affirm neither of the two contradictories: neither existence nor nonexistence,” he should be told:

“Suppose you say this with your tongue and believe neither alternative in your heart, choosing instead to turn away from knowing Allah, worshipping Him, and remembering Him, so that you never remember Him, worship Him, supplicate to Him, place your hope in Him, or fear Him. Your denial of Him would then be greater than that of Iblīs, who acknowledged Him. Yet your refusal to affirm either of the two contradictories does not entail that neither holds in reality, for it is impossible for neither of two contradictories to hold. Rather, in reality, anything—whatever it may be—must be either existent or nonexistent: it either is or is not. There is absolutely no middle ground between negation and affirmation. We are speaking of what is actually the case, whether you deny it or acknowledge it, and whether

---

## Page 2217

you mention it or turn away from it. A person’s refusal to look at the sun, the moon, the stars, and the sky does not negate their existence, nor does it prevent one of the two contradictories from holding true. Rather, ‘the sun’ must necessarily be either existent or nonexistent. How, then, could your heart and tongue turning away from the remembrance of Allah negate His existence and entail that neither contradictory holds? In reality, He must be either existent or nonexistent.”

Likewise, whoever says, “I do not say that He is existent; rather, I say that He is not nonexistent,” should be told:

“Negating one of two contradictories affirms the other. You have merely changed the wording, since saying that He is not nonexistent necessarily entails that He is existent. If He is not nonexistent, either He is existent or He is neither existent nor nonexistent. This ‘third alternative’ entails that neither contradictory holds, which is self-evidently invalid. Thus, if He is not nonexistent, He must be existent.”

If he says, “Rather, I commit myself to saying that He is nonexistent,” he should be told:

“Observation and reason establish that existing things exist. It is also known that some of them come into being after not having existed. We know, for example, that we ourselves came into being after not existing, and that clouds, rain, plants, and animals come into being. These and similar things are among the signs to which Allah Most High draws attention in His words:

‘Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that sail the sea with what benefits people, and the water Allah sends down from the sky, thereby bringing the earth to life after

---

## Page 2218

its death, and spreading throughout it every kind of creature, and the shifting of the winds and the clouds held subject between heaven and earth, are signs for people who reason.’

These familiar things that come into being cannot be necessary existents in themselves. For whatever exists necessarily in itself cannot be nonexistent and must have existed without beginning. These things, however, were nonexistent and then came into existence. Their existence after nonexistence therefore demonstrates that both their existence and their nonexistence are possible, since both have actually occurred. Thus, it is self-evidently known that among existing things there is something that has come into being and is contingent.

We then say:

An existing thing that has come into being and is contingent must have a cause that brings it into existence, exists without beginning, and exists necessarily in itself. For something that comes into being cannot bring itself into existence, just as a person cannot create himself. This is among the most evident, self-evident truths. Even after a person has come into existence and attained strength, he cannot add a limb to his body or increase its size: he cannot make a tall person shorter or a short person taller, nor make his own head larger or smaller than it is. Likewise, his parents cannot do any of these things.

It is self-evidently known that whatever comes into being after not existing must have someone who brings it into being. This is a self-evident proposition known through the innate disposition, even to children. If someone strikes a child while he is unaware and cannot see the person, he will ask, ‘Who struck me?’ If he is told, ‘No one struck you,’ his mind will not accept that the blow occurred without someone causing it. Rather, he knows that whatever occurs must have someone who causes it. Then, if he is told, ‘So-and-so struck you,’ he cries until he strikes the person who struck him. Thus, his innate disposition included acknowledgment

---

## Page 2219

of the Maker and of the revealed law, whose foundation is justice. Hence Allah Most High says:

“Or were they created by nothing, or are they the creators?”

The two Sahih collections relate from Jubayr ibn Mut‘im that, when he came to ransom the captives of Badr, he said: “I found the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, reciting Sūrat al-Tūr during the Maghrib prayer. When I heard this verse, ‘Or were they created by nothing, or are they the creators?’ I felt my heart split open.”

This is an exhaustive division of the possibilities, which Allah presents as a rhetorical question rejecting these alternatives, to show that these premises are self-evidently known and cannot be denied. He says:

“Or were they created by nothing?”

That is, without a creator who created them? Or did they create themselves? They know that both alternatives are false. It therefore follows that they have a Creator who created them—glorified and exalted is He.

There are many ways to establish this. For example, one may say: Whatever exists either has no beginning or has come into being, and whatever has come into being must depend on something without beginning. An existent is either necessary or contingent, and whatever is contingent must depend on something necessary. There are other arguments of this kind.

In every case, it necessarily follows that among existing things there is a being that has no beginning and exists necessarily in itself, and a contingent being that came into existence after not existing. Both share in what is denoted by “existence.” Yet he can conceive of no existent in the observable world except a body. He is therefore subject to the same charge he has brought against others: likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him.

It is thus clear that anyone’s denial of any of Allah’s attributes on the basis of such a method is false

---

## Page 2220

even if revelation had not affirmed it, nor reason established it. How, then, can such an argument be used to deny what both revelation and reason establish? It therefore becomes clear that anyone who denies any of the attributes—on the grounds that affirming them entails likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him—is subject to the very charge he levels against others. The rebuttal thus applies equally to both sides. Moreover, if this consequence follows on every possible assumption, then using it to deny that which entails it is clearly invalid, since that which entails it exists and cannot possibly be denied.

For this reason, such reasoning is not found in the words of any of the early generations of this Ummah or its leading scholars. Rather, it was introduced by the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, and many people adopted it from them. A person denies of the Lord what must indeed be denied of Him, such as imperfections from which He must be declared free: ignorance, inability, need, and the like. Declaring Him free of these is correct. Yet this person argues that they must be denied because they entail attributing corporeality to Allah and likening Him to creation. He is then challenged with what he himself affirms, and so falls into contradiction.

Through this opening, the heretical esotericists gained influence among Muslims, until they turned vast numbers away from Islam. They began saying to anyone who denied something of the Lord—such as someone who denied some or all of His attributes, or His most beautiful names—“Did you not deny this to avoid likening Allah to creation and attributing corporeality to Him?”

He replies, “Yes.”

They then say, “But this same consequence follows from what you affirm.”

He thus finds himself obliged to agree with them in denying one thing after another, until he reaches the point where he neither knows Allah in his heart, nor remembers Him with his tongue, nor worships Him, nor calls upon Him—even if he does not categorically affirm His nonexistence, but instead divests himself of faith in Him. The inconsistency of these people is already known.

Yet you ultimately made that which is eternal, without beginning, and necessarily existent in its own right into multiple bodies that resemble others in many respects, possess attributes, and undergo motions—despite their dependence and need. Each celestial sphere also depends on something other than itself, besides the other indications of their imperfection and need.”

## Page 2222

The point here is this: the person who refused to acknowledge that the Eternal, Necessary Existent exists and possesses attributes of perfection—lest this entail the likeness to creation and corporeality he mentioned, and who took the negation of this supposed consequence as proof for denying what he claimed entailed it—ultimately fell into the very thing he sought to escape: making the Necessary Existent a body resembling other things. Moreover, he ascribed to it attributes of imperfection from which the Lord must be declared free, while also denying the Creator, majestic is His glory. Thus, besides committing disbelief greater than that of polytheists in general—for they acknowledged the Maker despite worshipping others besides Him—he proved to be among the most ignorant of Adam’s descendants, the most unsound in intellect and reasoning, and the most inconsistent.

## Page 2224

The reason for this is that the terms “body” and “likening Allah to creation” are ambiguous and liable to cause confusion, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills. These negationists do not mean by the “body” they deny what the word means in ordinary language. As all rational people agree, something possessing attributes need not be a body in the linguistic sense recorded by the lexicographers. We shall explain this later. Rather, by “body” they mean something they believe to be composed of parts, and they believe that anything in which attributes subsist is composed of parts. This belief is false. Rather, the Lord possesses attributes without being a body composed of indivisible substances or of matter and form, as they claim. We shall explain this, if Allah Most High wills. Thus, the existence of the attributes does not entail the impossibility they allege; rather, they have erred in asserting this necessary connection. Whatever is unquestionably entailed, however, must be affirmed and may not be denied of Allah Most High.

Their error therefore arose from using an ambiguous expression, while one of the two premises is false—either the first or the second—as will be explained, if Allah Most High wills. These are concise, comprehensive principles, which are discussed at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 2225

Section

With this established, the questioner’s words, “How does He descend?” are like asking, “How did He rise over the Throne?” or “How does He hear? How does He see? How does He know and decree? How does He create and provide?”

The answer given by the imams of Islam to such questions has already been mentioned, including that of Mālik ibn Anas and his teacher, Rabī‘ah ibn Abī ‘Abd al-Rahmān. It has been related through several routes that someone asked Mālik about His saying:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.”

“How did He rise over it?” Mālik lowered his head until he was covered in perspiration, then said: “Rising over the Throne is known; its manner is unknown. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation. I consider you nothing but an evil man.” He then ordered that the man be removed.

A similar answer is reliably established from Rabī‘ah, Mālik’s teacher. This answer has also been narrated from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, both as her own statement and as a statement traced back to the Prophet, but its chain of transmission is not reliable.

The statements of all the other imams likewise agree with Mālik’s: we do not know the manner of His rising over the Throne, just as we do not know the manner of His essence. We do, however, know the meaning conveyed by the revealed words. Thus, we know the meaning of rising over the Throne, but not its manner. Likewise, we know the meaning of descent, but not its manner. We know the meanings of hearing, sight, knowledge, and power, but not their manner. We know the meanings of mercy, anger, pleasure, joy, and laughter, but not their manner.

---

## Page 2226

As for the questioner’s question, “Is the Throne left without Him, or not?”: if the respondent refrains from answering because he does not know what answer to give, he is refraining from answering about something whose reality he does not know. If the questioner asks this to deny what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed, he is mistaken. If he seeks guidance, that is commendable. If he seeks to expose the respondent’s ignorance, then a distinction must be made.

Someone who affirms only what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed, while disclaiming knowledge of its manner, has spoken soundly; this question cannot refute him. The objection of anyone who challenges him with this question is invalid, for it does not undermine the respondent’s answer.

The respondent’s statement, “This is an innovated statement and a newly devised opinion”—an evasion of the question—indicates that he does not know the sound answer. Yet this does not establish that the objector is right to deny what the Messenger conveyed, nor that his interpretation of the descent as the descent of Allah’s command and mercy is correct.

This is further clarified by the following: either this objector acknowledges that Allah is above the Throne, or he does not. If he does not acknowledge this, then his question, “Is the Throne left without Him, or not?” is invalid, because this division into alternatives presupposes that He is over the Throne.

If the objector says:

“I introduced this division into alternatives to deny His descent and His being above. For if he says, ‘The Throne is left without Him,’ it follows that He would no longer be rising over the Throne or above it, and that, at the time of descent, He would not be the Most High, the Highest. Rather, He would be within the world, with the world surrounding Him. If he says, ‘The Throne is not left without Him,’ he is told: ‘If the Throne is not left without Him, then He has not descended, for His descending without the Throne being left without Him is inconceivable.’”

Then this objector is told:

---

## Page 2227

This objection is invalid and does not help your case, for the existence of the Creator—glorified and exalted be He—is established by self-evident knowledge, revelation, reason, and common agreement. Either He is separate from the world and above it, or He is within the world, occupying the same space as it, or He is neither.

If you say that He occupies the same space as the world, your argument fails. For if you allow that He descends while He Himself is in every place, then, in your view, it would not be impossible for what is above the Throne to be without Him. Indeed, it is always without Him, since, according to you, nothing exists there. You are then asked: “Is it conceivable, on this account, that He is in every place and nevertheless descends to the lowest heaven?”

If you say, “Yes,” you are asked: “When He descends, are some places left without Him, or not?”

If you say, “Some places are left without Him,” this is analogous to the Throne being left without Him. If you say, “No place is left without Him,” this is analogous to the Throne not being left without Him. If you allow that no place is left without Him, your opponent may allow that the Throne is not left without Him.

Thus, your own position entails the very consequence entailed by your opponent’s. Indeed, your position is further removed from what is rationally conceivable, for the descent of One who is above the world is more readily conceivable than the descent of one who indwells the entire world. The latter’s descent is wholly inconceivable. You have fallen into the equivalent of the very indwelling you sought to avoid. Indeed, your opponent, who allows that He is above the world, that He is greater than the world, and that He descends to the world, shows greater reverence for Allah than you do.

He is also asked: “Is it conceivable that there are two independently existing entities, one occupying the same space as the other?”

If he says, “No,” his position is invalidated. If he says, “Yes,” he is told: “Then let it be conceivable that He is above the Throne and descends to the lowest heaven without the Throne being left without Him, for this is more rationally conceivable than your saying that He indwells the world.”

---

## Page 2228

If, however, you say that He is neither separate from the world nor within it, you are asked: “Can one conceive of two independently existing entities, neither of which is separate from the other nor occupies the same space as it?” Most rational people maintain that the invalidity of this is self-evident.

If he says, “Yes, that is conceivable,” he is told: If an independently existing entity can exist without being either separate from the world or occupying the same space as it, then it is more rationally conceivable that One who is separate from the world should descend to it without what is above the world being left without Him. For if you affirm the existence only of what you can conceive as having a reality outside the mind, you cannot conceive, in external reality, of two independently existing entities, neither of which is within the other nor occupies the same space as it. If, however, you affirm something whose reality outside the mind you cannot conceive, then the existence of two entities, one separate from the other, is more rationally conceivable. And His descending without what is above the Throne being left without Him is more rationally conceivable than His being neither above the world nor within it. Thus, if you judge by analogy, analogy counts against you, not for you; and if you do not judge by it, you cannot validly use it to argue against your opponent.

As for the questioner’s statement, “This does not answer my question; rather, it evades the answer,” he is told: There are “two kinds” of response: a response to an objector who denies His descent and His being above creation, and a response to someone who affirms His descent and His being above creation. You did not ask as someone seeking guidance, but as an objector intent on denial.

It has already been made clear to you that this objection is invalid and does not help your case. Whether it is said that the Throne is left without Him or that it is not left without Him, neither statement lends validity to your claim that He is neither within the world nor outside it, or to your claim that He Himself is in every place. And if

---

## Page 2229

these two claims are false, the “third” necessarily follows: that He, glorified and exalted, is above His heavens, over His Throne, separate from His creation. If that is so, the objector’s claim is invalid.

This applies if the objector does not acknowledge that He is above the Throne. One of the leading proponents of the denial of Allah’s being above creation was asked about His descent and replied, “His command descends.” The questioner said to him, “Then who descends? In your view, there is nothing above the world, so from whom does the command descend? From sheer nonexistence?” He was left speechless.

If, however, the objector affirms Allah’s being above creation and says that Allah is above the Throne, but does not acknowledge His descent, instead maintaining that an angel descends, or that His command descends—meaning the thing commanded, which is one of His created things—then he makes the descent a newly originated effect that Allah brings into being in heaven. Similar claims are made concerning His rising over the Throne.

He is then told: This same division of possibilities applies to you. If you say, “When He descends, the Throne is left without Him,” the first unacceptable consequence follows. If you say, “The Throne is not left without Him,” you have affirmed a descent without the Throne being left without Him, and this is inconceivable on your own principles.

If he says, “I affirm this only of some of His created things,” he is told: Whatever you affirm while denying a voluntary act subsisting in Him Himself cannot be understood from this statement; it cannot possibly be what is intended by it. Moreover, you have distorted words from their proper meanings. You have thus combined two things: affirming something that cannot be understood from the words of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and distorting the words of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

If you say, “The one who descends is an angel,” the reply is: This is false for several reasons:

---

## Page 2230

One is that the angels continually descend to the earth by night and by day, as Allah, exalted is He, says:

“He sends down the angels with revelation by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants.”

And He, exalted is He, says:

“We descend only by the command of your Lord.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah and Abū Sa‘īd, may Allah be pleased with them both, report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Angels take turns among you by night and by day, meeting at the dawn and afternoon prayers. Then those who spent the night among you ascend to Him, and their Lord asks them—though He knows best about them—‘How did you leave My servants?’ They reply, ‘We came to them while they were praying, and we left them while they were praying.’”

It is likewise authentically reported in the Sahīh from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has additional angels who roam about, seeking gatherings of remembrance. When they pass people remembering Allah, exalted is He, they call out, ‘Come to what you seek!’ Then they surround them with their wings up to the lowest heaven.” He said, “Their Lord asks them—though He knows best about them—‘What are My servants saying?’” He said, “They reply, ‘They glorify You, proclaim Your greatness, praise You and extol Your majesty.’”

In a version narrated by Muslim:

“Allah has angels who roam about, in addition to those who record people’s deeds, seeking gatherings of remembrance. When they find a gathering in which Allah is remembered, they sit with them and surround one another until they fill the space between them and the lowest heaven. When the people disperse, they ascend—or rise—to heaven.” He said, “Then Allah, mighty and majestic, asks them—though He knows best about them—‘Where have you come from?’ They reply, ‘We have come

---

## Page 2231

from Your servants on earth, who glorify You, proclaim Your greatness and Your oneness, praise You, and ask of You.’” The hadith continues at length.

(The second point is that he said in it:

“Who asks Me, that I may give to him? Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

These are not words that an angel may utter on Allah’s behalf. Rather, what an angel says is illustrated by the authentic report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When Allah loves a servant, He calls Gabriel: ‘I love so-and-so, so love him.’ Gabriel then loves him and calls out in heaven: ‘Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.’ The inhabitants of heaven then love him, and acceptance is granted to him on earth.”

Something similar was mentioned concerning hatred. Thus, when an angel makes a proclamation on Allah’s behalf, he does not speak in the first person. Rather, he says, “Allah has commanded such-and-such,” or, “He has said such-and-such.”

Likewise, when a ruler commands a herald to make a proclamation, the herald says, “O people! The ruler has commanded such-and-such, forbidden such-and-such, and decreed this.” He does not say, “I have commanded such-and-such and forbidden such-and-such.” Indeed, were he to say that, he would promptly be punished.

This is one of the Jahmiyyah’s longstanding interpretations. They interpreted Allah’s speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, to mean that He commanded an angel to speak to him. The people of the Sunnah replied to them: Had an angel spoken to him, he would not have said:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

Rather, he would have spoken as the Messiah, peace be upon him, did:

“I told them only what You commanded me: ‘Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.’”

The angels are Allah’s messengers to the prophets. They speak as Gabriel, peace be upon him, used to speak

---

## Page 2232

to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“We descend only by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs whatever is before us, whatever is behind us, and whatever lies between.”

He would say, “Allah commands you to do such-and-such, and says such-and-such.” No angel can say:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

Nor can he say:

“Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who asks Me, that I may give to him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

Nor can he say, “No one but Me asks about My servants,” as reported by al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Mājah, and others. Both al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah transmit it with an authentic chain, stating that He says:

“I do not ask anyone else about My servants.”

This also refutes the argument advanced by someone who cited a version transmitted by al-Nasā’ī through one of the hadith’s chains, stating that He commands a herald to make a proclamation. If this is authentically established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then the Lord says those words and commands a herald to proclaim accordingly; it does not mean that the herald says, “Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him?” Whoever reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that the herald says this, we know that he is lying about the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Besides contradicting the widely disseminated, mass-transmitted wording that the Muslim community has passed down from generation to generation, this is rationally untenable. It is therefore known to be one of the falsehoods fabricated by certain proponents of religious innovation—just as some of them narrated it as yunzilu (“He causes to descend”), with an initial u-vowel, and just as some of them recited, “And Allah spoke directly to Moses,” and other such distortions of both wording and meaning.

If someone interprets this as the descent of His mercy, or something else, he is told: The mercy you affirm must be either a self-subsisting entity or an attribute subsisting in something else.

---

## Page 2233

If it is a self-subsisting entity that has descended to the lowest heaven, it cannot say, “Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him?”—just as an angel cannot say this. If it is an attribute, it does not subsist independently; rather, it must subsist in something. Moreover, neither the attribute nor that in which it subsists can speak these words. Furthermore, if mercy descends to the lowest heaven but does not descend to us, what benefit do we derive from that?

If he says:

“Rather, mercy is what He sends down at that hour upon the hearts of those who stand in prayer at night: the sweetness of intimate prayer and worship, the delight of supplication and knowledge, the increase in knowledge of Allah, faith in Him and remembrance of Him that arises in their hearts, and His manifestation to the hearts of His devoted servants. This is something familiar to those who stand in prayer at night.”

He is told: That these things arise in their hearts is true. However, this descends to earth, to the hearts of His servants; it does not descend to the lowest heaven, nor does it ascend after descending. What is found in their hearts remains after dawn. Yet this light, blessing and mercy within their hearts are effects of what He has described concerning Himself: that He Himself descends—glorified and exalted is He.

Likewise, He has described Himself as “descending on the afternoon of the Day of ‘Arafah” in several authentic hadiths. Among them is the report in Sahīh Muslim from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is no day on which Allah frees more servants from the Fire than the Day of ‘Arafah. He, mighty and majestic, draws near, then boasts of them before the angels, saying, ‘What do these people seek?’”

Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“On the Day of ‘Arafah, Allah descends to the lowest heaven and boasts of the people of ‘Arafah before the angels, saying, ‘Look at My servants: they have come to Me dishevelled and dusty

---

## Page 2234

, exposed to the sun, from every distant pass.’”

Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah descends to the lowest heaven and boasts of the people of ‘Arafah before the angels, saying, ‘Look at My servants: they have come to Me dishevelled and dusty.’”

Thus, He is described as drawing near to the lowest heaven on the afternoon of ‘Arafah and boasting of the pilgrims before the angels, saying, “Look at My servants: they have come to Me dishevelled and dusty. What do these people seek?” It is well known that faith, mercy, light and blessing descend upon the pilgrims’ hearts on the afternoon of ‘Arafah to an extent beyond expression. Yet what is in their hearts is not what draws near to the lowest heaven and boasts of the pilgrims before the angels.

The Jahmiyyah and others like them who deny the divine attributes affirm only something created without a Creator, an effect without a cause, and something done without a doer. This is well known from their fundamental principles, and this is one of the implications of the Jahmiyyah’s doctrines.

He may also be told: His description of Himself as descending is like His descriptions in the Quran: that He

“created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne”;

that He turned to the heaven while it was smoke; that He called to Moses and spoke privately with him in the blessed spot, from the tree; and that He comes, as He says:

“And your Lord comes, with the angels, rank upon rank.”

He also says:

“Are they waiting for anything but for the angels to come to them, or for your Lord to come, or for some of your Lord’s signs to come?”

There are many mass-transmitted hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the Lord’s coming on the Day of Resurrection, and likewise His coming to the people of Paradise on Friday. This is among the evidence the early generations cited against those who denied the hadith: they explained that the Quran confirms the meaning of this hadith, just as it was cited by Ishāq

---

## Page 2235

ibn Rāhawayh against some of the Jahmiyyah in the presence of the emir ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir, the governor of Khurāsān.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Ribātī said:

“One day I attended the gathering of the emir ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir. Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh was also present and was asked whether the hadith concerning the descent was authentic. He replied, ‘Yes.’ One of ‘Abd Allāh’s commanders asked him, ‘Abū Ya‘qūb, do you maintain that Allah descends every night?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ The man asked, ‘How does He descend?’ Ishāq said, ‘Affirm that He is above, and then I will describe His descent to you.’ The man replied, ‘I affirm that He is above.’ Ishāq then said to him, ‘Allah Most High says: “And your Lord comes, with the angels, rank upon rank.”’

“The emir ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir said, ‘Abū Ya‘qūb, that is on the Day of Resurrection.’ Ishāq replied, ‘May Allah honour the emir! Who can prevent the One who comes on the Day of Resurrection from coming today?’”

Then there is the further question: when He descends, is the Throne left without Him or not? “This is a separate issue.” Those who affirm the divine attributes have discussed it. Some said that the Throne is not left without Him. This position has been transmitted from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal in his letter to Musaddad, and from Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Hammād ibn Zayd, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī and others.

Others rejected this and challenged the authenticity of the letter, saying, “The person who transmitted it from Ahmad ibn Hanbal is unknown and unrecognized.” The first position, however, is well known among such imams as Hammād ibn Zayd and Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh

## Page 2236

and others. Al-Khallāl said in Kitāb al-Sunnah (The Book of the Sunnah):

Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-Firyābī narrated to us: Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Muqaddamī narrated to us: Sulaymān ibn Harb narrated to us, saying:

Bishr ibn al-Sarī asked Hammād ibn Zayd, “Abū Ismā‘īl, concerning the reported hadith, ‘Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven’—does He move from one place to another?” Hammād ibn Zayd remained silent, then said, “He is in His place and draws near to His creation however He wills.”

Ibn Battah also transmitted it in his book al-Ibānah (The Elucidation), saying:

Abū al-Qāsim Hafs ibn ‘Umar al-Ardabīlī narrated to me: Abū Hātim al-Rāzī narrated to us: Sulaymān ibn Harb narrated to us, saying:

Bishr ibn al-Sarī asked Hammād ibn Zayd, “Abū Ismā‘īl, concerning the reported hadith, ‘Allah descends to the lowest heaven’—does He move from one place to another?” Hammād ibn Zayd remained silent, then said, “He is in His place and draws near to His creation however He wills.”

Ibn Battah also said:

Abū Bakr al-Najjād narrated to us: Ahmad ibn ‘Alī al-Abbār narrated to us: ‘Alī ibn Khashram narrated to us, saying: Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh said:

I went in to see ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir, who asked, “What are these hadiths that you narrate?”

I replied, “Which ones, may Allah set the emir’s affairs aright?”

He said, “You narrate that Allah descends to the lowest heaven.”

I replied, “Yes. They were transmitted by the trustworthy narrators who transmit hadiths concerning legal rulings.”

He asked, “Does He descend and leave His Throne?”

I replied, “He is able to descend without the Throne being left without Him.”

He said, “Yes.”

I said, “Then why do you raise this question?”

Al-Lakā’ī also transmitted it through a disconnected chain of transmission, with wording different from this. This chain is sounder. Both this account and the preceding one are authentic, and their transmitters are trustworthy imams.

Thus Hammād ibn Zayd says, “He is in His place and draws near to His creation however He wills,” thereby affirming His nearness to His creation together with

---

## Page 2237

His being above His Throne. ‘Abd Allāh ibn Tāhir—one of the finest men to govern Khurāsān—knew that Allah is above the Throne, but found His descent difficult to understand because he imagined that it required the Throne to be left without Him. Imam Ishāq affirmed his understanding that Allah is above the Throne and asked him, “Can He descend without the Throne being left without Him?”

The emir replied, “Yes.” Ishāq then asked him, “Why, then, do you raise this question?”

His point was that, if Allah is able to do this, His descent does not necessarily leave the Throne without Him. It is therefore impermissible to object to His descent on the grounds that it necessarily leaves the Throne without Him. This objection was less serious than that of someone who says, “There is nothing above the Throne,” thereby denying both His being above it and His descent.

A similar account was narrated by Abū Bakr al-Athram in al-Sunnah (The Sunnah). He said:

Ibrāhīm ibn al-Hārith—meaning al-‘Abbādī—narrated to us: Al-Layth ibn Yahyā narrated to me, saying: I heard Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ash‘ath say: I heard al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād say, “If a Jahmī says, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who moves from His place,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’”

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, may Allah have mercy on him, intended to oppose the Jahmī who says that no acts performed by choice subsist in Allah, so that no approach, coming, descent, rising, or any other acts performed by choice and subsisting in Him can be conceived of Him.

Al-Fudayl therefore said, “If a Jahmī says to you, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who moves from His place,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’” He thus instructed him to believe in the Lord who performs whatever acts He wills that subsist in His own Being. He did not mean the things He brings into being that are separate from Him. Similar statements are reported from al-Awzā‘ī and others among the early generations: concerning the hadith of descent, they said, “Allah does whatever He wills.”

Al-Lālakā’ī said:

Al-Musayyar ibn ‘Uthmān narrated to us: We were told by

---

## Page 2238

Ahmad ibn al-Husayn: Ahmad ibn ‘Alī al-Abbār narrated to us, saying: I heard Yahyā ibn Ma‘īn say, “If you hear a Jahmī say, ‘I disbelieve in a Lord who descends,’ say, ‘I believe in a Lord who does whatever He wills.’”

For some who revere these authorities but deny that acts performed by choice subsist in Him—such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr and his followers, Ibn ‘Aqīl, al-Qādī ‘Iyād, and others—construe their words, “He does whatever He wills,” as meaning that He brings into being something separate from Himself, without any act whatsoever subsisting in Him.

This interpretation follows necessarily from two principles they hold:

(The first is that, in their view, the act is identical to what it produces, and creation is identical to the created thing. Thus, they interpret His transitive acts, as in His saying, “He created the heavens and the earth,” and similar statements, to mean that these things came into existence through His power, without any act proceeding from Him and subsisting in His own Being. Rather, His state before creating and after creating is the same. In their view, nothing new has arisen except a relation and a connection, which is something non-existent, not existent.

They say the same concerning His hearing His servants’ voices and seeing their deeds, His having spoken to Moses and others, His having sent down the Quran or abrogated whatever He abrogated of it, and other such matters. In their view, nothing new has arisen except a mere “connection” and “relation” between the Creator and the created, which is something non-existent, not existent.

They likewise say this concerning His rising over the Throne, if they affirm that He is above the Throne. This is the position of Ibn ‘Aqīl and others, and it was the earlier of al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā’s two positions. Ibn ‘Aqīl calls this “connection” states; perhaps he likens it to the “states” affirmed by those speculative thinkers who affirm them

---

## Page 2239

and say that these states are neither existent nor nonexistent, as maintained by Abū Hāshim, the two qādīs—Abū Bakr and Abū Ya‘lā—and Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī in the earlier of his two positions.

Most people disagreed with them on this principle and affirmed that He, Most High, performs an act subsisting in His own Being, and that creation is distinct from the created thing—this is called “bringing into being.” This is the position of the early Kullābīs, as stated by al-Thaqafī, al-Duba‘ī, and other companions of Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Khuzayma in the creed they wrote and read to Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzayma when the dispute concerning “the question of the Quran” arose among them. This was also the later of al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā’s two positions, and is the position of the majority of Hanafīs and Hanbalīs and the leading scholars of the Mālikī and Shāfi‘ī schools. It is what al-Baghawī reported from Ahl al-Sunnah in Sharh al-Sunnah, and what al-Bukhārī reported as the consensus of the scholars, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The “second principle” is their denial that matters connected with His power and will can subsist in Him. They call this “the inherence of temporal events.” Since they denied this, they deemed it impossible for any act performed by choice through His power and will to subsist in Him, whether intransitive or transitive: neither descending, coming, rising over the Throne, approaching, creating, giving life, causing death, nor anything else of this kind.

For this reason, they interpreted the early scholars’ statement concerning the descent—that “He does whatever He wills”—as meaning that a created thing separate from Him comes into being. Yet the early scholars’ words explicitly show that this was not what they meant. Rather, they meant an act performed by choice that subsists in Him.

---

## Page 2240

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād—may Allah have mercy on him—did not mean that the Throne is left without Him; rather, he intended to oppose the Jahmiyyah. His statement, “He does whatever He wills,” does not entail that He must be beneath the Throne. Rather, his words are of the same kind as those of his peers among the early scholars, such as al-Awzā‘ī, Hammād ibn Zayd, and others.

Some of them rejected what is reported from Ahmad in his letter to Musaddad, saying: “Its transmitter from Ahmad is unknown; no one named Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barda‘ī is known among Ahmad’s companions.”

The scholars of hadith hold three positions on this matter. Some reject saying either that the Throne is left without Him or that it is not. This is the position of the hadith master ‘Abd al-Ghanī al-Maqdisī and others.

Others say that the Throne is indeed left without Him. Abū al-Qāsim ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn Mandah wrote a work refuting those who say that the Throne is not left without Him. He entitled it “A Refutation of Those Who Claim That Allah Is Everywhere, Those Who Claim That Allah Has No Place, and Those Who Interpret the Descent as Something Other Than Descent.”

He mentioned that he had been asked about a report recorded by Abū Sa‘īd al-Naqqāsh in “Statements of Ahl al-Sunnah,” from Abū al-Hasan Muhammad ibn ‘Alī al-Marwazī, from Muhammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Dīnawarī, from ‘Alī ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Mūsā, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barda‘ī al-Tamīmī, who said: “When Musaddad ibn Musarhad became uncertain about the Sunnah and the controversies into which people had fallen concerning ‘predestination’
