## Page 2271

the same about the claim made by some philosophers: “The celestial sphere is eternal and without beginning, yet He originated it by His power and will.”

The majority of people of sound reason say that any particular thing, whether an entity or an attribute, cannot be eternal without beginning if it comes about through the Lord’s will and power.

It was a principle of Ibn Kullāb and those who agreed with him—such as al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, the judges Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, Abū Ya‘lā ibn al-Farrā’, Abū Ja‘far al-Sammānī, and Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, and other prominent figures, such as Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī and those like him, as well as Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl, Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, and those like them—that nothing which comes about through the Lord’s will and power subsists in Him. They express this by saying that temporally originated events do not subsist in Him. In this they agreed with Jahm ibn Safwān and his followers among the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah. Consequently, they adopted one of two positions concerning the Lord’s attributes mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah: either they regard them all as created things separate from Him.

Thus they say: “Allah’s speech is created and separate from Him; no speech subsists in Him.” Likewise, His pleasure, anger, joy, coming, arrival, descent, and everything else of this kind are created and separate from Him. In their view, the Lord is not characterized by anything subsisting in Him.

When they say that these things are attributes of action, they mean that they are separate and distinct from Allah and are attributed to Him—not that they are attributes subsisting in Him.

---

## Page 2272

For this reason, many of them say: “These are verses of attribution and hadiths of attribution,” and object to anyone calling them verses and hadiths concerning the attributes.

Or else they regard all these meanings as eternal and without beginning. They say: “His descent, coming, arrival, joy, anger, pleasure, and the like are eternal and without beginning,” just as they say that the Quran is eternal and without beginning. Some of them regard it as a single meaning, while others regard it as letters, or letters and sounds, eternal and without beginning, despite its being internally ordered. They say: “There is a distinction between the ordering of its existence and the ordering of its essence.” We have discussed these matters at length elsewhere, examining these views, those who hold them, and their scriptural and rational proofs.

The point here is that none of these views is the position of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the Muslim imams renowned for their leadership—the imams of the Sunnah and the community, and the scholars of hadith—such as al-Awzāʿī, Mālik ibn Anas, Hammād ibn Zayd, Hammād ibn Salamah, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and others like them.

Rather, the statements of the early generations—the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the imams of religion and Muslim scholars who followed their path—are preserved in books that transmit their exact words through well-known chains of transmission from them. These can be found in many books, such as The Sunnah and Refutation of the Jahmiyyah

---

## Page 2273

by Muhammad ibn Abd Allāh al-Juʿfī, al-Bukhārī’s teacher; and by Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī, Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Bakr al-Athram, Hanbal ibn Ishāq, Harb al-Kirmānī, Uthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī, Nuʿaym ibn Hammād al-Khuzāʿī, Abū Bakr al-Khallāl, Abū Bakr ibn Khuzaymah, Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Hātim, Abū al-Qāsim al-Tabarānī, Abū al-Shaykh al-Asbahānī, Abū Abd Allāh ibn Mandah, Abū Amr al-Talamankī, and Abū Umar ibn Abd al-Barr.

A substantial body of this material also appears in Quran commentaries that transmit reports with their chains of transmission, such as the commentaries of Abd al-Razzāq, Abd ibn Humayd, Duhaym, Sunayd, Ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī, Abū Bakr ibn al-Mundhir, and Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Hātim, as well as other commentaries that convey the exact words of the Companions and their Successors concerning the meanings of the Quran through well-known chains of transmission.

Understanding what the Messenger and the Companions intended is the foundation of knowledge and the wellspring of guidance. Yet many who describe and report the position of the early generations have no familiarity with any of this material. For example, they suppose that the position of the early generations concerning the verses and hadiths about the divine attributes is that no one understands their meanings—neither the Messenger nor anyone else. They suppose that this is the meaning of His words:

“And no one knows its interpretation except Allah.”

They also argue for stopping at this point in the recitation. Thus, they portray the position of the early generations as being that the Messenger conveyed a Quran whose meaning cannot be understood, and, moreover, that he spoke the hadiths concerning the divine attributes without understanding their meaning himself; that Gabriel was likewise, and that the Companions and their Successors were likewise.

---

## Page 2274

This is grave misguidance, one of the forms of error concerning the words of Allah and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. These include the assumptions of those who advocate imaginative representation, those who distort and alter the texts, and those who attribute ignorance of their meanings. This has been discussed at length elsewhere. May Allah guide us and all our brothers to His straight path, the path of those He has blessed among the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

The purpose here is to discuss those who say that He descends without the Throne becoming empty of Him. The hadith scholars hold three positions on this issue. Some reject saying either that the Throne becomes empty of Him or that it does not. This is the position of the hadith master Abd al-Ghanī and others.

Others say that the Throne does indeed become empty of Him. Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mandah wrote a work refuting those who say, “He does not leave the Throne,” or, “The Throne does not become empty of Him”—some of his words have already been quoted. Many hadith scholars refrain from saying whether it becomes empty of Him or not. Most of them, however, hold that the Throne does not become empty of Him.

Many refrain from saying whether it becomes empty of Him or not because they are uncertain about this and neither answer has become clear to them. Alternatively, even when one of them finds one of the two positions more convincing, he refrains from speaking on the matter because it is not stated in the hadith

---

## Page 2275

and because he fears being censured for it. As for categorically asserting that the Throne becomes empty of Him, this has reached us from only a small group among them. The third position—which is correct and is transmitted from the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars—is that He remains above the Throne, and the Throne does not become empty of Him, even as He draws near and descends to the lowest heaven; the Throne is not above Him. The same applies on the Day of Resurrection, as stated in the Book and the Sunnah. His descent is not like the bodily descent of human beings from a rooftop to the ground, leaving the roof above them. Rather, Allah is exalted above that. We shall discuss this, Allah willing; this issue requires an extensive explanation.

As for the claim of one who denies His descent, “Only His command and His mercy descend,” this is erroneous for several reasons. This has already been pointed out on the assumption that those who deny His descent nevertheless affirm His being above. If, however, someone denies both His being above and His descent, he may also be answered in several ways:

(First: “Command” and “mercy” must mean either entities subsisting in their own right, such as angels, or attributes and accidents. If the former is intended, angels descend to the earth at all times, whereas the hadith specifies descent in the depth of the night and makes the lowest heaven its endpoint. The angels’ descent is restricted neither to this time nor to this place. If attributes and accidents are intended—such as the tenderness, humble entreaty, sweetness of worship, and the like that arise in worshippers’ hearts in the hours before dawn—these occur on earth; their endpoint is not the lowest heaven.

---

## Page 2276

Second: The authentic hadith states:

“He descends to the lowest heaven, then says, ‘I ask no one else about My servants.’”

It is well known that these are Allah’s words, which no one else can say.

Third: He said:

“He descends to the lowest heaven and says, ‘Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will ask of Me, that I may give him? Who will seek My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?’—until dawn breaks.”

It is well known that none but Allah answers supplications, forgives sins, and grants every petitioner what he asks. His command and His mercy do none of these things.

Fourth: His command and His mercy can only descend from Him. This therefore requires that He be above the world, so the very interpretation he advances invalidates his own position. Thus, one of those who deny this said to someone who affirms it, “His command and His mercy descend.” The latter replied, “From whom, then, do they descend? According to you, there is nothing above, so neither command nor mercy nor anything else can descend from Him.” The denier was confounded, although he was a leading figure among them.

(Fifth: Several hadiths contain the wording, “Then He ascends,” and another wording states, “Then He rises.”

Sixth: If it were supposed that the one descending is an angel who calls out on Allah’s behalf—as some have distorted the wording of the hadith, reporting it as “yunzilu” (“He sends down”), using the transitive Form IV verb, meaning that He commands a herald to call out—then the angel would have had to say, “Who will call upon Allah, that He may answer him? Who will ask of Him, that He may give him? Who will seek His forgiveness, that He may forgive him?” This is as established in the two Sahīh collections and the Muwatta’ of

---

## Page 2277

Mālik, the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other works, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When Allah loves a servant, He calls out in heaven, ‘O Gabriel, I love so-and-so, so love him.’ Gabriel then loves him. Then Gabriel calls out, ‘Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.’ The inhabitants of heaven then love him, and he is granted acceptance on earth.”

He said something similar concerning hatred.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, thus clarified the difference between Allah’s call and Gabriel’s call. Concerning Allah’s call, he said:

“O Gabriel, I love so-and-so, so love him.”

Concerning Gabriel’s call, he said:

“Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.”

This is what the language in which we have been addressed requires—indeed, what all languages require. The first-person pronoun is used only by the speaker himself, whereas someone speaking about another uses that person’s name and third-person pronouns.

They liken Allah’s call to a ruler’s proclamation, saying, “One may say, ‘The ruler proclaimed,’ when he commanded someone else to make the proclamation.” This is like what the thoroughgoing Jahmiyyah said concerning Allah’s speaking to Moses: “He commanded someone else to speak to him; He Himself was not the speaker.”

They should be told: When a ruler commands someone else to make a proclamation, speak to another person, or address him, the herald calls out, “O people! The ruler has commanded such-and-such,” or “has decreed such-and-such.” He does not say, “I myself have commanded you to do that.” Were he to say this, people would treat him with contempt and say, “Who are you to command us?”

Yet the One who calls out every night says:

“Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will ask of Me, that I may give him? Who will seek My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

This is just as in His call

---

## Page 2278

to Moses, peace be upon him:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

And He said:

“I am Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

It is clear that if Allah commanded an angel to call out every night, or to call out to Moses, the angel would not say:

“Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will ask of Me, that I may give him? Who will seek My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

Nor would he say:

“I ask no one other than Myself about My servants.”

As for the objection that night begins earlier or later and varies in length according to the land and the season, the response is this: The answer is the same as the answer to your question, “Does the Throne become vacant of Him, or not?” If it is possible for Him to descend without the Throne becoming vacant of Him, the same applies to His descent occurring earlier or later and lasting longer or shorter, since this descent cannot be measured against the descent of created beings.

In sum, questions of this kind may be answered in several ways.

(First: to show that the disputant who denies this is committed to implications even further removed from what he himself acknowledges to be rational than those entailed by the position of one who affirms it. If the rational argument invoked is sound, the denial must be false, and affirmation must therefore follow, since the truth cannot lie outside two contradictory propositions. If the argument is invalid, it does not invalidate affirmation and thus cannot counter what is established by innate reason and the prophetic law.

An example is someone saying, “If He were above the Throne, He would be a body, and that is impossible.”

He is told: There are three positions on this matter:

---

## Page 2279

Some say: “He is above the Throne and is not a body.”

Others say: “He is above the Throne and is a body.”

Still others say: “He is above the Throne, but I say neither that He is a body nor that He is not a body.” Among this last group, some refrain from either denial or affirmation because both are innovations in religion. Others seek clarification of what is meant by “body.” If it is explained as something from which the Lord must be declared free, they deny it and explain that His being above the Throne does not entail it. If it is explained as something that does describe the Lord, they do not deny that meaning.

In ordinary Arabic, “body” means the bodily frame, and Allah is exalted above that. Speculative theologians may use “body” to mean something composed of indivisible atoms or of matter and form. Many of them dispute that created bodies are composed of either of these. Indeed, most rational people hold that the heavens are composed neither of indivisible atoms nor of matter and form. How, then, could the Lord of all worlds be composed of either?

Whoever says, “Allah is a body,” and means by “body” a composite of this kind is mistaken. Whoever intends to deny such composition of Allah is correct in denying it of Him, but should use wording that makes his meaning clear. The term “composition” may mean that something was assembled by someone, that its parts were separate and then came together, or that it can be taken apart. Allah is exalted above all of this.

---

## Page 2280

The terms “body” and “that which occupies space” may also mean something that can be pointed towards, in the sense that hands are raised towards it in supplication and that it can be said to be here or there. They may also mean something self-subsisting, or simply something that exists. There is no doubt that Allah exists and is self-subsisting. According to the early generations and Ahl al-Sunnah, hands are raised towards Him in supplication, and He is above the Throne. If someone calls whatever possesses these characteristics a “body,” this is like someone else calling whatever is living, knowing and powerful a “body,” or another calling whatever possesses life, knowledge and power a “body.”

It is well known that all these usages are contested on three grounds:

First: calling whatever possesses these attributes a “body” is an innovation both in religious usage and in the language. The authorities on the language do not call this a “body”; rather, for them, the term means the bodily frame, as several leading lexicographers have reported and as is well known from the dictionaries. Al-Jawharī says in his well-known Sihāh:

“Abū Zayd said: ‘Al-jism means the body, as do al-jusmān and al-juthmān.’ Al-Asma‘ī said: ‘Al-jism and al-juthmān mean the body, and al-juthmān means the person.’ He said: ‘Al-ajsam means larger in bodily build.’ Ibn al-Sikkīt said: ‘Tajassamtu al-amr means that I undertook its greatest and most substantial part—that is, its main part.’ He said: ‘Likewise, tajassamtu al-rajul wa-l-jabal means that I took on the man or the mountain at its largest part.’”

Allah mentions the term “body” in two places in the Quran. He, Exalted is He, says:

“and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature”

and:

“When you see them, their bodies impress you.”

“Body” may also be understood as an attribute inhering in something, namely its size and thickness, as when one says: “This garment

---

## Page 2281

has body, whereas this one does not”—that is, it has thickness and bulk, unlike the other. “Body” may also mean thickness and bulk themselves.

Certain groups among the speculative theologians who espouse negation have claimed that, in ordinary language, a body is something compounded and composite, and that their use of the term “body” for everything that can be pointed towards accords with linguistic usage. They say:

“Anything that can be pointed towards has one part distinguishable from another. Whatever is like this is composed either of individual atoms, each of which is an indivisible part with no side distinguishable from another, or of matter and form, which are two intelligible substances, as some philosophers maintain.”

They say:

“If, then, such a thing is composite and compounded, a body in the Arabic language is something compounded and composite. The evidence is that the Arabs say ‘a large-bodied man’ and ‘Zayd is larger-bodied than ‘Amr’ when his extension in the various directions is greater. By the intensive force of ‘larger-bodied’ and ‘large-bodied,’ they mean only the greater number of parts joined together and their composition. For they do not say ‘larger-bodied’ of someone because his knowledge, standing, or other activities and attributes have increased, apart from aggregation. Only when the aggregation in him increases through an increase in his parts do they say ‘larger-bodied’ or ‘a large-bodied man.’ This shows that their expression jassama (‘to make into a body’) conveys composition.”

This is the basis of the position of these proponents of negation. It rests on two premises: one based on transmitted linguistic usage, and the other on rational reflection and innate understanding. As for the premise based on transmitted linguistic usage, it is their claim that speakers of the language apply the term “body” to what is composite

---

## Page 2282

and they cite as evidence the expression “He is larger-bodied,” used when someone is thicker and extends farther in the various directions, arguing that this implies that they took the greater number of parts into account.

The reply is as follows:

As for the “first premise”—that speakers of the language call everything possessing a magnitude, such that it can be larger or smaller than something else, a body—this usage is entirely absent from the Arabic language. No one can report that the Arabs call the air between heaven and earth a body, nor do they call the human spirit a body. Rather, it is well known that they distinguish between body and spirit. Hence the Exalted says:

“When you see them, their bodies impress you.”

This means their physical bodies, not their inner spirits. Lexicographers have stated that, in their usage, jism (body) means jasad (physical body).

It is also well established in the language that this word conveys thickness and density. Thus, they do not call independently existing things bodies when they are subtle, such as air and the human spirit, even though these possess a magnitude by which some may be larger than others. Such things are nevertheless not called bodies in the language. Nor, when one exceeds another in size, do they say, “This is larger-bodied than that.” They do not say, “This spacious place is larger-bodied than that narrow place,” even though it is larger and—even according to those who hold that it is composed of parts—its parts outnumber those of the other. Thus, not everything that, in their view, is composed of parts is called a body. Nor does one find in their speech the expressions “He took his body,” or “He ascended with his body to heaven,” or that Allah takes

---

## Page 2283

our bodies wherever He wills and returns them wherever He wills. Rather, they call that a spirit, distinguishing what is meant by “spirit” from what is meant by “body,” just as they distinguish between bodily frame and spirit, and between physical body and spirit. They do not apply the word jism (body) to air. In their usage, jism resembles jasad (physical body).

Al-Jawharī said:

“Jasad means badan (body). Its corresponding verb is tajassada (to take bodily form), just as tajassama is the corresponding verb for jism.”

As previously quoted from the leading lexicographers, jism means jasad. Thus, these two words are synonymous, or nearly so. Hence, they speak of a fabric as having jasad (body), just as they speak of it as having jism (body), when it is thick, substantial, and closely woven. Scholars say that an impurity may have a substantial physical form, as with blood and carrion, or may lack such a form, as with moisture. They also call blood jasad, as al-Nābigha said:

“No, by the life of Him whom I have visited year after year,
And by the blood poured out upon the sacrificial stones.”

Likewise, they say that it has jism (body). This disproves their claim concerning linguistic usage: that people call anything in which one part can be distinguished from another a body.

As for the “second premise”: even if that were conceded, their claim that people apply the expression “This is a body” when the number of parts increases rests on the view that bodies are composed of indivisible atoms. Even supposing this were true, speakers of the language did not take it into account, nor did any of them say such a thing. It is therefore clear that they considered only its thickness and density.

As for their supposedly taking into account whether the parts are more or fewer, this is something not conceived of by

---

## Page 2284

most rational human beings, let alone something that all speakers of the language can be reported to have intended by the words jasīm (large-bodied) and ajsam (larger-bodied). A word’s commonly understood meaning cannot refer to something understood by only a few people. Belief in indivisible atoms is confined to certain people; hence, the word “body” in ordinary language cannot designate something known only to certain people—namely, a composite of such atoms.

As for the “second rational principle,” it is their assertion that anything one can point to as being here or there must be composed either of indivisible atoms or of matter and form. This is a question for rational investigation. Most rational human beings—both speculative theologians and others—deny that such things are composed of indivisible atoms or of matter and form. This denial is the position of Ibn Kullāb and his followers, the Kullābiyya—he was the authority whom al-Ashʿarī followed in matters concerning the divine attributes. It is also the position of the Hishāmiyya, the Najjāriyya, the Dirāriyya, and some of the Karrāmiyya.

Those who affirmed the “indivisible atom” claimed that neither through sensory perception nor through self-evident knowledge do we know that Allah has brought into existence anything subsisting in itself. They further claimed that everything we witness being created—clouds, rain, animals, plants, minerals, human beings, and other beings—involves no more than His producing states in indivisible atoms, such as aggregation, separation, motion, and rest. They denied that, when Allah created us, He brought our bodies into existence as entities subsisting in themselves, or brought into existence trees, fruit, or anything else subsisting in itself. According to them, He produced only accidents. As for the indivisible atoms, they had existed all along.

Then, among those who hold that these atoms came into existence, some say that they knew this because the atoms have never been free of events that begin to exist, and whatever has never been free of such events must itself have begun to exist.

---

## Page 2285

They said: “Through this ‘rational proof’ and others like it, we have learned that He has not originated anything subsisting in itself; for what we witness is the inherence of observable events, such as clouds and rain.”

Their discussion of “bodily resurrection” rests on this principle. Some say that He separates the constituent parts and then gathers them together. Others say that He annihilates them and then restores them to existence. Here they became confused over how resurrection would occur when one animal has eaten another. Some claimed that Allah annihilates all the constituent parts of the world. Others say: “This is possible, but we do not know whether or not it occurs.” According to them, “resurrection” then requires Him to originate these atoms anew.

Jahm ibn Safwān, who is one of them, maintains that they will cease to exist thereafter, and that Paradise and Hell will perish, because he considers an unending succession of events in the future impossible, just as he considers it impossible in the past. Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf maintains that motions will cease.

These people deny that bodies can be transformed into one another, or that one kind can turn into another. Rather, according to them, atoms are identical in nature, and bodies are composed of them. There is nothing beyond a change in composition: no conversion or transformation takes place. Undoubtedly, most rational people, Muslims and others, reject this. Physicians and jurists are among those who affirm that bodies can be transformed into one another, as is found in their books. In their view, bodies are not identical in nature: water differs from air, air differs from earth, and human bodies differ from plants.

Thus, according to those who deny the divine attributes, whenever someone affirms any attribute, this necessarily makes the being possessing it a body—and, in their view, bodies are identical in nature. They therefore label such a person someone who likens Allah to created beings, on the basis of these premises, which commit them to the like of

---

## Page 2286

what they impute to others. These premises are contradictory: no sound argument can conceivably be constructed from them. All are rejected by the great majority of rational people. They contain distortions of language and reason introduced through these fallacies and specious arguments, leaving a man bewildered. He finds it hard to set aside his reason and religion and abandon faith and the Quran, for all of these concur in affirming the divine attributes. Yet he also finds it hard to accept what they insist his position entails: that the Lord is composed of parts and resembles created beings. He knows that this, too, is false, and that the Lord, mighty and majestic, must be declared free of it. For He, glorified is He, is the One, the Self-Sufficient Master. “The One” excludes any likeness to Him, while “the Self-Sufficient Master” excludes His being susceptible to separation, division, or having parts—glorified and exalted is He—let alone His being something assembled and composed: put together and assembled from parts.

Thus they lead those they address to believe that the attributes with which the Lord has described Himself are conceivable only in a body like the human body. Indeed, they may state this explicitly, saying, “Speech can only proceed from a composite structure, such as the human mouth,” and making other such claims.

When “the deniers” tell them, “Whenever you say that He can be seen, it follows that He is composed and assembled, because whatever is seen must lie in some direction from the beholder; whatever lies in some direction from the beholder must be a body; and a body is assembled and composed of parts”; or say, “If the Lord has spoken the Quran or any other speech, this necessarily follows; and if He is above the Throne, this necessarily follows”—the Muslim acquainted with what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said knows that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter, on the basis of the mass-transmitted reports to that effect that have reached him from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

---

## Page 2287

and likewise knows that Allah has spoken the Quran and other speech, and knows that Allah is above the Throne, through the mass-transmitted reports from the Messenger indicating this, together with the corresponding innate truths upon which Allah created His servants.

When they tell him, “This entails that Allah is composed of discrete parts, and whatever is composed must have someone who composes it. It therefore follows that Allah is brought into existence, since a composite depends upon its parts, and its parts are other than itself. Whatever depends upon something other than itself cannot be self-sufficient and necessarily existent in itself”—they bewilder him and fill him with doubts, if they do not actually cause him to reject what the Messenger brought and renounce some of the faith he previously held. Yet his doubt and bewilderment themselves undermine his faith, religion, knowledge, and reason.

They should therefore be told:

As for the claim that the Lord, glorified and exalted is He, is a composite assembled by another, this is among the most obviously false claims. Its falsity is known by rational necessity. Whoever says this is among the most disbelieving and ignorant of people, and among those most fiercely at war with Allah. None of the well-known groups holds this view.

Likewise, if He is said to be assembled or composed—meaning that His parts were once separate and were then brought together, just as the components of compound foods, medicines, garments, and buildings are brought together—then whoever believes that Allah is composed in this sense is among the most disbelieving and misguided of people. No well-known group within the Muslim community has held this belief. Indeed, most rational people hold that the creatures of

---

## Page 2288

the Lord are not composed in this way. Only those who affirm indivisible atoms maintain this.

Likewise, whoever claims that the Lord is assembled and composed, meaning that He is susceptible to separation, division, and partition, is among the most disbelieving and ignorant of people. His view is worse than that of those who say that Allah has a child, meaning that a part separated from Him and became His child. We have discussed this at length in the commentary on “Say, ‘He is Allah, One,’” and elsewhere.

Likewise, if He is said to be a body, meaning that He is composed of indivisible atoms or of matter and form, this is false. Indeed, it is false even of created things, so how much more so of the Creator, glorified and exalted is He! This view may have been held by some corporealists among the Hishāmiyya, the Karrāmiyya, and others reported to hold corporealist views. Some of these maintain that every body is composed of indivisible atoms, while also saying that the Lord is a body. I believe this is the position of some of the Karrāmiyya, for they differ over the existence of indivisible atoms, although they all agree that He, glorified is He, is a body.

They are, however, reported to disagree over what is meant by “body”: does it mean that He exists and subsists in Himself, or that He is composite? The position commonly reported from Abū al-Haysam and other speculative theologians among them is that the intended meaning is that He exists, subsists in Himself, and can be pointed to—not that He is assembled and composed.

Even those who deny that Allah is a body have acknowledged that these people are not unbelievers, since they have not affirmed any unsound meaning concerning Allah Most High. They have, however, said that these people erred in calling everything that subsists in itself, or whatever is

---

## Page 2289

in existence, a “body” on linguistic grounds. They said: “Arabic speakers apply the word ‘body’ only to what is composite.”

The truth is that both parties misuse the language: those who call everything that subsists in itself a body, and those who call everything that can be pointed to and toward which hands are raised a body, claiming that everything of this kind is composite and that Arabic speakers apply the word “body” to everything composite. Thus, both parties share in linguistic error and religious innovation.

As for the meanings intended, whoever among either party affirms what Allah and His Messenger have denied, or denies what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed, is mistaken according to reason just as he is mistaken according to revelation.

Indeed, the former say to the latter: “We and you agree that, outside the point at issue, whatever subsists in itself is called a body. You then claim that the Creator, who subsists in Himself, has a distinguishing feature that precludes applying this designation, which we and you have agreed upon. We have shown that He has no such distinguishing feature, because that claim rests on the premise that bodies are composite. We dispute this and say that they are not composed of indivisible atoms.”

For this reason, the early generations and the leading scholars—such as Imam Ahmad and others—disapproved of countering an innovation with another innovation. Thus, when Ahmad debated the Jahmiyya and they argued that the Quran was created, Abū ‘Īsā Muhammad ibn ‘Īsā Burghūth sought to compel him to accept that, if it were uncreated, Allah would necessarily be a body, which was ruled out. Ahmad would agree neither to deny this nor to affirm it. Rather, he said:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One;
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor is born,
nor is there to Him any equivalent.’”

---

## Page 2290

And Ahmad pointed out that it is not known what they mean by this expression. When a speaker’s intended meaning is unknown, one should agree with him neither in affirming it nor in denying it. If he mentions a meaning affirmed by Allah and His Messenger, we affirm it; and if he mentions a meaning denied by Allah and His Messenger, we deny it—in clear Arabic. We have no need for expressions that are innovations in religion, distortions of language, and rationally contradictory in meaning, thereby corrupting revelation, language, and reason—as has been done by the innovators who engage in false speculative theology contrary to the Quran and Sunnah.

The same applies to the expression “compulsion.” The early generations disapproved of saying either “He compelled” or “He did not compel.” Al-Khallāl related in his book al-Sunnah, from the imam Abū Ishāq al-Fazārī, who said:

“Al-Awzā‘ī said to me, ‘Two men came to me and asked me about divine decree. I wanted to bring them to you so that you could hear what they have to say and answer them.’

“I said, ‘May Allah have mercy on you; you are better qualified to answer.’

“Then al-Awzā‘ī came to me with the two men and said, ‘Speak.’

“They said, ‘Some adherents of the Qadariyya came to us and disputed with us concerning divine decree. “He said, ‘Answer them, Abū Ishāq.’

“I said, ‘May Allah have mercy on you; you are better qualified to answer.’

“He said, ‘Answer them.’ I was reluctant to go against him, so I said, ‘You two! Those who brought these claims to you have introduced an innovation and brought something new into religion. “He said, ‘You have answered well, Abū Ishāq.’”

It was also related from Baqiyya ibn al-Walīd, who said:

“I asked al-Zubaydī and al-Awzā‘ī about compulsion. Al-Zubaydī said, ‘Allah’s command is too great, and His power too great, for Him to compel or obstruct; rather,

an innovation, they go to greater lengths in answering it.’ He also said, ‘Whoever responded to them with an innovation must seek his Lord’s forgiveness.’ He disapproved of anyone responding with such theological discourse without a precedent from an earlier imam.”

I say: These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is simply to point out that the early generations adhered to the wording of the Quran and hadith in what they affirmed or denied concerning Allah’s attributes and actions. They did not introduce newly coined, innovated expressions into their affirmations and negations. Rather, every sound meaning is encompassed by what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed.

Innovated expressions have no fixed standard governing their usage. Each group intends by them a meaning different from that intended by others—as with the expressions “body,” “direction,” “spatial location,” “compulsion,” and the like. This is unlike the Messenger’s expressions: his intended meaning can be known, just as his intended meaning in all his other expressions can be known. If a person knew his intended meaning, he would be obliged to believe what he said in general terms. Even if a sound meaning were posited—and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had not spoken

## Page 2293

of it—no one would be permitted to introduce it into the religion of the Muslims. This is unlike what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed, for believing it is obligatory. Innovated statements entail denying much of what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. This is recognized by anyone who understands both the Messenger’s intended meaning and that of those who advance these innovated statements.

When newly introduced theological discourse spread, incorporating ideas that contradicted the Quran and Sunnah, and people began using it to oppose them, explaining what they meant by these expressions and the linguistic and rational arguments they offered for them became a means of showing the believer how to avoid innovation and misguidance—or escape them if he had already fallen into them—and how to ward off, inwardly and outwardly, whatever in this discourse conflicts with his faith in the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought cannot be dismissed through ambiguous expressions such as “corporealism” and others, which may encompass a false meaning, while the person denying them denies both truth and falsehood. When false meanings are mentioned, hearts recoil. When they press upon someone their claim that his position entails corporealism, he recoils when they tell him, “This entails corporealism, because this can only be conceived of in a body,” and he cannot adequately refute what they have said or unravel their argument. Yet they are all inconsistent. In reality, their argument is that the attributes with which the Lord has described Himself can only be conceived as they are in

---

## Page 2294

a small number of the created things we observe, such as human bodies. This is the height of ignorance, for there are created beings we have not seen, such as the angels and jinn, and even our own souls. What the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has conveyed need not resemble these, so how could it necessarily resemble what they have observed? This concerns the word “body” from the standpoint of language. As for revelation, it is well known that none of the prophets, the Companions, the Successors, or the early generations of the Muslim community is reported to have said that Allah is a body or that Allah is not a body. Rather, both affirming and denying this are innovations in religion.

As for rational inquiry, they disagree about those things they agree to call bodies, such as the heavens, the earth, wind, water, and similar things that can be pointed to, lie in a particular direction, and occupy space. They dispute whether such things are composed of indivisible atoms, of matter and form, or of neither. Most rational thinkers hold the third view. Each of the first two views is held by a group of speculative thinkers: the first is widespread among speculative theologians, and the second among philosophers. Yet both groups’ positions are false, and those who hold the third view know through reason that they are false.

That being so, if someone says: “I affirm that He is above the Throne, that hands are raised to Him, and the like; yet not everything of this kind is composed of individual parts

---

## Page 2295

nor of matter and form as conceived by the intellect,” then the discussion with him concerns whether the former necessarily entails the latter.

If the other person says, “Rather, everything that is above something else, and everything that can be pointed to with the hands, must be composed in one or the other of these two ways,” this is equivalent to someone else saying: “Everything that is living, powerful and knowing must have this composition”; or: “Everything that possesses life, knowledge and power must have this composition”; or: “Everything that hears, sees and speaks must have this composition.” This rests on the premise that every self-subsisting existent is a body, and that every body has this composition. It is well known, by their own agreement, that this is false in the view of the vast majority of scholars and rational thinkers.

Indeed, I know of no group of recognized rational thinkers who have said both, “He is a body,” and, “He has this composition.” Rather, what I know is that those who have said, “He is a body,” such as the Hishāmiyyah and the Karrāmiyyah, do not all define a body as something having this composition. This has only been reported from some of them. Statements may also be attributed to some of them which others among them deny, as in the reprehensible statements attributed to Muqātil ibn Sulaymān and Hishām ibn al-Hakam. Many people have rejected the attribution of these statements to Muqātil ibn Sulaymān. As for their attribution to Hishām, many of his followers have rejected it.

If anyone is assumed to have said this, then his assertion is false, like that of anyone else who speaks falsely about Allah. Such are the reports concerning some Jews, Rāfidah and corporealists, who describe Him with imperfections far above which Allah is exalted: that He is hollow; that He wept until His eyes became inflamed and the angels visited Him in His illness; that He bit His fingers until they bled; and that He descends on the afternoon of the Day of ‘Arafah upon a gray camel.

---

## Page 2296

and similar statements containing lies about Allah Most High and attributing imperfections to Him—statements whose falsehood is established by clear reason and authentic revelation.

Likewise, someone may say: “If He descended to the lowest heaven, this would necessarily entail movement and passage from one place to another, which are exclusive to bodies.” Or he may say: “It would necessarily follow that the Throne would be vacant of Him, and that is impossible.” People hold three positions on this.

(One is the position of those who say: “He descends, but He is not a body.” Another is that of those who say: “He descends, and He is a body.” The other is that of those who neither deny nor affirm that He is a body. They either refrain from both because such terminology constitutes an innovation and creates confusion, as explained above; or they clarify the intended meaning, affirm what is true, reject what is false, and explain the correct rational meanings that have become confused in this matter.

For example, one may say: “Descent, ascent, coming, approaching, and similar acts are varieties of movement. We do not concede that they are exclusive to the technically defined body whose affirmation and negation the speculative theologians debate. Rather, these descriptions apply more broadly than that.”

There are then two approaches here. The first is that these descriptions apply to both bodies and accidents. Thus, one says: “The cold has come,” “The heat has come,” “The fever has come,” and similarly of other accidents. Since accidents can be described as coming and approaching, it is known that these are not exclusive to bodies. Thus, it is not permissible to describe Him with these

---

## Page 2297

acts in a literal sense while He is not a body. This is the approach of al-Ash'arī and those who followed him among the speculative thinkers of the people of hadith, the followers of the four imams, and others, such as al-Qādī Abū Ya'lā. This is the meaning of what he reported in al-Maqālāt concerning the people of the Sunnah and hadith.

For this reason, Ibn Kullāb, al-Ash'arī, al-Qalānisī, and those who agreed with them among the followers of the four imams and others, including the followers of Ahmad and others, held that establishment over the Throne is an act that the Lord brings about in the Throne. They say the same concerning descent. What this means is that He brings about a proximity in the Throne, thereby becoming established over it, without any voluntary act subsisting in Him Himself—whether or not they identify the act with its effect. They understand descent in the same way. Thus, they treat intransitive acts as though they were transitive. This is because they believed that no voluntary act subsists in Him, since such an act has a temporal beginning; its subsistence in Him would therefore entail that temporal events subsist in Him. They denied this on account of that principle which they held.

(The second approach is to say: Coming, approaching, ascending, and descending are descriptions applied to the human spirit, which departs from a person at death and is also called the soul. They are also applied to the angels. The spirit’s descent and ascent are not of the same kind as the body’s descent and ascent. The believer’s spirit ascends above the heavens and then descends to the earth between the time it is taken and the time the deceased is placed in his grave. This is a short interval: the body cannot ascend above the heavens and then descend to the earth in such a time.

---

## Page 2298

The same is true of its ascent and subsequent return to the body during sleep and wakefulness. For this reason, some people liken its descent into the grave to a ray of sunlight, but this is not an exact analogy. The sun itself does not descend. The light that appears on the earth is an accident produced by the sun; it is neither the sun itself nor an attribute subsisting in it. The spirit itself, however, ascends and descends.

For in the well-known hadith of al-Barā' ibn 'Āzib—may Allah be pleased with him—concerning the taking of the soul and the trial of the grave—a hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad and others, also narrated in abridged form by Abū Dāwūd, as well as by al-Nasā'ī and Ibn Mājah, and narrated in full by Abū 'Awānah in his Sahīh. In the latter's narration, Zādhān says, “I heard al-Barā',” which disproves the claim that he did not hear it from him. Al-Hākim also narrated it in his Sahīh through Abū Mu'āwiyah, who said: Al-A'mash narrated to us: al-Minhāl ibn 'Amr narrated to us, from Abū 'Amr Zādhān,

“From al-Barā' ibn 'Āzib—may Allah be pleased with them both—who said: ‘We went out with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for a funeral. We reached the grave, but its burial niche had not yet been dug.’”

He then related the hadith in full. Al-Hākim also narrated it through Muhammad ibn al-Fadl, who said: Al-A'mash narrated to us; he then related it.

At its end, he said: Fudayl narrated to us: My father narrated to me, from Abū Hāzim, from Abū Hurayrah, this same hadith, except that he said:

“He was put to sleep, like one whom none but his dearest loved one awakens.”

He said: Shu'bah, Zā'idah, and others also narrated it from al-A'mash, and Mu'ammal narrated it from

Another such report is the hadith narrated by Ibn Abī Dhi’b, from Muhammad ibn ‘Amr ibn ‘Atā’, from Sa‘īd ibn Yasār, from Abū Hurayrah. Imam Ahmad related it in his Musnad, as did others.

The hadith scholar Abū Nu‘aym al-Asbahānī said:

“The uprightness of this hadith’s transmitters is agreed upon. Both imams, Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl al-Bukhārī and Muslim ibn al-Hajjāj, accepted Ibn Abī Dhi’b, Muhammad ibn ‘Amr ibn ‘Atā’, and Sa‘īd ibn Yasār; these narrators meet their criteria. Leading early scholars narrated it from Ibn Abī Dhi’b, including Ibn Abī Fudayk, from whom Duhaym ibn Ibrāhīm narrated it.”

I say:

Several narrators related it from Ibn Abī Dhi’b, but the wording given here is that of Ibn Abī Fudayk’s narration, in view of his precedence.

Ibn Abī Fudayk said:

Muhammad ibn Abī Dhi’b narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn ‘Amr ibn ‘Atā’, from Sa‘īd ibn Yasār, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Angels attend the dying person. If he is a righteous man, they say, ‘Come out, good soul that dwelt in a good body! Come out praiseworthy, and receive glad tidings of rest and provision, and a Lord who is not angry.’

“They continue saying this until it comes out. It is then taken up to the lowest heaven, and permission is sought for it to enter. It is asked, ‘Who is this?’

“They reply, ‘So-and-so.’ Then they say, ‘Welcome to the good soul that dwelt in a good body! Enter praiseworthy, and receive glad tidings of rest and provision, and a Lord who is not angry.’ This is said to it until it is brought to the heaven in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is.

“But if the man is evil,” he said, “the words are: ‘Come out, wicked soul that dwelt in a wicked body! Come out blameworthy, and receive tidings of scalding water, ghassāq, and more of the same kind

---

## Page 2306

in many varieties.’

“They continue saying this until it comes out. It is then taken up to heaven, and permission is sought for it to enter. It is asked, ‘Who is this?’

“The reply is, ‘So-and-so.’ They then say, ‘No welcome to the wicked soul that dwelt in a wicked body! Return blameworthy, for the gates of heaven will not be opened to you.’ It is then released between heaven and earth and returns to his grave.

“The righteous man sits in his grave, neither frightened nor distressed. Then he is asked, ‘What did you used to say about Islam?’ (1)

“He then says, ‘Who is this man?’

“He replies, ‘Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah. He brought us clear proofs from Allah, so we believed and accepted the truth.’” He then related the remainder of the hadith.

The point is that Abū Hurayrah’s hadith contains the words, “It returns to his grave,” just as in the hadith of al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib. Abū Hurayrah’s hadith has been narrated through chains that corroborate the hadith of al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib. Some versions give the account found in al-Barā’s hadith in full, as al-Hākim mentioned. Moreover, the other authentic, mass-transmitted hadiths indicate that the soul returns to the body. The view that the body is questioned without the soul was held by a group of people but rejected by the majority. Likewise, Ibn Maysarah and Ibn Hazm held that the soul is questioned without the body. If that were so, however, the grave would have no special connection with the soul.

Ibn Hazm claimed that only Zādhān narrated “the return” from al-Barā’, and he declared him weak. But the matter is not as he stated: others besides Zādhān narrated it from al-Barā’, and it was also narrated from people other than al-Barā’, such as ‘Adī ibn Thābit and others. Al-Dāraqutnī collected its chains of transmission in a separate work. Moreover, Zādhān

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Thus in the original.
