## Page 2307

is among the trustworthy narrators. He narrated from leading Companions such as ‘Umar and others, and Muslim included his narrations in his Sahīh, as did others. Yahyā ibn Ma‘īn said, “He is trustworthy.” When Humayd ibn Hilāl was asked about him, he said, “He is trustworthy. The reliability of men like him need not be questioned.” Ibn ‘Adī said that his hadiths are acceptable when transmitted from him by a trustworthy narrator. He used to follow al-Karābīsī, and those who criticized him did so only because he talked a great deal. As for al-Minhāl ibn ‘Amr, he is among al-Bukhārī’s narrators. The hadith concerning “the soul’s return” has also been narrated from others besides al-Barā’. Zādhān’s hadith is among those that the earlier and later generations have unanimously transmitted and accepted.

The souls of the believers are in Paradise, although they may nevertheless be returned to their bodies, just as they may be in their bodies while being taken up to heaven, as happens during sleep. There are hadiths stating in general terms that they are in Paradise. Ahmad and other scholars explicitly affirmed this, citing both general transmitted hadiths and specific hadiths concerning sleep and other matters.

An example of the former is the well-known hadith of al-Zuhrī, which Mālik narrated from him in his Muwatta’, as did Shu‘ayb ibn Abī Hamzah and others. Imam Ahmad also narrated it in his Musnad, as did others. Al-Zuhrī said:

“‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ka‘b ibn Mālik informed us that Ka‘b ibn Mālik al-Ansārī—one of the three whose repentance was accepted—used to relate that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘The believer’s soul is a bird that feeds among the trees of Paradise until Allah returns it to his body.’”

Thus, he stated that it feeds among the trees of Paradise until it returns to his body

---

## Page 2308

—that is, in the life to come.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mandah said:

It was also narrated by Yūnus, al-Zubaydī, al-Awzā‘ī and Ibn Ishāq. ‘Amr ibn Dīnār and al-Zuhrī’s nephew narrated it from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Ka‘b, from his father, who said: … Sālih ibn Kaysān and al-Zuhrī’s nephew narrated it from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Ka‘b, who had been informed that Ka‘b said: …

It was narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī, who said: “A good and authentic hadith.”

I say:

The well-known hadith transmitted by Muhammad ibn ‘Amr, from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was narrated by Abū Hātim in his Sahīh and also by the leading hadith scholars. He said:

“The deceased indeed hears the sound of their sandals as they turn away from him. If he was a believer, prayer will stand at his head, fasting to his right, zakat to his left, and his good deeds—charity, maintaining ties of kinship, kindness and benevolence towards people—at his feet.

“He will be approached from the direction of his head, and prayer will say, ‘There is no way in from my side.’ Then he will be approached from his right, and fasting will say, ‘There is no way in from my side.’ Then he will be approached from his left, and zakat will say, ‘There is no way in from my side.’ Then he will be approached from the direction of his feet, and his good deeds—charity, maintaining ties of kinship, kindness and benevolence towards people—will say, ‘There is no way in from my side.’

“He will then be told, ‘Sit up.’ He will sit up, and the sun will be made to appear before him as though it were nearing sunset. He will be asked, ‘What about this man who was among you? What do you say about him?’

“He will reply, ‘Let me pray first.’

“They will say, ‘You will do so. Tell us about what

---

## Page 2309

we are asking you about.’

“He will say, ‘What are you asking me about?’

“They will say, ‘What do you say about this man who was among you? What do you testify concerning him?’

“He will say, ‘I testify that he is the Messenger of Allah and that he brought the truth from Allah.’

“He will be told, ‘Upon that you lived, upon that you died, and upon that you will be resurrected, if Allah Most High wills.’ Then a gate of Paradise will be opened for him, and he will be told, ‘That is your place there, and that is what Allah has prepared for you therein.’ His joy and happiness will increase. Then a gate of Hell will be opened for him, and he will be told, ‘That would have been your place there, and that is what Allah would have prepared for you therein had you disobeyed your Lord.’ His joy and happiness will increase. Then his grave will be widened for him by seventy cubits and illuminated for him. His body will be restored to its original state, and his soul will be placed amid fragrant breezes; it is a bird that feeds among the trees of Paradise.”

In another wording: “And he is in a bird that feeds among the trees of Paradise.” Abū Hurayrah said: Allah Most High said:

“Allah makes those who believe firm with the firm word, in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.”

In another wording: “Then the body is returned to that from which it originated.” This return is the one mentioned in the words of the Most High:

“From it We created you, into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you forth once again.”

It is not the second creation.

Al-Hākim also narrated it in his Sahīh, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, from Qasāmah ibn Zuhayr, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“When the believer is at the point of death, the angels of mercy come to him with a piece of white silk and say, ‘Come out, well pleased and pleasing to Allah, to rest and fragrance and a Lord who is not angry.’ It comes out like the sweetest scent of musk, so much so that some of them pass it

---

## Page 2310

to one another, inhaling its fragrance, until they bring it to the gate of heaven. They say, ‘How sweet is this fragrance that has come to you from the earth!’ They say this at every heaven they reach, until they bring it to the souls of the believers. They are more delighted to receive him than any of you is when an absent loved one returns. They ask him, ‘What has become of so-and-so?’

“He said: They then say, ‘Leave him until he has rested, for he was amid the sorrows of this world.’ When he says to them, ‘Has he not come to you? He has died,’ they say, ‘He has been taken to his mother—the Abyss.’

“As for the disbeliever, the angels of punishment come to him and say, ‘Come out, displeased and subject to Allah’s displeasure, to Allah’s punishment and wrath.’ It comes out with the foulest stench of a carcass. They take it to the gate of the earth and say, ‘How foul this smell is!’ They say this at every earth they reach, until they bring it to the souls of the disbelievers.”

Al-Hākim said: “Hishām al-Dastawā’ī also transmitted it from Qatādah. Hammām ibn Yahyā narrated something similar from Qatādah, from Abū al-Jawzā’, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. All these narrations are sound, and they are corroborated by the hadith of al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib.”

The hadith scholar Abū Nu‘aym likewise narrated it through al-Qāsim ibn al-Fadl al-Hadhā’ī, as Ma‘mar narrated it.

He said: “Abū Mūsā and Bundār narrated the same report from Mu‘ādh ibn Hishām, from his father, from Qatādah, tracing it back to the Prophet. Some of Qatādah’s students narrated it as a report stopping at the Companion. Hammām narrated something similar from Qatādah, from Abū al-Jawzā’, from Abū Hurayrah, tracing it back to the Prophet.”

This hadith was also narrated by al-Nasā’ī, al-Bazzār in his Musnad, and Abū Hātim in his Sahīh.

---

## Page 2311

Muslim also narrated in his Sahīh that Abū Hurayrah said:

“When the believer’s soul departs, two angels receive it and ascend with it.” He mentioned its pleasant fragrance and musk, then said: “The inhabitants of heaven say, ‘A good soul has come from the earth. May Allah bless you and the body you used to inhabit.’ It is then taken to its Lord, and it is said, ‘Take him away until the end of the appointed term.’”

He said: “When the disbeliever’s soul departs”—he mentioned its stench and a curse—“the inhabitants of heaven say, ‘An evil soul has come from the earth.’” He said: “Then it is said, ‘Take him away until the end of the appointed term.’” Abū Hurayrah said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then drew the cloth he was wearing over his nose like this.”

It is also established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say when going to sleep:

“In Your name, my Lord, I lay down my side, and by You I raise it. If You retain my soul, forgive it; and if You release it, protect it as You protect Your righteous servants.”

It is likewise reported in the Sahīh that he used to say:

“O Allah, You created my soul, and You take it at death. Its death and life belong to You. If You retain it, have mercy on it; and if You release it, protect it as You protect Your righteous servants.”

These hadiths, in describing the soul’s ascent to heaven and its return to the body, make clear that its ascent is of a different kind, unlike the body’s ascent and descent.

We have also transmitted from the hadith scholar Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn Mandah, in his book al-Rūh wa-al-Nafs (The Spirit and the Soul): “Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to us: ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hasan al-Harrānī narrated to us: Ahmad

---

## Page 2312

ibn Shu‘ayb narrated to us: Mūsā ibn Ayman narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from Ja‘far ibn Abī al-Mughīrah, from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning the interpretation of this verse:

‘Allah takes souls at the time of their death, and, during sleep, those that have not died.’

He said: ‘The souls of the living meet the souls of the dead during sleep, and they question one another. Allah then retains the souls of the dead and returns the souls of the living to their bodies.’”

The hadith scholar Abū Muhammad ibn Abī Hātim also narrated in his Tafsīr: “‘Abd Allāh ibn Sulaymān narrated to us: al-Hasan narrated to us: ‘Āmir narrated to us, from al-Furāt: Asbāt narrated to us, from al-Suddī, concerning the words:

‘And, during sleep, those that have not died.’

He said: ‘He takes them during their sleep.’ He said: ‘The soul of the living person and the soul of the dead person meet, converse, and recognize one another.’ He said: ‘The living person’s soul then returns to his body in this world for the remainder of his appointed lifespan.’ He said: ‘The dead person’s soul wishes to return to his body, but is held back.’”

This is one of the two interpretations: that His words,

“He then retains those for whom He has decreed death,”

refer to those who had already died and met the soul of a living person. The second interpretation—which is held by the majority—is that both souls, the one retained and the one released, have been taken in sleep. As for the soul taken in death, that constitutes a third category, mentioned first in His words:

“Allah takes souls at the time of their death.”

This is what the Book and the Sunnah indicate, for Allah said:

“Allah takes souls at the time of their death, and, during sleep, those that have not died. He then retains those for whom He has decreed death and releases the others until an appointed term.”

Thus, He mentioned retaining those for whom He has decreed death from among these souls that He took during sleep. As for those that

---

## Page 2313

He takes at the time of their death, He did not describe them as either retained or released. Nor does the verse mention the dead meeting those who are asleep. The correct understanding is that the verse encompasses both kinds, for Allah mentions two forms of taking souls: taking them in death and taking them during sleep. He also mentions retaining the souls taken and releasing the others. It is well known that He retains every soul that has died, whether it died during sleep or before that, and releases those that have not died.

His words,

“He takes souls at the time of their death,”

include those who die while awake and those who die during sleep. Having mentioned the two forms of taking souls, He states that He retains the soul in one and releases it in the other. This is the wording’s apparent meaning and what it indicates without any strained interpretation. The reported meeting of the souls of sleepers and the dead does not contradict the verse, but its wording does not indicate such a meeting. However, His words,

“He then retains those for whom He has decreed death,”

entail that He retains them and does not release them as He releases the souls of sleepers, whether He took them while awake or during sleep. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O Allah, You created my soul, and You take it. To You belong its death and its life. If You retain it, have mercy on it; and if You release it, protect it as You protect Your righteous servants.”

He thus described the soul, when taken during sleep, as either retained or released.

Ibn Abī Hātim said: My father narrated to us: ‘Umar ibn ‘Uthmān narrated to us: Baqiyyah narrated to us: Safwān ibn ‘Amr narrated to us: Sulaym ibn ‘Āmir al-Hadramī related to me that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said to ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him: “I marvel at a man’s dreams: he goes to sleep and sees something

---

## Page 2314

that has never crossed his mind, yet his dream is as clear as if he were being led by the hand; whereas a man may see something and his dream amounts to nothing.”

‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib said: “Shall I explain this to you, Commander of the Faithful? Allah says:

‘Allah takes souls at the time of their death, and during sleep those that have not died. He then retains those for whom He has decreed death and releases the others until an appointed term.’

“Allah takes all souls. Whatever they see while they are with Him in heaven is a true dream. As for what they see when they are released to their bodies, the devils meet them in the air and deceive them, telling them falsehoods and lying in their visions.” ‘Umar marvelled at what he said.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Mandah mentioned this in his book al-Rūh wa-l-Nafs (The Spirit and the Soul), saying: “This is a well-known report from Safwān ibn ‘Amr and others.” His wording is:

‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib said: “Commander of the Faithful, Allah Most High says:

‘Allah takes souls at the time of their death, and during sleep those that have not died. He then retains those for whom He has decreed death and releases the others until an appointed term.’

“Souls are taken up during sleep. Whatever they see while in heaven is true. When they are returned to their bodies, the devils meet them in the air and deceive them. Whatever they see as a result of that is false.”

Imam Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mandah said: “It was also reported from Abū al-Dardā’.” He said: “Ibn Lahī‘ah narrated from ‘Uthmān ibn Nu‘aym al-Ru‘aynī, from Abū ‘Uthmān al-Asbahī, from Abū al-Dardā’, who said: ‘When a person sleeps, his soul is taken up until it is brought to the Throne.’ He said: ‘If the person is in a state of ritual purity, the soul is permitted to prostrate; but if he is in a state of major ritual impurity, it is not permitted to prostrate.’” Zayd ibn al-Hubāb and others narrated it.

---

## Page 2315

Ibn Mandah also narrated the report of ‘Alī and ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, traced back to the Prophet: Abū Ishāq Ibrāhīm ibn Muhammad narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Shu‘ayb narrated to us: Ibn ‘Ayyāsh ibn Abī Ismā‘īl narrated to us. Al-Hasan ibn ‘Alī also informed us: ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Muhammad informed us: Qutaybah and al-Rāzī narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us: Abū Zuhayr ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Maghrā’ al-Dawsī narrated to us: al-Azhar ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Azdī narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn ‘Ajlān, from Sālim ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, from his father, who said:

“‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb met ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and said, ‘Abū al-Hasan, sometimes you were present when we were absent, and sometimes we were present when you were absent. There are three matters I wish to ask you about. Do you have any knowledge of them?’

“‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib asked, ‘What are they?’

“He said, ‘A man loves another man although he has never received any kindness from him; and a man dislikes another man although he has never suffered any harm from him.’

“He replied, ‘Yes. I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: “Souls are troops assembled together. They meet in the air and catch one another’s scent. Those that recognize one another come together in harmony, while those that find one another unfamiliar remain at odds.”’

“‘Umar said, ‘That is one.’

“‘Umar continued, ‘A man is recounting something when he forgets it; then, while it has slipped his mind, he suddenly remembers it.’

“He replied, ‘Yes. I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: “There is no heart without a cloud like the cloud that covers the moon. While the moon is shining, a cloud suddenly covers it and it grows dark; then the cloud clears away and it shines again. Likewise, while the heart is engaged in thought, the cloud covers it and it forgets; then the cloud clears away and it remembers.”’

“‘Umar said, ‘That is two.’

“He continued, ‘A man has dreams: some come true and others prove false.’

“He replied, ‘Yes. I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: “Whenever a servant falls into deep sleep, his soul is taken up towards the Throne. If he does not awaken before reaching the Throne, that is the dream that comes true. But as for one who awakens before reaching the Throne

---

## Page 2316

that is the dream that proves false.”’

“‘Umar said, ‘These are three matters whose answers I had been seeking. Praise be to Allah that I have found them before death.’”

He also narrated it through a third chain, in which Ibn ‘Abbās questioned ‘Umar about it. He said: Ahmad ibn Sulaymān ibn Ayyūb narrated to us: Yazīd ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Samad narrated to us: Ādam ibn Abī Iyās narrated to us: Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ayyāsh narrated to us, from Tha‘labah ibn Muslim al-Khath‘amī, from Ibn Abī Talhah al-Qurashī, that Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said to ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, “Commander of the Faithful, may I ask you about some matters?”

He replied, “Ask whatever you wish.”

He said, “Commander of the Faithful, what causes a man to remember, and what causes him to forget? What causes dreams to come true, and what causes them to prove false?”

‘Umar replied, “As for your question about what causes a man to remember and what causes him to forget, there is a cloud over the heart like the cloud that covers the moon. When it envelops the heart, the son of Adam forgets; when it clears away from the heart, he remembers what he had forgotten. As for what causes dreams to come true or prove false, Allah says:

‘Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die, during their sleep.’

“Those souls that enter the dominion of heaven have dreams that come true, while those that remain short of the dominion of heaven have dreams that prove false.”

I say: These two chains of transmission state that false dreams occur when the ascent to the heights is not completed. The first states that they arise from what happens after the soul’s return. Both are possible, for the outcome varies according to whether a necessary condition is absent or an impediment is present.

‘Ikrimah and Mujāhid said, “When a person sleeps, he has a connection along which the soul travels

---

## Page 2317

while its root remains in the body. It reaches wherever Allah wills, and as long as it is away, the person remains asleep. When it returns to the body, the person awakens. It is thus like a ray falling upon the earth while remaining connected at its source to the sun.”

Ibn Mandah said:

I was informed on the authority of ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Samarqandī, from ‘Alī ibn Yazīd al-Samarqandī—who was a man of learning and letters, with knowledge of medicine and dream interpretation—that he said:

“Souls extend outward from a person’s nostril, while their vehicles and their source remain within the body. Were the soul to leave, the person would die, just as a lamp’s flame would go out if separated from its wick. Do you not see that the flame rests upon the wick, while its light and radiance fill the house? Likewise, during sleep, the soul extends outward from a person’s nostril until it reaches heaven, roams through the lands, and meets the souls of the dead.

“When the angel entrusted with the souls of Allah’s servants sees it, he shows the person what he wishes him to see. If that person, while awake, is sensible, intelligent, and truthful, paying no heed to anything false, his soul returns to him and faithfully conveys to his heart what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has shown him, in proportion to his truthfulness.

“But if he is frivolous and rash, fond of falsehood and watching it, then, when he sleeps and Allah shows him something good or bad, his soul returns and pauses wherever it encounters any of Satan’s tricks or anything false, just as he pauses over such things while awake. It conveys these things to his heart as well, so he cannot comprehend what he saw, because he has mixed truth with falsehood. No dream interpreter can interpret it for him once truth has become mixed with falsehood.”

Imam Ibn Mandah said:

“What supports this account is what we have related from ‘Umar, ‘Alī, and Abū al-Dardā’, may Allah be pleased with them.”

I say: Ibn Qutaybah also recorded a report in his book Ta‘bīr al-Ru’yā (Dream Interpretation), saying: “There narrated to me

---

## Page 2318

Husayn ibn Hasan al-Marwazī, who said: ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak informed us: al-Mubārak narrated to us from al-Hasan, who said: ‘I have been informed that when a servant falls asleep while prostrating, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: “Look at My servant: his soul is with Me, while his body is obeying Me.”’”

If the soul ascends to heaven while remaining in the body, it follows that its ascent is not of the same kind as bodily ascent, for which this is impossible. The ascent and descent of the angels are of the same kind as the soul’s ascent and descent, not those of the body. The ascent of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is above all this and more exalted than all of it. For He, Exalted is He, is further removed from resembling any created being than one created being is from resembling another.

If it is said, “Ascending, descending, coming, and arriving are all forms of motion,” the response is: Motion itself comprises different kinds. The soul’s motion is not like the body’s motion, nor is the angels’ motion like the body’s motion.

“Motion” may mean the displacement of a body or physical object from its location, but it may also mean other things, as many naturalists and philosophers maintain. These include motion in quantity, such as growth; motion in quality, such as a person’s transition from ignorance to knowledge, or a colour or clothes changing from black to white; and motion in place, such as the motion occurring in growing bodies—plants and animals—as they grow and increase, or wither and diminish. Yet here no body moves from one spatial region to another.

Whoever says that indivisible atoms move from place to place is mistaken, as has been explained at length in its proper place.

---

## Page 2319

Likewise, the colours, tastes, and smells of bodies change. A body becomes black after being white, and sweet after being bitter, having previously been otherwise. These are motions, transformations, and transitions, even though no body moves from one spatial region to another. Similarly, a body rotating in one place, such as a wheel or a celestial sphere, does not, as a whole, leave its spatial region, although it never ceases moving.

All these motions occur in bodies. As for spirits, the soul passes from hatred to love, from displeasure to contentment, from aversion to desire, and from ignorance to knowledge. A person experiences the motions and transitions of his own soul, its ascent and descent. These belong to a different kind from the motions of his body. Once this is understood, the angels likewise have motions befitting them, while what is attributed to the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, is more perfect, higher, and more complete than all of this.

Thus, if the early generations and leading scholars—such as Hammād ibn Zayd, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and other leading scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah—say that He descends while the Throne is not left without Him, it is not permissible to say that this is impossible. Rather, if one created being can be described in these respects in ways that are impossible for another—the soul being described in ways that cannot apply to the body—then this is all the more possible with regard to the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, than with regard to created beings, such as human souls and angels.

Whoever supposes that what is attributed to the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, can only be like what is attributed to human bodies is far more mistaken than someone who supposes that what is attributed to the soul is like what is attributed to bodies.

---

## Page 2320

The underlying principle is that “His nearness—glory be to Him—and His drawing close to some of His creatures” do not entail that He Himself ceases to be above the Throne. Rather, He is above the Throne and draws near to His creation however He wills, as those of the early generations who held this view affirmed. Such was His nearness to Moses when He spoke to him from the tree. The Exalted says:

“When Moses said to his family, ‘I have perceived a fire. I will bring you some news from it, or bring you a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves.’ When he came to it, he was called: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds! O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise. Throw down your staff.’ When he saw it writhing as though it were a snake, he turned and fled without looking back. ‘O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers have no fear in My presence, except one who has been wronged.’”

He says in the other surah:

“When Moses had fulfilled the term and was travelling with his family, he perceived a fire on the side of the Mount. He said to his family, ‘Stay here. I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you some news from it, or a burning piece of wood, so that you may warm yourselves.’ When he came to it, he was called from the right bank of the valley, at the blessed spot, from the tree: ‘O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”

The Exalted also says:

“And mention Moses in the Book. Indeed, he was chosen, and he was a messenger and a prophet. We called him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near in intimate converse.”

Thus He states that He called him from the side of the Mount and brought him near in intimate converse. The Exalted says:

“We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, after We had destroyed the earlier generations, as enlightenment for the people, guidance and mercy, so that they might be reminded. You were not on the western side when We entrusted the command to Moses, nor were you among the witnesses. But We raised up generations, and a long time passed over them. You were not dwelling among the people of Midian, reciting Our verses to them, but it was We who sent messengers. Nor were you on the side of the Mount when We called. Rather, it is a mercy from your Lord, so that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, so that they might be reminded.”

And the Exalted says:

---

## Page 2321

“Has the story of Moses reached you? When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwā: ‘Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. And say, “Would you be willing to purify yourself, and let me guide you to your Lord so that you may fear Him?”’ Then he showed him the greatest sign.”

Ibn Abī Hātim said in his Tafsīr (Quran commentary): ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn narrated to us; ‘Uthmān ibn Abī Shaybah narrated to us; Mu‘āwiyah ibn Hishām narrated to us; Sharīk narrated to us, from ‘Atā’, from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ‘Abbās—may Allah be pleased with him—who said concerning the Exalted’s words,

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it.’”

He said: “That was the fire.” He said: “Allah is the One in the light. And the call was made: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the light.’”

‘Alī ibn al-Husayn narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Hamzah narrated to us; ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn ibn Wāqid narrated to us, from his father, from Yazīd al-Nahwī, who said: ‘Ikrimah narrated to me from Ibn ‘Abbās, concerning the words, “Blessed is whoever is in the fire,” that he said: “That fire was His light.” And “whoever is around it” means: “Blessed is whoever is in the light and whoever is around the light.”

He likewise transmitted, through his chain of narration, from ‘Atiyyah’s Quran commentary, from Ibn ‘Abbās, concerning the words,

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the fire.’”

He meant Himself. He said: “The light of the Lord of the worlds was in the tree and around it.”

My father narrated to us; Ibrāhīm ibn Sa‘īd al-Jawharī narrated to us; Abū Mu‘āwiyah narrated to us, from Shaybān, from ‘Ikrimah, concerning the words, “Blessed is whoever is in the fire.” He said: “Allah was in His light.”

Abū Zur‘ah narrated to us; Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated to us; ‘Alī ibn Ja‘far al-Madā’inī narrated to us, from Warqā’, from ‘Atā’ ibn al-Sā’ib, from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, concerning the words, “Blessed is whoever is in the fire.” He said: “He called to him while He was in the light.”

---

## Page 2322

‘Alī ibn al-Husayn al-Manjānī narrated to us; Sa‘īd ibn Abī Maryam narrated to us; Mufaddal ibn Abī Fadālah narrated to us; Ibn Damrah narrated to me, concerning the words:

“When he came to it, he was called: ‘Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it.’”

He said: “Moses was on the bank of the valley”—until he said—“When he stood up, he saw the fire and walked towards it. When he reached it, ‘he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire.’” He said: “It was not a fire; rather, it was the light of Allah. He was the One in that light, and that light was from Him alone, while Moses was around it.”

Abū Sa‘īd ibn Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān narrated to us; Makkī ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to us; Mūsā ibn ‘Ubaydah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka‘b, concerning His words, Mighty and Majestic:

“Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it.”

He said: “The fire was the light of mercy.” He said: “A radiance from Allah Most High.” As for “whoever is around it,” he said: “Moses and the angels.”

It was also narrated through his chain of transmission from Ibn ‘Abbās, concerning “whoever is around it,” that he said: “The angels.” He said: “The same was narrated from ‘Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr and Qatādah.” It was narrated from al-Suddī alone, concerning “Blessed is whoever is in the fire,” that he said: “There were angels in the fire.”

In Sahīh Muslim, it is narrated from Abū ‘Ubaydah, from Abū Mūsā, who said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stood among us and made four statements, saying: ‘Allah does not sleep, nor is it fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the balance and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before

the deeds of the night. His veil is light—or fire. Were He to remove it, the splendours of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.’”

Tūr means “mountain.” Thus, the call came from the right-hand side of the mountain and of the valley, since the bank of a valley is its side. He says:

That is, on the western side—the side of the western location. This indicates that this right-hand side was the western side, not the eastern side. Thus, He mentions that the call came from a specific place: the sacred valley of Tuwā, from the right-hand bank of the valley, from the right-hand side of Mount Tūr, from the tree.

He also mentions that He brought him near for intimate conversation. He called to him and spoke intimately with him, and the One who called to him and spoke intimately with him was Allah, Lord of the worlds, and no other. His calling and His intimate speech subsist in Him; they are not something created and separate from Him, as claimed by those who say: “No speech subsists in Allah; rather, His speech is separate from Him and created.”

He, glorified and exalted is He, called to him and spoke intimately with him at that time, as the Quran indicates—not as claimed by those who say: “He had always been calling to him and speaking intimately with him, but at that time He created in him the perception of the eternal call, which has always existed and will always exist.”

His nearness to His servants as they draw near to Him is acknowledged by all who affirm that He is above the Throne, whether or not they also maintain that acts of His own choosing subsist in Him.

Among the meanings of nearness—and one that none of these groups denies—is the nearness of the One who is known and worshipped to the hearts of those who know and worship Him. For whoever loves something must know it, and it must be close to his heart, whereas whatever he hates is distant from his heart. This does not mean, however, that His very essence dwells in the hearts of those who know and worship Him. Rather, what is in their hearts is knowledge of Him, worship of Him, love for Him, and faith in Him. Yet knowledge corresponds to what is known.

This faith within the hearts is the “highest description” that belongs to Him in the heavens and the earth. This is the meaning of His words, Most High:

and His words:

“Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

## Page 2328

the descent of human bodies from a rooftop to the ground. This resembles the claim that the Throne becomes vacant of Him, so that some created things are above Him and others below Him. If the descent is conceived in this way, it would be impossible, for the reason they mentioned: He would remain beneath the Throne most or all of the time, since the time difference between the two extremities of the inhabited world is approximately one night.

For it is said that the inhabited world extends from east to west over approximately one hundred and eighty celestial degrees. Every fifteen degrees correspond to one equinoctial hour. An equinoctial hour is one of the twelve hours of night or day when night and day are equal—as they are at the beginning of spring, which the Arabs call summer, and at the beginning of autumn, which they call spring. This differs from the situation in which one is longer than the other, yet each is divided into twelve hours: those hours vary in length. Thus, the sun sets for the people of the east before it sets for the people of the west, just as it rises for the former before the latter, by approximately twelve hours or more.

Wherever the sun reaches its full elevation above the earth, as it does at midday, it illuminates what lies ahead of it and behind it, to the east and west: ninety degrees eastward and ninety degrees westward. Together, these correspond to twelve hours of its motion: six eastward and six westward. This is the daylight period when day and night are equal. The sun always has this daylight period, but its light is obscured because of its inclination toward the north

---

## Page 2329

and south; for the inhabited part of the earth lies in its northern region, north of the equator, which corresponds to the celestial equator and bears the same relation to both poles—the northern and the southern. Thus, the motion of the celestial sphere at that location is described as wheel-like, resembling a wheel; at the poles, it is millstone-like, resembling the motion of a millstone; and in the inhabited part of the earth, it is belt-like, resembling sword-belts.

The inhabited, populated portion of the earth is said to extend over sixty-odd degrees, a little more than one-sixth.

A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere. There we have presented evidence from the Quran and Sunnah, the statements of the Companions and Successors, and the other Muslim scholars who followed them, showing that the “celestial sphere” is round. Several scholars have reported the consensus of Muslim scholars on this, including Imam Abū al-Husayn ibn al-Munādī, who authored some “four hundred works” and belonged to the second generation of Ahmad’s followers; Abū Muhammad ibn Hazm; Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī; and others.

The point here is that when the sun rises over the easternmost lands, it is then either setting or approaching sunset over the westernmost lands. Its light extends ninety degrees ahead of it and ninety degrees behind it; this is the limit of its illumination. When it rises upon them, ninety degrees separate it from them, and the same applies to every land over which it rises. The astronomer distinguishes between degrees just as he distinguishes between hours, for each of the unequal, seasonal hours comprises fifteen degrees reckoned according to the time in question

so there are likewise ninety degrees between it and the west, in the westward direction. If this is so—and the descent mentioned in the prophetic hadith (may the finest blessings and peace be upon its speaker), recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim and unanimously deemed authentic by hadith scholars, occurs:

As for the versions mentioning a half or two-thirds, Muslim alone recorded them through some of its chains of transmission. Al-Tirmidhī said that the most authentic version reported from Abū Hurayrah is:

If the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also mentioned “the descent” when the first third of the night has passed and when half the night has passed, then his statement is true, for he is the truthful one whose truthfulness is confirmed.

The descent would then be of three kinds: first, when the first third of the night has passed; then, when half the night has passed, which is more pronounced; then, when a third of the night remains, which is the most pronounced of the three kinds.

When the expressions “night and day” are used without qualification in the language of the Lawgiver, daytime begins at dawn

However, when the Lawgiver, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, says “midday,” he means the midpoint of the daytime beginning at sunrise. Neither he nor any Muslim scholar ever uses “midday” to mean the midpoint of the daytime beginning at dawn, since that midpoint falls before the sun passes its zenith.

This is why a certain later jurist made a mistake upon reading the scholars’ statement that someone observing a voluntary fast may form the intention to fast before midday, while there are two opinions on whether he may do so afterward, both transmitted from Ahmad. He assumed that “daytime” here meant the fasting day, which begins at dawn. His mistake arose from failing to distinguish between what “daytime” denotes when used without qualification and what “midday” denotes. The day whose midpoint is meant in the words of the Lawgiver and the scholars of his community begins at sunrise, whereas daytime, when used without qualification in connection with the times of prayer and fasting, begins at dawn.

## Page 2333

As already explained, the third of the night in an eastern land occurs before the third of the night in a western land. The inhabited world extends over twelve hours of longitude, or 180 degrees. If it is said that their summer nights are short, the reply is that their winter nights are long: the one offsets the other, and whatever is lost from their summer nights is added to their winter nights. Hence the report:

“Winter is the believer’s spring: he fasts its days and spends its nights in prayer.”

This being so, if the descent were as some ignorant people imagine—that He comes to be beneath the heavens, above the lowest heaven, and beneath the Throne for a third of the night in each land—it would not merely follow that He remains beneath the Throne and beneath the heavens at all times. For that alone would be the necessary consequence only if all the inhabitants of each sixth of the inhabited world shared the same third of the night, making six thirds altogether. If He were then assumed to remain over these people for one third, then over those others for one third, it would follow that He remains at all times beneath the Throne, or beneath the heavens, or wherever the ignorant person imagines Allah to be confined, and thus is never above the Throne.

## Page 2335

But if each land has a third of the night distinct from the others, and the beginning in each land follows the other third by a reckoned interval, then likewise the third of the night in an eastern land ends before the third of the night in a western land ends. Moreover, even if these periods overlap, the descent over each land must continue throughout its people’s third of the night until their dawn breaks. This necessarily entails reckoning as many thirds as there are lands.

Furthermore, just as the third of the night varies with a land’s longitude, it also varies with its latitude. The farther north a land lies, the longer its nights are in winter and the shorter they are in summer. A land near the equator has shorter winter nights and longer summer nights than that northern land, so its nights and days are more nearly equal. Accordingly, the divine descent to each people lasts for the duration of their third of the night. Its duration thus varies according to the length of the night in the north and south, just as it varies in the east and west.

Moreover, when the final third of the night begins for one people, a moment later it begins in lands near them. Thus, the divine descent reported by the truthful Prophet whose truth is confirmed also takes place for those people when a third of their night remains, and so on to the farthest reaches of the inhabited world.

If, then, it were as the ignorant person imagines—that He is beneath the Throne, with a heaven above Him and a heaven beneath Him—this would be impossible in many respects.

“They have not given Allah His due honour. On the Day of Resurrection, the whole earth will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand. Glorified and exalted is He above what they associate with Him!”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections, in a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will grasp the earth and roll up the heavens in His right hand, and He will say: ‘I am the King! I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”

---

## Page 2341

The hadith of Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, is even more emphatic. The following wording is Muslim’s, reporting that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will roll up the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, then take them in His right hand. Then He will roll up the earths in His left hand and say: ‘I am the King! Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?’”

Muslim narrated it from Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah. ‘Uthmān ibn Abī Shaybah also narrated it, with the wording:

“Allah will roll up the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, then take them in His right hand and say: ‘I am the King! Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?’ Then He will roll up the earths, take them in His left hand, and say: ‘I am the King! Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?’”

In a hadith transmitted by ‘Abdullāh ibn Miqsam, ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Umar said:

“I saw the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on the pulpit, saying: ‘The Compeller takes hold of His heavens and His earth’—he clenched his hand, then began closing and opening it—‘and says: “I am the Most Merciful! I am the King! I am the All-Holy! I am the Source of Peace! I am the Giver of Security! I am the Guardian! I am the Almighty! I am the Compeller! I am the Supremely Great! I am the One who brought this world into being when it was nothing! I am the One who will bring it back! Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?”’ The Messenger of Allah swayed to his right and to his left, until I saw the pulpit moving from its very base, and I wondered: ‘Will it collapse beneath the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’”

This was narrated by Ibn Mandah, Ibn Khuzaymah, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī, Sa‘īd ibn Mansūr, and other leading hadith scholars, renowned for their mastery, critical discernment, and expertise. So if He, glorified be He, rolls up all the heavens in His right hand, and such is their magnitude in relation to Him—as

---

## Page 2342

Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah Most High be pleased with them both, said:

“The seven heavens, the seven earths, and everything within and between them are, in the hand of the Most Merciful, no more than a mustard seed in the hand of one of you.”

He, glorified be He, has made His greatness known to us to the extent that we can comprehend it, as ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Mājishūn said:

“By Allah, nothing conveyed to them the immensity of what He has described of Himself and what His grasp encompasses except the smallness of its counterpart in their own experience. Indeed, that is what He instilled in their minds and created their hearts to recognize.”

Allah Most High has said:

“No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision.”

Ibn Abī Hātim said in his Tafsīr (Quran commentary): Abū Zur‘ah narrated to us; Minjāb ibn al-Hārith narrated to us; Bishr ibn ‘Umārah narrated to us, from Abū Rawq, from ‘Atiyyah al-‘Awfī, from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning His words, glorified and exalted is He, “No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision”:

“If the jinn, humankind, devils, and angels, from their creation until their extinction, were arrayed in a single row, they would never encompass Allah.”—then how could any created thing, whether a heaven or anything else, contain One whose greatness is such? How could it be said that, when He descends to the lowest heaven, the Throne comes to be above Him, or that any created thing comes to contain and encompass Him, glorified and exalted is He?

If someone says, “He has power to do whatever He wills,” the reply is: Then say, “He, glorified and exalted is He, has the power to descend while remaining above His Throne.” If you appeal indiscriminately to absolute power and greatness, then whatever expresses greater power and greatness is more fitting to attribute to Him than what is not

---

## Page 2343

so. For if someone imagines that the Great One, than whom none is greater, can become so small that His tiny creature encompasses Him, and regards this as an expression of power and greatness, then his saying that He descends while retaining His greatness and His elevation above the Throne expresses still greater power and greatness. It also accords with revelation and reason.

This resembles what some people say, among them Abū Tālib al-Makkī, who said:

“If He wills, the smallest thing contains Him; if He wills, nothing contains Him. If He wishes, everything knows Him; if He does not wish, nothing knows Him. If He pleases, He is found with everything; if He does not please, He is found with nothing. He transcends bounds and measure, and precedes speech and decrees. His attributes are beyond enumeration, and His greatness has no limit. He is neither confined to a form, nor restricted to an attribute, nor subject to judgment by words. He does not manifest Himself with the same attribute twice, nor appear in the same form to two people. No two utterances come from Him with the same meaning. Rather, every manifestation of His has a form; for every servant there is an attribute when He appears; from every gaze comes speech, and through every word comes understanding. His manifestations have no end, and His attributes have no limit.”

I say: Abū Tālib—may Allah have mercy on him—and his companions, the Sālimiyyah, are followers of Shaykh Abū al-Hasan ibn Sālim, the companion of Sahl ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Tustarī. They are renowned for their spiritual knowledge, worship, asceticism, and adherence to the Sunnah and the community on most of the well-known positions of Ahl al-Sunnah. They affiliate themselves with two great imams of the Sunnah: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Sahl ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Tustarī. Some of them studied jurisprudence according to the school of Mālik ibn Anas, such as the household of Shaykh Abū Muhammad and others, while some follow the school of al-Shāfi‘ī.

---

## Page 2344

Thus, those with whom they affiliate themselves, whom they venerate and seek to follow, are imams of guidance—may Allah be pleased with them all. In this regard, they are like their counterparts among Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah. Scarcely any group among the later generations has been free of some error in its statements, owing to the many specious arguments spread by the people of innovation. Thus, in many works on the principles of jurisprudence, the foundations of religion, jurisprudence, asceticism, Quranic commentary, and hadith, an author mentions several views on a major foundational issue and recounts all manner of opinions, yet fails to mention the position with which Allah sent His Messenger. This is because he does not know it, not because he dislikes what the Messenger upheld.

Certain things appeared in their statements—they objected to some of what appeared in Abū Tālib’s statements concerning the divine attributes, such as indwelling and the like—which the imams of knowledge and religion condemned, accusing them of indwelling on that account. For this reason, Abū al-Qāsim ibn ‘Asākir criticized Abū ‘Alī al-Ahwāzī when the latter wrote an account of Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī’s faults, while the former wrote an account of his merits. Abū ‘Alī al-Ahwāzī belonged to the Sālimiyyah, and some people therefore accused them of indwelling. Judge Abū Ya‘lā also wrote a book refuting the Sālimiyyah.

The disputes between them and their opponents—such as Judge Abū Ya‘lā and others, as well as the followers of al-Ash‘arī and their other opponents—are like disputes among people generally: sometimes both truth and falsehood in their positions are rejected; sometimes something true in their position is rejected; sometimes falsehood is refuted with falsehood; and sometimes falsehood is refuted with truth.

---

## Page 2345

Likewise, al-Khatīb al-Baghdādī mentioned in his History that a number of scholars objected to certain statements of Abū Tālib concerning the divine attributes. Some of the indwelling expressed in Abū Tālib’s words spread to other shaykhs who learned from him, such as Abū al-Hakam ibn Barrajān and others.

As for Abū Ismā‘īl al-Ansārī, the author of Stations of the Wayfarers, his words contain nothing of universal indwelling. They do, however, contain something of particular indwelling with regard to the servant endowed with spiritual knowledge who reaches what he himself called “the station of divine oneness.” He disclosed concerning this what Abū Tālib did not disclose, though he expressed it allusively. As for “universal indwelling,” a considerable amount of it appears in Abū Tālib’s words, despite his disavowal of the term “indwelling.” He made many fine statements about divine oneness, such as:

“He is All-Knowing, never unknown; All-Powerful, never incapable; Ever-Living, never dying; Ever-Sustaining, never heedless; Forbearing, never foolish; All-Hearing, All-Seeing; a Sovereign whose dominion never passes away; eternal without time; the Last without limit; ever existent.”

He continued until he said:

“He is before everything, behind everything, above everything, and with everything. He hears everything and is nearer to everything than that thing is to itself. Yet He is not a locus for things, nor are things a locus for Him. He rose over the Throne as He willed, without specifying how or likening Him to creation. He has knowledge of all things and power over all things, and of all things

---

## Page 2346

He is all-encompassing.”

He mentioned further remarks concerning created things and how some encompass others, according to his understanding. He then said:

“Allah—majestic is His glory and exalted is His greatness—is a Being who exists independently, unique in His attributes and distinct from all His creation. He does not indwell bodies, nor do accidents inhere in Him. Nothing other than Him is within His Essence, nor is anything of His Essence within anything other than Him. Within creation there is only creation, and within the Essence there is only the Creator.”

I say: This negates indwelling, just as he negated it at the outset.

He then said:

“Section: The Testimony to Divine Oneness and a Description of Its Affirmation by Those Endowed with Certainty

The testimony of one endowed with certainty consists in his certainty that Allah is before everything and nearer than everything. He is the Giver and the Withholder, the One who guides and the One who leads astray. None gives or withholds, harms or benefits, except Allah, just as there is no god but Allah. He witnesses Allah’s nearness to him, His watching over him, His power over him, and His encompassing him. Thus his gaze and concern turn first to Allah, before anything else. He remembers Him in everything, empties his heart of everything else for Him, turns back to Him in everything, and worships Him to the exclusion of everything else.

He knows that Allah is nearer to his heart than his vein, nearer to his spirit than his life, nearer to his sight than his gaze, and nearer to his tongue than his saliva—with a nearness that He Himself has described, without drawing nearer or coming closer—and that He, exalted is He, is above the Throne throughout all this; that He is exalted, far above the earth, just as He is exalted, far above the Throne; and that His nearness to the earth and to everything is like His nearness

---

## Page 2347

to the Throne; and that the Throne does not touch Him in any sensory manner, nor has He taken up residence within it. He is not remembered within it through an inward thought; no eye gazes upon Him, nor can He be encompassed and thereby comprehended, for He, exalted is He, is veiled by His power from all His creation. The Throne has no share of Him except like the share of one who knows Him with certainty and experiences what He has enabled him to experience of Him: that Allah is above it, that the Throne rests secure through Him, and that Allah encompasses His Throne, above everything and above the underside of everything. Thus He is above the ‘above,’ beneath the ‘beneath.’ He is not bounded by a ‘beneath’ such that there would be an ‘above’ over Him, for He is the Most High, the Highest. Wherever He may be, no place is devoid of His knowledge and power. He is not bounded by any place; He is neither absent from any place nor located in any place.

‘Below’ pertains to what is lower, and ‘above’ to what is higher. He, glorified is He, is above every ‘above’ in height and above every ‘below’ in exaltedness. He is above the angels of the earth just as He is above the angels of the Throne and all possible places.

His place is His will, and His existence is His power. The Throne, the earth, and everything between them mark the bounds of creation, lower and higher, and are like a mustard seed in His grasp. He is higher than all this, encompassing it all, just as reason cannot comprehend Him and imagination cannot conceive how He is. There is no end to His height, nothing above His exaltedness, and no remoteness in His nearness.”

He went on to say:

“And nothing veils Allah from anything, nor is anything remote from Him. He is near to everything through His attribute, namely power and perception, while things are kept distant by their own attributes:

---

## Page 2348

namely, remoteness and veiling. Remoteness and distancing are governed by His will, while boundaries and regions are veils belonging to His creation.”

He went on to say:

“‘He is Allah in the heavens and on earth.’

‘Then He rose over the Throne.’

‘And He is with you wherever you are.’

He is neither joined to creation nor separate from it, neither in contact with the universe nor distant from it. Rather, He stands alone in Himself, unique in His attributes. He is not paired with anything, nor is anything coupled with Him. He is nearer than anything, with a nearness that is His attribute, and He encompasses everything with an encompassing that is His attribute. He is with everything, above everything, before everything and behind everything, through His exaltedness and His closeness, which is His nearness. He is beyond the surrounding expanse that lies beyond the bearers of the Throne, and He is nearer than the jugular vein, which is the spirit. Yet He is above everything and encompasses everything.

In all this, He, exalted is He, is not a place for anything, nor is anything a place for Him. Nothing is like Him in any of this. He has no partner in His dominion, no helper in His creation, no equal among His servants, and none resembles Him in His bringing things into existence. He is First in His lastness, with a firstness that is His attribute; Last in His firstness, with a lastness that is His attribute; Hidden in His manifestness, with a hiddenness that is His nearness; and Manifest in His hiddenness, with a manifestness that is His exaltedness. He has always thus been First and will forever thus be Last; He has always thus been Hidden and will forever thus be Manifest.”

He went on to say:

“He is upon His Throne, as He has declared concerning Himself. The Throne is the uppermost boundary of His creation, but He is not bounded by His Throne. The Throne needs a place, whereas the Lord, mighty and majestic, has no need of it. As He, exalted is He, says:

‘The All-Merciful rose over the Throne.’

‘The All-Merciful’ is a name, and rising over the Throne

---

## Page 2349

is His attribute, connected with His essence, while the Throne is His creation, separate from His attributes. He has no need of a place to contain Him or a bearer to carry Him.”

He went on to say:

“Nothing encompasses Him but His will. He appears only in the lights of His attribute and is found only in the vastness of expansion. When He contracts, He conceals what He has revealed; when He expands, He restores what He has concealed. Likewise, His fashioning in every form is a coming into being, and His action through every name is a place, whether great and manifest or subtle and hidden. Nothing encompasses Him but His will, in His nearness. He is known only through witnessing Him and seen only by His light. This belongs to His close servants today, in their hearts, while He remains unseen; and it will be theirs when they behold Him with their eyes. He is known only by His will: if He wills, the least thing encompasses Him; if He does not will, not even all things encompass Him. If He wishes, everything knows Him; if He does not wish, nothing knows Him. If He so loves, He is found with everything; if He does not so love, He is not found in anything.”

He then cited the remainder of his words, as we related earlier.

I say:

What he mentions here concerning His nearness and His being unrestricted, and that He does not manifest Himself with the same attribute twice or appear in the same form to two people, describes what appears to some spiritual wayfarers of His nearness to their hearts and His manifestation to their hearts. It does not mean that this describes Him as He actually is, or that these differing manifestations will occur to their eyes on the Day of Resurrection just as they occur here.

This is a matter in which many spiritual wayfarers fall into error: they witness things in their hearts and suppose that these things exist in external reality just as they witness them. Indeed, many of them, both earlier and later, suppose that they see Allah with their eyes because of what overwhelms their hearts

---

## Page 2350

of knowledge, remembrance, and love. They become oblivious to all else through witnessing what has arisen in their hearts, experiencing self-effacement and utter absorption. They imagine that this is something witnessed with their eyes, although it occurs only in the heart. Thus, many of them have imagined that they see Allah with their own eyes in this world.

This has happened to a number of people, both earlier and later, and it is an outright error. Indeed, their claims have even caused uncertainty among speculative thinkers and theologians who acknowledge, in principle, the possibility of seeing Allah but lack sufficient knowledge of the Sunnah to determine whether this occurs in this world. Some mention two opinions concerning its occurrence in this world, while others say that it is possible. All of this is misguidance. The imams of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah agree that no one sees Allah with their own eyes in this world. Their disagreement concerns only our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Several reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, state that we do not see Him in this world. Among them is the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said when speaking of the Dajjāl: ‘Know that none of you will see his Lord until he dies.’”

Moses son of Imrān, peace be upon him, asked to see Him. Allah, glorified is He, recounted His words:

“You will not see Me,”

and the loss of consciousness that befell Moses.

Some of these people say that Moses did see Him, and that the mountain was a veil between them; when He leveled the mountain, Moses saw Him. This appears in the writings of Abū Tālib and others like him. Others identify the seer with the One seen, namely Allah. They speak of union and say that He caused Moses to lose awareness of himself until

---

## Page 2351

the seer became the One seen. Thus, according to them, it was not Moses who saw Him; rather, He saw Himself through Himself. This is also what they claim for themselves. Yet union and indwelling are false. Even according to those who profess this, it occurs only inwardly, in the heart, not outwardly. At most, it amounts to what the Christians say about Christ, yet they have not claimed that anyone saw the inward divine nature clothed in human nature.

This error occurs frequently among those treading the spiritual path. They experience things inwardly and imagine that these exist outside themselves. In this respect, they resemble speculative philosophers and others who fall into error: they conceive things in their minds, such as universals, abstract entities, and the like, then imagine that these exist externally, whereas they exist only in their minds.

For this reason, Abū al-Qāsim al-Suhaylī and others say:

“We seek refuge in Allah from philosophical syllogisms and Sufi fantasies.”

This is why so many contradictions appear in the statements of both groups. As for those who combine unsound philosophical views with worthless Sufi fantasies, such as Ibn ʿArabī and his like, they are among the most misguided people on earth.

Al-Junayd, may Allah be pleased with him, the leader of the Sufis, was an imam of guidance who understood what some spiritual wayfarers experience. Thus, when asked about tawhīd, he said:

“Tawhīd is to distinguish the originated from the eternal.”

He thereby made clear that one must distinguish what has a beginning from what has none, warning against indwelling and union. Then came

---

## Page 2352

heretics such as Ibn ʿArabī and his like, who rejected this statement of al-Junayd because it invalidates their corrupt doctrine. Al-Junayd and those like him are imams of guidance; whoever opposes him in this matter is misguided. Other shaykhs likewise discussed what spiritual wayfarers experience and the lights and other things they see within their hearts, warning them not to suppose that these are Allah’s very essence, exalted is He.

ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr once asked ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar for his daughter’s hand in marriage while the latter was circumambulating the Kaʿbah. He replied:

“Do you speak to me about women while we behold Allah in our circumambulation?”

By all such statements, they did not mean that every veil between the heart and Allah is lifted until Allah’s very essence directly encounters the soul, as He sees Himself. This is not possible for anyone in this world. Those who considered it possible allowed it only for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as in Ibn ʿAbbās’s statement:

“Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice.”

Rather, this manifestation occurs through intermediaries, according to the servant’s faith, knowledge, and love. People’s experiences therefore vary, just as their visions of Allah Most High in dreams vary: each person sees Him according to his faith, and He is seen in various forms.

Statements such as these made by Abū Tālib and these men would be approximately correct if understood as referring to what occurs within hearts, although some of them remain open to question. But to say that the Lord Most High is like this in Himself is not correct.

As for his statement:

“Closer to the spirit than its life, closer to the faculty of sight than its seeing, and to

---

## Page 2353

the tongue than its saliva, with a nearness that is His attribute,” and his statement, “Closer than the jugular vein”—none of this is found in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Nor was it said by any of the early generations: neither the Companions, nor those who followed them in righteousness, nor the four imams and their peers among the imams of the Muslims, nor the exemplary shaykhs of spiritual knowledge and Sufism.

The Quran nowhere describes the Lord Most High as near to everything. Rather, the nearness mentioned in the Quran is particular, not universal, as in His words, Most High:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I respond to the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.”

He, glorified is He, is near to whoever calls upon Him. Likewise, the two Sahīh collections report from Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī that they were travelling with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and were raising their voices in proclaiming Allah’s greatness. He said:

“O people, take it easy on yourselves! You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who hears and is near. The One upon whom you call is nearer to each of you than the neck of his mount.”

He said, “The One upon whom you call is nearer to each of you.” He did not say that He is near to every existing thing. Similarly, the words of Sālih, peace be upon him:

“So seek His forgiveness, then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Near and Responsive,”

are like the words of Shu‘ayb:

“Seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.”

It is clear that His words “Near and Responsive” are linked to repentance and seeking forgiveness. What is meant is that He is near and responsive to those who seek His forgiveness and repent to Him, just as He is merciful and loving toward them. He has paired “Near” with “Responsive.” It is clear that He is not described as responsive to every existing thing; rather, He responds to those who ask Him and call upon Him. The same applies to His nearness, glorified and exalted is He.

---

## Page 2354

Allah’s names, when used without qualification—such as the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the All-Forgiving, the Most Appreciative, the Responsive, and the Near—need not apply to every existing thing. Rather, each name applies to what is appropriate to it. His name the All-Knowing applies to everything because everything can be known.

As for His words, Most High:

“We created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein, when the two recording angels record, seated on the right and on the left. Not a word does he utter without an observer beside him, ready to record.”

And His words:

“Then why, when the soul reaches the throat, while you are looking on at that moment—and We are nearer to him than you are, though you do not see—”

What is meant is His nearness to him through the angels. This is the interpretation known from the early Quran commentators among the righteous predecessors. They said: “The Angel of Death is nearer to him than his family, but you do not see the angels.”

One group interpreted “We are closer to him” as meaning through knowledge. Some said through knowledge and power; others used the wording “through power and sight.” These views are weak, for neither the Book nor the Sunnah describes Him as having a universal nearness to every existing thing, such that they would need to explain it as nearness through knowledge, power, and sight. However, when some people assumed that He was described as near to everything, they interpreted this to mean that He knows everything and has power over everything. It is as though they thought that the expression “nearness” was like the expression “being with.” For the expression “being with” in the surahs of

---

## Page 2355

al-Hadīd and al-Mujādalah occurs in His words, Most High:

“He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from heaven and what ascends into it. He is with you wherever you are, and Allah sees all that you do.”

And His words, Most High:

“There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth, nor among five but He is their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more but He is with them wherever they may be. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection.”

It is authentically reported that the righteous predecessors said: “He is with them through His knowledge.”

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and others stated that this was the consensus of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness. No one whose opinion carries weight disagreed with them on this. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Dahhāk, Muqātil ibn Hayyān, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others.

Ibn Abī Hātim said in his Quran commentary: “My father narrated to us: Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Maʿmar narrated to us, from Nūh ibn Maymūn al-Madrūb, from Bukayr ibn Maʿrūf, from Muqātil ibn Hayyān, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words, ‘He is with you wherever you are.’ He said: ‘He is upon the Throne, and His knowledge is with them.’”

He said: “It is also reported from Sufyān al-Thawrī that he said: ‘His knowledge is with them.’”

He also said: “My father narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Dawraqī narrated to us: Nūh ibn Maymūn al-Madrūb narrated to us: Bukayr ibn Maʿrūf narrated to us, from Muqātil ibn Hayyān, from al-Dahhāk ibn Muzāhim, concerning His words, ‘There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth,’ through to His words, ‘wherever they may be’:

---

## Page 2356

he said: ‘He is upon the Throne, and His knowledge is with them.’”

He also related it through another chain from this same Muqātil ibn Hayyān, who is trustworthy in Quranic exegesis and whose reliability has not been impugned as that of Muqātil ibn Sulaymān has.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ahmad said: “My father narrated to us: Nūh ibn Maymūn al-Madrūb narrated to us, from Bukayr ibn Maʿrūf: Abū Muʿāwiyah narrated to us, from Muqātil ibn Hayyān, from al-Dahhāk, concerning His words, Most High:

‘There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth, nor among five but He is their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more but He is with them wherever they may be.’

He said: ‘He is upon the Throne, and His knowledge is with them.’”

ʿAlī ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqīq said: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā, the companion of ʿUbādah, narrated to us: Maʿdān narrated to us—Ibn al-Mubārak said: ‘If anyone in Khurāsān is one of the abdāl, it is Maʿdān’—saying: ‘I asked Sufyān al-Thawrī about His words, “He is with you wherever you are.” He replied: “His knowledge.”’”

Hanbal ibn Ishāq said in his book al-Sunnah: “I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal: ‘What is the meaning of His words, Most High, “He is with you wherever you are,” and “There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth,” through to His words, Most High, “but He is with them wherever they may be”?’

He replied: ‘His knowledge. He is the Knower of the unseen and the seen, encompassing everything and witnessing it. He is the All-Knower of all that is unseen; He knows the unseen. Our Lord is upon the Throne, without limit or description. His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth.’”

Imam Ahmad discussed the meaning of Allah’s being with His creation at length in al-Radd ʿalā al-Jahmiyyah (Refutation of the Jahmiyyah).

The expression denoting Allah’s being with His creation occurs in the Book of Allah in a general sense, as in these two verses, and in a specific sense, as in His words:

---

## Page 2357

“Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good,”

and His words:

“Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see,”

and His words:

“Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us.”

If the intended meaning were that He is with everything in His essence, the general statement would contradict the specific one. For it is known that the words, “Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us,” were intended to single out the Prophet and Abū Bakr, excluding their unbelieving enemies. Likewise, His words, “Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good,” single them out, excluding the wrongdoers and the wicked.

Moreover, neither in Arabic usage nor anywhere in the Quran does the expression “being with” mean that one essence intermingles with another. Examples include His words:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those who are with him,”

and His words:

“Those will be with the believers,”

and His words:

“Fear Allah and be with the truthful,”

and His words:

“And strove alongside you.”

There are many such examples. Thus, His words, “He is with you,” cannot indicate that His essence is intermingled with the essences of created beings. Furthermore, He began the verse by mentioning knowledge and ended it by mentioning knowledge, so the context indicates that He meant that He knows them.

This matter has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it was explained that although the expression “being with” in Arabic conveys being together, companionship, and association, His being with His servants does not conflict with His being above His Throne. The implications of His being with them vary according to the context: He is with all creation through His knowledge, power, and sovereignty, while singling out some of them for His assistance, victory, and support.

Ibn Abī Hātim said: “I read to Muhammad ibn al-Fadl, who related: Muhammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqīq narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Muzāhim narrated to us: Bukayr ibn Maʿrūf narrated to us, from Muqātil ibn Sulaymān

---

## Page 2358

concerning the words of the Most High: ‘He knows what penetrates into the earth’—of rain; ‘and what emerges from it’—of vegetation; ‘and what descends from the heaven’—of rainfall; ‘and what ascends into it’—the angels who ascend to heaven. ‘And He is with you wherever you are’ means that He is with you through His power, sovereignty, and knowledge, wherever you are.

Through this same chain of transmission, Muqātil ibn Sulaymān said: ‘It has reached us—and Allah knows best—concerning the words of the Most High: “He is the First”—he said: before everything; “and the Last”—he said: after everything; “and the Outward”—he said: above everything; “and the Inward”—he said: nearer than everything. By nearness, we mean only His knowledge and power, while He is above His Throne. “And He has knowledge of all things”—He knows their private conversations and hears their speech, then on the Day of Resurrection He will inform them of everything they uttered, whether evil or good.’”

This report is not as widely known from Muqātil as the first, which has been transmitted from him through several routes. He did not assert what he said with certainty, but instead said, “It has reached us.” It was he who explained “the Inward” as “the Near,” then explained nearness in terms of knowledge and power. There is no need for this. It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You are the First, and there is nothing before You. You are the Last, and there is nothing after You. You are the Outward, and there is nothing above You. You are the Inward, and there is nothing beyond You.”

Reports have also come from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through Abū Hurayrah and Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with them both, explaining these names, as well as the hadith of “lowering.” We have discussed these at length in our treatment of the question of encompassing.

---

## Page 2359

Qatādah likewise mentioned this hadith in his commentary. It makes clear that “the Inward” does not mean nearness, nor does the word itself indicate that. Moreover, nearness is not spoken of in the Book and Sunnah with the same universal scope as being with. Nor, in Arabic and the Quran, does nearness have the same meaning as being with. When someone says, “This is with that,” he means togetherness, association, and companionship. This does not indicate that one of the two entities is near the other or intermingled with it.

Thus, when it is said, “He is with them,” this indicates that His knowledge, power, and sovereignty encompass them, while He is nevertheless above His Throne, as the Quran and Sunnah inform us. The Most High says:

“He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He knows what penetrates into the earth and what emerges from it, what descends from heaven and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are.”

He, glory be to Him, thus informs us that, despite being high above His Throne, He knows everything. His being on high does not prevent Him from knowing all things. Likewise, in the hadith of the mountain goats, recorded in the Sunan, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“And Allah is above His Throne, and He knows your circumstances.”

No comparable statement concerning nearness has been transmitted in which He says that He is above His Throne and near to everything. Rather, He says:

“Indeed, Allah’s mercy is near to those who do good.”

And He says:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. The One upon whom you call is All-Hearing, Near.”

Ibn Abī Hātim said: My father narrated to us: Yahyā ibn al-Mughīrah narrated to us: Jarīr narrated to us, from Abadah ibn
