Abī Barzah al-Sijistānī, from al-Salt ibn Hakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, who said:

When you instruct them to call upon Me and they call upon Me, I answer them.

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.”

He thus declared that He is near and answers supplications. A group among Ahl al-Sunnah interpret “nearness” in the verse and the hadith as knowledge, since this is what is sought: when He knows and hears the supplicant’s prayer, the supplicant’s aim is fulfilled. This is what led some to say that He is near to everything in the sense of knowledge and power. Some of the early generations said this, as previously related from Muqātil ibn Hayyān, as did many later scholars. However, none of them said that His very essence is near to everything. All Muslims acknowledge this meaning, both those who say that He is above the Throne and those who say that He is not above the Throne.

Ibn Abī Hātim related, with his chain of transmission, from Abd al-Azīz ibn Abd Allāh ibn Abī Salamah al-Mājishūn, who said:

He knows, while being thus, what is whispered by

## Page 2362

and cannot ward off death from him. Allah Most High has said:

And He Most High has said:

I say:

Several Quran commentators, including al-Thaʿlabī, Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī, and others, have likewise given this explanation of His words:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

As for His words, “And We are nearer to him than you are,” Abū al-Faraj mentioned both interpretations: that this refers to the angels—which he related from Abū Sālih, from Ibn ʿAbbās—and that it means nearness through knowledge.

Their point, in every case, is that these words do not mean that the Creator Himself—glorious and exalted is He—is near the servant’s jugular vein or the dying person. Since they understood this to refer to His nearness alone, rather than the angels’ nearness, they explained it in terms of knowledge and power, as with the wording concerning His being with His servants. Yet there is no need for this, for His words, “And We are nearer to him than you are,” mean “through Our angels” in both verses.

This differs from the wording concerning His being with His servants. He did not say, “And We are with him.” Rather, He identified Himself as the One who is with His servants and stated that He will inform them on the Day of Resurrection of what they did. He Himself is the One who created the heavens and the earth, and He Himself is the One who rose over the Throne. One expression must therefore not be treated like another when the Quran distinguishes between them.

Abū Hāmid likewise said the following, agreeing with Abū Tālib al-Makkī in some of what he said and differing with him in other respects. For he is among those who deny that Allah Himself is above the Throne; according to him, what is meant is only that He has power and dominion over it, or that He is superior to it.

He said:

“And He is established over the Throne in the manner He has stated

---

## Page 2363

and with the meaning He intended—an establishment free of contact, settling, occupying a place, indwelling, or movement from place to place. The Throne does not bear Him; rather, the Throne and its bearers are sustained by His subtle power and held subject within His grasp. He is above the Throne and above everything, down to the furthest depths of the earth.

His being above does not bring Him any closer to the Throne or heaven. Rather, He is exalted in rank above the Throne just as He is exalted in rank above the earth. Yet He is near every existing thing, nearer to the servant than his jugular vein, and a witness over all things. His nearness does not resemble the nearness of bodies, just as His essence does not resemble the essence of bodies. He does not dwell within anything, nor does anything dwell within Him.” He went on to say:

“He is distinct from His creation in His attributes. Nothing other than Him is within His essence, nor is His essence within anything other than Him.”

I say:

The being above that he mentions concerns power and dominion—“superiority in power”—and means that He is superior to created beings. The “nearness” he mentions is knowledge, or knowledge and power.

Muslims agree that His knowledge, power, and dominion encompass everything. A number of scholars have interpreted His nearness in this way because they thought that the nearness mentioned in the verse was His nearness alone. They therefore explained it as knowledge, since they understood it to apply universally. They said: “He is near every existing thing in the sense of knowing it.” Yet there is no need for this, as explained above.

His words:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein”

cannot mean knowledge alone. Someone who knows a thing better than another does is not said to be nearer to it than the other merely because of his knowledge of it, nor merely because of his power over it.

---

## Page 2364

Moreover, He—glorified and exalted be He—knows what is said secretly and what is said openly, and He knows the servant’s deeds. There is therefore no reason to single out the jugular vein by saying that He is nearer to the servant than it is. The jugular vein is close to the heart, not to the servant’s outward speech, whereas He knows both the outward and inward aspects of the human being.

The Most High says:

“Whether you conceal your speech or declare it openly, He knows well what is within the hearts.”

“Does He who created not know, when He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?”

The Most High also says:

“He knows the secret and what is even more hidden.”

And He says:

“Do they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private conversations, and that Allah is the Knower of all unseen things?”

And He says:

“Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Indeed We do, and Our messengers are with them, recording.”

And He says:

“Do you not see that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth? No three converse privately without Him being their fourth, nor five without Him being their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more without Him being with them wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah knows all things.”

Further evidence that nearness here does not mean knowledge is His saying:

“We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

“When the two recording angels record, one seated on the right and the other on the left.”

He states that He knows what the person’s soul whispers to him, then says:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

Thus He affirms knowledge and affirms nearness, presenting them as two distinct things; one must therefore not be equated with the other. He also qualifies this nearness by saying:

“When the two recording angels record, one seated on the right and the other on the left.”

“He utters no word but that beside him is”

## Page 2365

As for anyone who supposes that this means the Lord Himself is near the jugular vein, or that He Himself is nearer to the dying person than his family are, this interpretation is extremely weak. Those who say that He is everywhere, or that He Himself is near everything, do not single out some things rather than others. No Muslim could say that Allah is near the dying person but not his family, or near the jugular vein but not the other organs.

How could this statement be sound according to their own premise? In their view, He is throughout the human body, or near the entire human body; or He is within the dying person’s family just as He is within the dying person. How, then, could He say, “We are nearer to him than you are,” if He is with him and with them in exactly the same way? And could He be nearer to Himself than His own Self?

The context of both passages indicates that what is meant is the angels. For He says:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

“When the two recording angels record, one seated on the right and the other on the left.”

“He utters no word but that beside him is a watchful observer, ready.”

He thus qualifies this nearness by specifying this time: when the two recording angels record, one seated on the right and the other on the left. These are the two guardian angels who write down his deeds, as He says:

“He utters no word but that beside him is a watchful observer, ready.”

Clearly, if what was meant were the nearness of the Lord Himself, it would not be confined to this circumstance, and mentioning the two seated angels and the terms “watchful” and “ready” would have no relevant meaning.

The same applies to His words in the other passage:

“Then why, when the soul reaches the throat”

“while you at that moment

---

## Page 2366

look on.”

“And We are nearer to him than you are, but you do not see.”

Had He meant His own nearness, He would not have confined it to this circumstance, nor would He have said:

“But you do not see.”

Such a statement is only made when someone is present who can be seen under certain circumstances, but whom we do not see. Yet in this circumstance, neither the angels nor human beings see the Lord Most High.

Moreover, He says:

“And We are nearer to him than you are.”

He thus speaks of those who are nearer to the dying person than the people beside him at that moment. If the Lord Himself—glorified and exalted be He—is said to be in a place, or near every existing thing, this would not be confined to this time, place, or these circumstances; nor would He be nearer to one thing than another.

Nor can this mean the Lord’s special nearness, as in His words:

“And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near.”

That is His nearness to those who call upon Him or worship Him, whereas this dying person may be a disbeliever, a wicked person, a believer, or one brought near to Allah. Hence the Most High says:

“Then, if he is among those brought near,
there will be rest, bounty, and a Garden of Bliss.
And if he is among the companions of the right,
then peace be upon you from the companions of the right.
But if he is among the deniers who have gone astray,
then his welcome will be scalding water
and burning in Hellfire.”

Clearly, the Lord does not single out such a denier for His nearness rather than those around him, who may include believers.

Rather, those meant are the angels who attend both the believer and the disbeliever, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves.”

And He says:

“If you could but see when the angels take the disbelievers in death, striking their faces and their backs.”

And He says:

“If you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the throes of death and the angels are stretching out

their hands, saying, ‘Give up your souls! Today you will be repaid with the punishment of humiliation for saying what is untrue about Allah and arrogantly rejecting His signs.’”

When Allah Most High uses such wording in His Book, it indicates that He, glorified be He, performs the act through His hosts and helpers among the angels. For the form “We” is used by a great leader who is followed and obeyed, and who has hosts that carry out his commands. No one has hosts who obey him as the angels obey their Lord, who is their Creator and Lord. Thus He, glorified be He, knows what a person’s soul whispers to him, and His angels also know; the wording “We” is therefore appropriate here.

The same applies to His saying:

“And We know what his soul whispers to him.”

For He, glorified be He, knows this, and His angels know it too, as is established in the two authentic hadith collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said: “When a servant intends a good deed, one good deed is recorded for him; if he performs it, ten

---

## Page 2368

good deeds are recorded for him. When he intends an evil deed, it is not recorded against him; if he performs it, one evil deed is recorded against him. If he leaves it for Allah’s sake, it is recorded as a good deed.”

Thus, the angel knows what good or evil deed the servant intends. This does not mean that the angels possess the knowledge of the unseen that belongs exclusively to Allah. It is reported from Ibn ʿUyaynah that they smell a pleasant fragrance and know that the person has intended a good deed, and smell a foul odour and know that he has intended an evil deed. Yet even if they smell pleasant and foul odours, their knowledge does not depend on this. Rather, they know what is in the human heart; indeed, they see it and hear the soul’s whisperings. Satan even takes the person’s heart into his mouth: when Allah is remembered, he withdraws, and when the heart becomes heedless of remembering Him, he whispers. Satan knows whether the person remembers Allah or neglects His remembrance, and he knows the misguided desires that his soul craves, so he makes them attractive to him.

It is established in the Sahīh, in the hadith mentioning Safiyyah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Satan flows through the son of Adam as blood flows.”

The nearness of the angels and Satan to the human heart is attested by mass-transmitted reports, whether the servant is a believer or an unbeliever. But the notion that the Lord’s very essence is in the heart of every person, unbeliever or believer, is false. None of the early generations of this Ummah said this, nor is it stated in the Book or the Sunnah. Rather, the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus of the early generations, and reason all contradict it.

Thus, when Allah, glorified be He, mentioned His nearness to those who call upon Him and worship Him, He said:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I respond to the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.”

Here, it is He Himself, glorified be He

## Page 2369

and exalted, who is near and answers the supplicant’s call—not the angels. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith agreed to be authentic:

“You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and near. Indeed, the One upon whom you call is nearer to each of you than the neck of his mount.”

This is because Allah, glorified be He, is near to the supplicant’s heart, and thus nearer to him than the neck of his mount.

His nearness to the supplicant’s heart has one meaning agreed upon among those who affirm Allah’s attributes and hold that Allah is above the Throne, and another meaning over which there is disagreement. The meaning they agree upon consists in His drawing the supplicant’s heart near to Himself, just as He draws near to Himself the heart of the one prostrating. As is established in the Sahīh:

“The servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating.”

Thus, the Lord becomes near to the one prostrating, and his heart draws close to his Lord, even though his body is on the earth. Whenever either of two things draws near to the other, the other necessarily becomes near to it, even if we suppose that the other has itself made no movement—just as, when someone draws near to Mecca, Mecca becomes near to him.

Allah has described how those angels and human beings whom He brings near draw near to Him. He said:

“The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels brought near.”

And He said:

“And the foremost—the foremost! They are those brought near.”

And He, exalted be He, said:

“If he is one of those brought near, then there will be rest, bounty, and a Garden of Bliss.”

And He said:

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of approach to their Lord, each striving to be nearest.”

And He said:

“We called him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near in intimate converse.”

---

## Page 2370

As for the Lord’s nearness that subsists in Him through His own act, the Kullābiyyah deny this, as do those who deny that acts performed by His choice subsist in His essence. The early generations and the leading scholars of hadith and the Sunnah, however, do not deny it; nor do many speculative theologians. His descent every night to the lowest heaven, His descent on the afternoon of the Day of ‘Arafah, and similar acts fall into this category.

This is why His descent is specified as being to the lowest heaven. The same applies to His speaking to Moses, peace be upon him. For if what was intended were merely His bringing the pilgrims and those who stand in prayer at night near to Himself, His descent would not have been specified as being to the lowest heaven, just as no such specification was made regarding His answering the supplicant and the nearness of those who worship Him. Allah, exalted be He, said:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the supplicant’s call when he calls upon Me.”

And He said:

“Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by a cubit.”

In the agreed-upon sense, this increase consists in His bringing the servant nearer to Himself as a reward for the servant’s drawing near by his own choice. Whenever the servant draws near by a handspan of his own choice, the Lord brings him still nearer to Himself, until he is like one who has drawn near by a cubit. Likewise, the Lord’s nearness to the worshipper’s heart consists in the knowledge of the Lord and faith in Him that arise in the servant’s heart. This is the highest likeness, and there is no disagreement over this either.

Thus, the servant comes to love what the Lord loves and hate what He hates, to be an ally to those whom He befriends and an enemy to those whom He opposes. His will thus accords with what Allah commands, loves, and is pleased with. This is part of the servant’s allegiance to his Lord and the Lord’s friendship towards His servant. For friendship is the opposite of enmity: “friendship” entails love and agreement, whereas “enmity” entails hatred

---

## Page 2371

and opposition. It is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards a friend of Mine has challenged Me to war. Nothing brings My servant near to Me like fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he strikes, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I have never hesitated over anything I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike distressing him, yet he must inevitably face it.’”

Thus, He, glorified and exalted be He, has stated that the servant draws near through obligatory acts of worship and continues drawing near through voluntary acts until Allah loves him. The servant thus becomes beloved to Allah, as He, exalted be He, says:

“Indeed, Allah loves those who turn to Him in repentance and loves those who purify themselves.”

And He, exalted be He, says:

“In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.”

And He, exalted be He, says:

## Page 2372

Thus He has stated that He loves those who follow His Messenger and strive in His cause, and that He loves the God-fearing, the steadfast, those who turn to Him in repentance, and those who purify themselves. He, glorified be He, loves everything He has commanded, whether as an obligation or a recommendation.

His words:

“We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein”

entail that He, glorified be He, and His hosts entrusted with this know what the servant whispers within himself. As He says:

“Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Indeed We do, and Our messengers are with them, recording.”

Thus He hears, and those angels whom He wills hear—and whichever angels He wills.

As for recording, His messengers do the recording, as He says here:

“He does not utter a word except that beside him is an observer, ready to record.”

And He, exalted be He, says:

“Indeed, it is We who give life to the dead and record what they have sent ahead and the traces they leave behind.”

He thus speaks of recording using the word “We,” because His hosts record at His command. In the other verse, He distinguishes between hearing and recording, because He Himself hears, whereas deeds are recorded at His command, with the angels doing the recording.

His words:

“And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein”

are therefore like His words:

“And We record what they have sent ahead and the traces they leave behind.”

He said this because His angels draw near to the servant at His command, just as they record his deeds at His command. His nearness to everyone through the mediation of the angels is like His speaking to everyone through the mediation of the messengers, as He, exalted be He, says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who then reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

---

## Page 2373

Thus He speaks to all His servants through the mediation of the messengers; the other passage concerns His nearness to them at the approach of death and when words are spoken inwardly within the soul or outwardly upon the tongue. He, exalted be He, says:

“Indeed, over you are watchers—noble scribes who know whatever you do.”

Some have mistakenly thought that it is He Himself from whom the Quran is heard, and that He Himself recites it without an intermediary whenever any reciter recites it, just as they erred concerning nearness. These are a group drawn from the later adherents of hadith and the later Sufis.

Some people interpret the statement, “He is nearer to everything than that thing is to itself,” as meaning that things have no existence in themselves: they exist only because the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, creates them, and they endure because He sustains their existence. Whatever He, glorified and exalted be He, wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. Nothing exists except through His bringing it into existence, and nothing endures except through His sustaining it. If it were supposed that He had not willed to create them and bring them into being, they would have remained nonexistent, with no existence whatsoever. Thus He is nearer to them than their own selves are. Bringing a thing into being, creating it, and giving it existence are the acts of the Lord, glorified and exalted be He; through this, the thing exists and becomes an actual entity in the external world.

Whatever exists is always in need of its Creator and cannot dispense with Him for even the blink of an eye. It therefore exists in relation to its Creator, but is nonexistent in relation to itself, for, considered in itself, it has no claim to anything but nonexistence. In this respect, the Lord is nearer to created things than they are to themselves.

Some may interpret His words, exalted be He,

“Everything will perish except His Face,”

in this sense: all things, considered in themselves, are pure nonexistence and sheer negation; they exist only

---

## Page 2374

fully by virtue of their relation to the Creator, namely their dependence on Him and on His will and power. In this respect they exist, whereas considered in themselves they can only be nonexistent.

They may also interpret in this sense the words of Labīd:

“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.”

Nor should it be said that this proposition is correct in itself, for things would not exist had Allah not created them, nor would they endure had He not sustained them.

Speculative thinkers have debated the reason for their dependence on Him. Is it temporal origination—so that they need Him only when they are brought into being, as maintained by those among the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and others who hold this view? Or is it contingency, which is thought to obtain without temporal origination, with the contingent, caused being instead being eternal and beginningless, and its dependence during its continued existence being possible without temporal origination, as Ibn Sīnā and a group of others maintain?

Both views are mistaken, as has been explained at length elsewhere. It has also been shown that contingency and temporal origination necessarily entail one another. This is the position of the great majority of rational thinkers, both earlier and later, including even the ancient philosophers such as Aristotle and his followers. They too hold that every contingent being originates in time. It was only Ibn Sīnā and a group of others who differed with them on this point. For this reason, his fellow philosophers, such as Ibn Rushd and others, rejected this view of his.

Created beings depend on the Creator. Dependence is therefore an enduring, inseparable attribute of theirs: they never cease to need Him.

---

## Page 2375

And contingency and temporal origination are two indications of dependence; these two attributes do not make a thing dependent. Rather, things’ dependence on their Creator is inseparable from them and requires no cause, just as the Lord’s self-sufficiency is inherent in His essence and requires no cause. Likewise, a created being requires no cause to account for its dependence. It is dependent by its very nature: its essence cannot be anything but dependent, with a dependence inseparable from it, and it can find sufficiency only through Allah. This is one of the meanings of al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient): the One upon whom everything depends, while He needs nothing. Indeed, things depend on Him both in respect of His lordship and His right to worship. Whatever does not come into being through Him cannot exist; whatever is not for His sake cannot be sound, beneficial, or lasting.

This is the full import of His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Had He not created anything by His will and power, nothing would have existed. All actions are corrupt unless they are for His sake—with Him as the object of worship, the One sought and loved for His own sake. For movements require a final cause just as they require an efficient cause. Indeed, it is the final cause that makes the agent act; without it, the agent would not act.

Thus, were He not the One worshipped and loved for His own sake, no action or movement could ever be sound; rather, the world would fall into ruin. This is the meaning of His words:

“Had there been in them both gods besides Allah, both would have fallen into ruin.”

He did not say, “Both would have ceased to exist.” This is also the meaning of Labīd’s words:

“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.”

---

## Page 2376

And this is like the transmitted supplication:

“I testify that every object of worship, from Your Throne to the depths of Your earth, is false except Your noble Face.”

The term bātil (“vain” or “false”) can refer to what is nonexistent or to what brings no benefit, as in the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Every pastime a man engages in is vain except shooting with his bow, training his horse, and playing with his wife, for these are beneficial pursuits.”

Likewise, his words concerning ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him:

“This man does not love what is vain.”

Another example is the statement of al-Qāsim ibn Muhammad when asked about singing. He said, “When Allah separates truth from falsehood on the Day of Resurrection, in which of the two will He place singing?”

The questioner replied, “Among falsehood.”

He said, “What is there beyond truth except error?”

Another example is the saying of Allah Most High:

“That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood.”

For those deities exist, but worshipping and invoking them is vain and brings no benefit. The aim sought through them is not attained and is thus vain. Belief in their divinity is false—that is, it does not correspond to reality. Their possessing divinity in themselves is also false, but not in the sense of being nonexistent.

Another example is His saying, Exalted is He:

“Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes.”

And His saying:

“And say, ‘Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is bound to vanish.’”

A lie is false because it does not correspond to reality, and every act that brings no benefit is vain because it has no real, praiseworthy end.

## Page 2377

Thus, the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The truest words ever spoken by a poet are the words of Labīd: ‘Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.’”

means that every object of worship besides Allah is false, as in His saying:

“That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Such is Allah, your true Lord. What is there beyond truth except error? How, then, are you turned away?”

And He says:

‘Uthmān, or someone else, visited Ibn Mas‘ūd while he was ill and asked, “How do you feel?” He replied, “I feel that I am being returned to Allah, my true Master.”

Allah Most High says:

“On that Day Allah will pay them their just recompense in full, and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth.”

They had already acknowledged His existence in this world, but on that Day they will know that He alone, to the exclusion of all else, is the Manifest Truth. Hence His words, “He is the Truth,” employ a construction expressing exclusivity. For on that Day no one will still claim divinity, nor will anyone associate anyone with his Lord.

## Page 2378

Section

Once the Lord’s absolute freedom from all attributes of deficiency is understood, it follows that He must not be described as being below anything, nor may anything be above Him in any respect. Rather, He is the Most High, the Highest, who can only be above all. He is the Manifest, above whom there is nothing, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed us. Nothing is like Him in the actions ascribed to Him, whether intransitive or transitive—neither in His descending, nor in His rising, nor in anything else.

Alongside this, it is obligatory to affirm whatever He has affirmed of Himself in His Book and through His Messenger. Sound rational proofs agree with this and do not contradict it. Rather, revelation and reason contradict innovations that oppose the Book and the Sunnah. The early generations—indeed, the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness—affirmed His actions, such as His rising and descending, as they are.

Abū Muhammad ibn Abī Hātim said in his Tafsīr:

‘Isām ibn al-Rawwād narrated to us: Ādam narrated to us: Abū Ja‘far narrated to us, from al-Rabī‘, from Abū al-‘Āliyah, who explained the words, “Then He rose toward heaven,” by saying: “He rose.”

He said: “The same was also reported from al-Hasan—meaning al-Basrī—and al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas.”

Al-Bukhārī also mentioned in his Sahīh, in the Book of Divine Oneness: Abū al-‘Āliyah said:

---

## Page 2379

“He rose toward heaven”: He rose, then perfected their creation.

Mujāhid said:

“‘He rose over the Throne’: He rose above the Throne.”

Ibn Abī Hātim likewise mentioned this in his Tafsīr concerning the words, “Then He rose over the Throne.” Through this chain, reports were transmitted from Abū al-‘Āliyah, al-Hasan, and al-Rabī‘ to the same effect as Abū al-‘Āliyah’s statement. He also transmitted through his chain, concerning “Then He rose over the Throne,” the statement: “On the seventh day.”

Abū ‘Amr al-Talamankī said:

## Page 2380

Abū ‘Ubaydah Ma‘mar ibn al-Muthannā:

‘When you and those with you have boarded the ship.’

He also says:

‘So that you may mount their backs.’

And:

meaning that He rose above the Throne.

The statement of al-Hasan and that of Mālik are among the finest and most comprehensive answers given on this question: this answer rejects specifying how, while affirming rising in its understood meaning. The scholars have followed Mālik’s statement, considering it excellent and commendable.”

He then discussed the invalidity of interpreting ‘rose’ as ‘gained mastery.’

Al-Tha‘labī said: “Al-Kalbī and Muqātil said that ‘Then He rose over the Throne’ means ‘He settled.’” He said: “Abū ‘Ubaydah said: ‘He ascended.’ It was also said: ‘He gained mastery,’ and it was said: ‘He took possession.’”

He himself preferred the interpretation he reported from al-Farrā’ and a group of scholars: that it means He turned to creating the Throne and directed Himself to its creation. He said: “This is supported by His words, ‘Then He turned toward heaven while it was smoke,’ meaning that He directed Himself to creating heaven.”

This interpretation is among the weakest, for He has stated that the Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth. Likewise, it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah existed, and there was nothing before Him. His Throne was upon the water, and He recorded everything in the Record, then created the heavens and the earth.”

---

## Page 2381

If the Throne was created before the creation of the heavens and the earth, how could His rising mean that He directed Himself to creating it—even supposing that the expression “He rose over such-and-such” were known in the language to mean that He directed Himself to bringing it into being? Yet no such usage is known in the language at all, whether literal or figurative, in either poetry or prose.

Those who said that “rose” means “directed Himself” mentioned this in connection with His words:

“Then He turned toward heaven while it was smoke.”

This is because the verb is followed by the directional preposition “to,” just as one says, “I directed myself to such-and-such” or “I turned to such-and-such,” but not “I directed myself over such-and-such” or “I turned over it.” Nevertheless, the interpretation given for that verse is likewise unknown in the language, nor was it the view of any Quran commentator among the early generations. Rather, their interpretation was contrary to this, as we have already related from some of them.

This interpretation and others like it were only introduced into Islam when people began denying the Lord’s acts that subsist in Him and that He performs by His power, will, and choice. Some then began interpreting the Quran in ways incompatible with this, just as all other adherents of religious innovation interpret the Quran to suit their own doctrines. As for this interpretation being transmitted from any of the early generations, it was not. Rather, the statements reliably transmitted from them agree on this matter. They are not known to have held two differing views on it, as they sometimes did concerning certain verses. Although their expressions differed, their intended meaning was one: affirming Allah’s exaltedness above the Throne.

If it is asked: If Allah is always above created things, as explained earlier, how can it be said, “Then He rose to heaven while it was smoke,” or, “Then He rose above the Throne”?

The reply is: This is just as He has informed us

---

## Page 2382

that He descends to the lowest heaven and then rises; another reported wording is, “then He ascends.” He—glory be to Him—has always been above the Throne, for His ascent is of the same kind as His descent. If nothing among created things comes to be above Him when He descends, then He—glory be to Him—ascends even though none of them is above Him.

As for His words:

“Then He rose to heaven,”

they explained this as meaning that He rose because He had said beforehand:

“Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days, and set up equals to Him? That is the Lord of all worlds.”

“He placed firm mountains upon it, blessed it, and apportioned its sustenance in four days, equally for all who ask.”

“Then He rose to heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly.’ They both said, ‘We come willingly.’”

“So He formed them into seven heavens in two days.”

This was revealed in Surah (Hā Mīm) in Mecca. Then Allah revealed Surah al-Baqarah in Medina:

“How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were lifeless and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then bring you to life, and then to Him you will be returned.”

“He is the One who created for you everything on earth, then rose to heaven and fashioned them into seven heavens. And He has knowledge of all things.”

Since He stated that His rising to heaven occurred after He had created the earth and everything in it, this conveyed the meaning of ascent: heaven is above the earth, so rising to it means ascending to it.

If it is asked: Since He rose over the Throne only after creating the heavens and the earth in six days, does that mean He was not over the Throne before that?

The reply is: Rising over is a particular kind of elevation. Everything that has risen over something is above it, but not everything above something has risen over it. Hence, not everything above something else is said to rise over it or to have risen over it.

---

## Page 2383

but everything said to have risen over something else is above it. What Allah stated occurred after the creation of the heavens and the earth was “rising over,” not elevation as such. It is also possible that He had risen over it before creating the heavens and the earth, when His Throne was upon the water; then, when He created this world, He was above it without having risen over it; then, when He created this world, He rose over it. The fundamental principle is that His elevation above created things is an inseparable attribute of His, just as are His greatness, majesty, and power. As for “rising over,” it is an act that He—glorified and exalted be He—performs by His will and power. Hence His words:

“Then He rose over.”

For this reason, rising over is among the attributes known through revelation and established by transmitted reports. His elevation above created things, however, is regarded by the leading scholars who affirm the divine attributes as one of the attributes known through reason as well as revelation. This is the position adopted by Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb and others, the later of the two views held by al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, and the position of the vast majority of the people of the Sunnah and hadith and the thinkers who affirm the divine attributes.

This matter and others like it have confused many people only because they have come to suppose that the attributes ascribed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are of the same kind as those ascribed to their own bodies. They therefore think that this entails combining two opposites, since being above the Throne while descending would be impossible for bodies like theirs. Yet something that helps them understand how this is possible is knowledge of their own souls, their attributes, and their actions: the soul may ascend from a sleeping person to heaven without having left the body. As the Exalted says:

“Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others for a specified term.”

Likewise, concerning one who prostrates, it was said by

---

## Page 2384

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The closest a servant is to his Lord is while he is prostrating.”

Likewise, the soul draws near to Allah at times other than prostration, even while remaining in the body. Hence some of the early generations said: “Hearts wander: one heart wanders around the Throne, while another wanders around the privy.”

When the soul is taken, it is raised to Allah in the briefest time, then returned to the body and questioned while within it. If it were the physical body that ascended and descended, this would take a long time. The same applies to what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described concerning the state of the deceased in his grave and his questioning by Munkar and Nakīr. The hadiths concerning this are numerous. It is established in the two Sahīh collections, in a hadith narrated by al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the deceased is made to sit up in his grave, he is approached and then testifies that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah. This is what His words mean: ‘Allah makes those who believe steadfast with the firm word, in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.’”

Likewise, in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, Qatādah narrates from Anas that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a servant is placed in his grave and his companions depart—he can even hear the sound of their sandals—two angels come to him and sit him up. They ask him, ‘What did you use to say about this man, Muhammad?’ He replies, ‘I bear witness that he is Allah’s servant and Messenger.’ He is then told, ‘Look at your place in the Fire. Allah has replaced it with a place in Paradise.’” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “He sees them both.

---

## Page 2385

As for the disbeliever and the hypocrite, he says, ‘Ah, ah! I do not know. I used to say what people said. I heard people saying something, so I said it.’ He is told, ‘You neither knew nor followed!’ He is struck with an iron hammer between his ears and lets out a scream heard by those nearby, except mankind and jinn.”

People hold “three views” concerning such matters. Some deny altogether that the deceased is made to sit up, because his body is surrounded by stones and earth that would prevent him from sitting. He may be enclosed tightly within rock, or something may be placed upon his body and later uncovered, only to be found unchanged, and so forth. For this reason, some have concluded that the punishment of the grave affects the soul alone, as Ibn Maysarah and Ibn Hazm maintain. This view is rejected by Sunni Muslims generally.

Others hold that the body itself sits up, according to their understanding of the texts. Still others appeal to Allah’s power and the report of the truthful Messenger, without considering what is known through sense perception and direct observation. Allah’s power is real, and the truthful Messenger’s report is true; the issue, however, lies in their understanding.

When it is understood that a sleeper remains asleep while his soul sits up, stands, walks, goes about, and speaks, and various actions and activities take place within his body in conjunction with his soul, bringing pleasure and torment to both his body and soul—even though his body is lying down, his eyes are closed, and his mouth is shut

---

## Page 2386

and his limbs are motionless, although his body may move because of the strength of the movement within him, and he may rise, walk, speak, and cry out because of the intensity of what is happening within him—this provides an analogy for understanding the condition of the deceased in his grave. His soul sits up, takes its seat, is questioned, experiences bliss and punishment, and cries out, all in connection with his body, even while it lies in the grave.

What he experiences may become so intense that its effects appear in his body. He may even be seen outside his grave, undergoing punishment, with the angels of punishment appointed over him; his body moves, walks, and emerges from his grave. More than one person has heard the voices of those being punished in their graves. People have been seen emerging from their graves while undergoing punishment, and others have been seen whose bodies sit up when the experience becomes intense. But this does not necessarily happen to every deceased person, just as not every sleeper’s body sits up in response to what he sees in sleep. Rather, it depends on the intensity of the experience.

It is known that many bodies are not consumed by the earth, such as the bodies of the Prophets, of the steadfastly truthful who are not Prophets, of the martyrs of Uhud, and of others besides those martyrs. Reports of this are mass-transmitted. The point, however, is that the Prophet’s unqualified statement about the deceased being made to sit up—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—encompasses their sitting up inwardly, even while the outward body remains lying down.

Something similar is found in his account—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—of the Prophets he saw in the heavens on the night of the Ascension. He saw Adam, Jesus, John, Joseph, Idrīs, Aaron, Moses, and Abraham—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them. He also reported that he saw Moses standing in prayer in his grave, yet he also saw him in the heavens. It is known that the bodies of the Prophets are in their graves, except for Jesus and Idrīs. And if Moses was standing in prayer in his grave, and the Prophet then saw him in heaven

---

## Page 2387

—the sixth—within so short a time, then this is something that does not occur with the body.

The descent of the angels—Gabriel and others, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them—also falls into this category. Once it is understood that the movement, ascent, descent, and other actions ascribed to angels and human souls do not resemble the movement of human bodies or other things we see with our eyes in this world, and that things are possible for them which are not possible for human bodies, then such attributes ascribed to the Lord are all the more possible and all the further removed from resembling the descent of bodies. Indeed, His descent does not resemble the descent of angels or human souls, even though their descent is closer than the descent of their bodies.

If the deceased’s sitting in his grave is not like bodily sitting, then the expressions “sitting” and “being seated” concerning Allah Most High, found in reports from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—such as the hadith of Ja‘far ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and the hadith of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and other reports, are all the more unlike the attributes of the bodies of His servants.

---

## Page 2388

Section

The disagreement over the meaning of the “hadith of the descent” and similar passages in the Quran and Sunnah concerning intransitive acts attributed to the Lord—glorified and exalted is He—such as coming, arriving, ascending to heaven and rising over the Throne, and indeed concerning transitive acts such as creating, bestowing kindness, acting justly and so forth, arises from disagreement over two fundamental questions.

The first is whether any act subsists in the Lord Most High, such that His creation of the heavens and the earth is an act He performed, distinct from what He created; or whether His act is itself the thing acted upon, and creating is itself what is created. There are two well-known views on this.

The first is the view transmitted from the early generations. It is what al-Bukhārī reported from the scholars without qualification in his book The Creation of Human Acts, mentioning no disagreement on the matter. Likewise, al-Baghawī and others presented it as the position of Ahl al-Sunnah. Abū ‘Alī al-Thaqafī, al-Duba‘ī and other companions of Ibn Khuzayma also stated it in the creed which they and Ibn Khuzayma agreed represented the position of Ahl al-Sunnah. Al-Kalābādhī likewise stated it in his book “An Introduction to the Doctrine of

---

## Page 2389

Sufism,” identifying it as the doctrine of the Sufis. It is also the well-known position of the Hanafis. Some writers on “speculative theology,” such as al-Rāzī and others, frame the disagreement on this issue as a dispute with the Hanafis, leading readers to suppose that this view is peculiar to them. Yet it is the position of all the early generations and the great majority of the various groups. It is also the position of the majority of Ahmad’s followers—all the earlier ones and most of the later ones—and one of the two views held by al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā.

Likewise, it is the position of the leading Mālikīs, Shāfi‘īs and scholars of hadith, and of most speculative theologians—such as the Hishāmiyya—or many of them; of all the Karrāmiyya; of some of the Mu‘tazila; and of many leading philosophers, both early and later.

Other speculative theologians—the Jahmiyya, most of the Mu‘tazila and the Ash‘arīs—held that the act of creation is identical with the created thing itself. According to them, Allah’s making, acting, creating and originating are nothing other than the created things themselves. This is also the position of a group of later philosophers—if they affirm that the Lord is an originator—such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him.

The well-known argument of these speculative theologians is that, if He created things through an act of creation, that act must be either eternal or originated in time. If it were eternal, every created thing would necessarily be eternal, which is a denial of the obvious. If it originated in time and subsisted in the Lord, this would entail that events originating in time subsist in Him. If it did not subsist in Him, the act of creation would subsist in something other than the Creator, which is impossible. Whether it subsisted in Him or not, that act of creation would require another act of creation, entailing an infinite regress. This is their principal argument.

The early generations and the majority answer this argument by rejecting its premises, each group rejecting a particular premise. They thereby confront its proponents with an objection from which they have no escape.

---

## Page 2390

As for the first premise, namely their statement, “If the act of creation were eternal, the created thing would necessarily be eternal,” this is disputed by those who hold that creation is an eternal act subsisting in the Creator, while the created thing originates in time. This position is held by some among the Kullābiyya, Hanafis, Hanbalis, Shāfiʿīs, Mālikīs, Sufis and scholars of hadith. They say: “You agree with us that His will is eternal and beginningless, although what He wills comes later. Likewise, the act of creation is eternal and beginningless, although the created thing comes later. Whatever you say concerning the will, we will bind you to its counterpart concerning the act of creation.” This is a dialectical rebuttal that binds them to the implications of their own position, and they have no way out of it.

As for the second premise, namely their statement, “If the act of creation originated in time and subsisted in the Lord, this would entail that events originating in time subsist in Him, which is impossible,” this is disputed by the early generations, the leading scholars of hadith, the foremost philosophers and many of their early and later representatives, and many speculative theologians, such as the Hishāmiyya and the Karrāmiyya. They say: “We do not concede that this consequence is impossible.” This will be discussed, Allah Most High willing, under the “Second Principle.”

As for the third premise, namely their statement, “If it did not subsist in Him, that would be impossible,” this is disputed only by certain groups of speculative theologians among the Muʿtazila and others. Some of them say: “Rather, the act of creation subsists in the created thing.” Others say: “Rather, the act of creation is not in any substrate,” just as the Basran Muʿtazila speak of “an act through a will that subsists in no substrate.” This is impossible, and I know of no one among the early generations, scholars of hadith, jurists, Sufis or philosophers who held this view.

---

## Page 2391

As for the fourth premise, namely their statement, “An act of creation that originates in time requires another act of creation,” this is disputed by the great majority of those who affirm an act of creation originating in time among scholars of hadith, speculative theology, philosophy, jurisprudence and Sufism, and others. These include Abū Muʿādh al-Tūmanī, Zuhayr al-Ibarī, the Hishāmiyya, the Karrāmiyya, Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī al-Asbahānī and his followers, and the scholars of hadith and early generations mentioned by al-Bukhārī and others.

They say: “If He creates the heavens and the earth through an act of creation, it does not follow that this act of creation must require another act of creation. Rather, that act of creation comes about through His power and will, even though it originates in time.”

The proof that the consequence they seek to impose is invalid is that either power and will suffice to bring about something that originates in time, or they do not. If they do not suffice, their claim that created things come into existence through power and will alone, without an act of creation, is invalidated. Once their claim is invalidated, it becomes clear that a created thing must have a Creator who created it—which is precisely the point to be established.

If power and will suffice to bring a created thing into existence, then this act of creation, through which He creates created things, may likewise come about through power and will, without requiring another act of creation. Thus, on either supposition, it is not necessary to say, “Created things were created without an act of creation.” Rather, one may say, “They were created through an act of creation”—which is precisely the point to be established.

It also becomes clear that the proponents of negation never advance an argument based on a premise without having contradicted that premise elsewhere. Thus, all the premises of their argument are contradicted.

Moreover, it is rationally evident that an effect, separate from the agent who produces it, can only come about

---

## Page 2392

through an act that inheres in the agent himself. As for the act itself, which inheres in him, it requires no further act, but comes about through his power and will.

For this reason, those who hold this view say that the act of creation originates in time (hādith), but do not say that it is created. They differ, however, over whether it may be called muhdath (newly brought about), holding two views.

Likewise, they say that He speaks by His will and power, and that His speech is discourse (hadīth)—indeed, the finest discourse. They unanimously agree that it is not created, and it is described as both hadīth and hādith. They also hold two views on whether it may be called muhdath.

For those who customarily use the term muhdath only for a created thing separate from Allah—as was the prevalent usage among those who debated the Quran during the ordeal of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, and who understood muhdath to mean nothing other than a created thing separate from Allah—Ahl al-Sunnah do not permit the Quran to be called muhdath in this sense. Rather, whoever calls it muhdath has thereby called it created.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad objected to “Dāwūd” using this expression when he received a written report that Dāwūd had said it. Those who employed this terminology assumed that this was what Dāwūd meant, so the imams of the Sunnah rejected it. Yet Dāwūd himself did not intend this meaning. Rather, he and the leading scholars among his followers agree that Allah’s speech is uncreated. He intended only that it inheres in Allah Himself. This is the position of more than one imam of the early generations, including al-Bukhārī and others. The disagreement over this among Ahl al-Sunnah is “terminological”: they agree that it is not a created thing separate from Allah, and that Allah’s speech inheres in His essence. The imams of the Sunnah—

---

## Page 2393

such as Ahmad and his peers, al-Bukhārī and his peers, Dāwūd and his peers, Ibn al-Mubārak and his peers, Ibn Khuzaymah, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, and others—agreed that Allah speaks by His will and power. None of them said that the Quran is eternal; the first person widely known to have said this was Ibn Kullāb. Imam Ahmad used to warn against the Kullābiyyah and instructed that al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī be shunned because he belonged to them.

It has been reported that al-Hārith abandoned Ibn Kullāb’s position concerning the Quran and used to say that Allah speaks with a voice. Among those who related this about him was al-Kalābādhī in his book al-Ta‘arruf li-Madhhab al-Tasawwuf (An Introduction to the Doctrine of Sufism).

The point here is that the claim, “If His act of creating things were not identical with those things, the act of creation would require another act of creation, and would therefore itself be created,” is untenable. Rather, the act of creation comes about through the Lord’s power and will, while the created thing comes about through the act of creation.

As for the fifth premise, namely that this leads to an infinite regress, it can be formulated in two ways:

(First: the act of creation requires another act of creation, which in turn requires another act of creation, as discussed above.

Second: suppose that it does not require another act of creation; it nevertheless requires a cause through which the act of creation comes about, even if that cause is not called an act of creation. That cause became complete only upon the occurrence of

---

## Page 2394

the act of creation; its becoming complete is therefore a new occurrence, and every new occurrence must have a cause. For if that act of creation did not require a newly arising cause, this would entail something coming into being without a newly arising cause.

If it is said that the complete cause is eternal, this would entail the effect being delayed beyond its complete cause, which is impossible.

Those who maintain that the act of creation is distinct from the created thing, and that the act of creation comes into being, offer four answers here.

The first is the position of those who say that the act of creation, though it comes into being, requires no newly arising cause—neither another act of creation nor anything else. They say:

“All of you who dispute our position maintain that something can come into being without a newly arising cause. For whoever says that the created thing is distinct from the act of creation holds that all created things come into being without a newly arising cause. And whoever says that the act of creation is eternal must acknowledge that what is eternal is not confined to any particular time. Thus, no newly arising cause has come about for the created thing that comes into being at its appointed time.”

They say:

“Since this consequence follows on every supposition, the burden of answering it does not fall on us alone. Rather, we say that the created thing came into being through the act of creation, and that the act of creation came about through Allah’s power and His eternal will, without requiring any other cause.”

This is the position of many groups among the adherents of hadith and speculative theology, such as the Karrāmiyyah and others.

The second answer is the position of those among the Mu‘tazilah who say that the act of creation, which comes into being, subsists in the created thing, or subsists without a substrate. Similarly, they say that the will comes into being without subsisting in a substrate and without any cause necessitating its coming into being; rather, He brings it into being solely through His power.

---

## Page 2395

The third answer:

This is the answer of Ma‘mar and his followers, who are known as “Ahl al-Ma‘ānī.” They affirm an infinite regress within a single instant. They say that the act of creation itself has an act of creation, that this act of creation has another act of creation, and so on without end, all existing within a single instant. This position is well known to be theirs.

The fourth answer is the position of those who say:

An act of creation that comes into being requires a newly arising cause; that cause likewise requires another, and so on. This entails the perpetual occurrence of things of this kind, which is not impossible. For the position of the early generations is that Allah has never ceased to speak whenever He wills. His words have no end, and every utterance is preceded by another, without any finite limit. He, glorified be He, speaks by His power and His will.

They likewise say that whatever is living must be active, as al-Bukhārī stated and related from Nu‘aym ibn Hammād, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd, Ibn Khuzaymah, and others. It must likewise be in motion, as ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī and others stated. Each of the two mentions that this is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah. This is also affirmed by leading philosophers, both earlier and later, whose statements to this effect have been cited elsewhere.

They say that this is an infinite regress of effects, whereas demonstration establishes only the impossibility of an infinite regress of causes. The invalidity of the latter is known through clear reason, and rational thinkers agree that it is impossible, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 2396

As for His speaking words without end, glorified and exalted is He, and His speaking by His will and power, this is what sound transmitted evidence and clear reason establish. It is the position of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. The philosophers agree that this kind of activity continues perpetually, and their foremost early authorities agree that it subsists in Allah’s essence, as the leading Muslim scholars and early generations maintain. Those who declare this impossible are the adherents of speculative theology newly introduced into Islam—the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah. They argue that everything in which temporal occurrences subsist must itself have come into existence, on the grounds that a beginningless succession of occurrences is impossible.

This brings to light the second principle underlying the exalted Lord’s acts, whether pertaining to Himself or affecting others: do matters subject to His choice and connected with His power and will subsist in Him or not? The position of the early generations, the leading scholars of hadith, and many groups among the speculative theologians and philosophers is that this is possible. By contrast, those who deny the attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and the philosophers, together with the Kullābiyyah among those who affirm the attributes, maintain that such matters cannot subsist in Him.

As for the “deniers of the attributes,” they deny this and other attributes, saying: “All these are accidents. Accidents subsist only in a body, and bodies have come into existence. Thus, if attributes subsisted in Him, He too would have come into existence.”

As for the “Kullābiyyah,” they say: “We affirm that attributes subsist in Him, but we do not call them accidents, for an accident does not endure for two successive moments. In our view, the attributes of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, endure, unlike the accidents subsisting in created beings; for we hold that accidents do not endure for two successive moments.”

---

## Page 2397

The majority of rational thinkers, however, disputed this and said: “Rather, the blackness and whiteness that existed an hour ago are the very same qualities that exist now.” This has been discussed at length elsewhere; the purpose here is simply to draw attention to the different groups’ positions on this principle.

The “Kullābiyyah” said: “As for temporal occurrences, if they subsisted in Him, it would follow that He could never be free of them, since whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. If He could never be free of them, it would follow that He too had come into existence, for this is the very argument used to establish that bodies have come into existence.”

This is their principal argument concerning this principle. Their opponents may reject both premises or only one of them.

Many speculative theologians and hadith scholars rejected the first premise, including the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, Abū Mu‘ādh, and Zuhayr al-Ibrī. Likewise, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and other Ash‘arīs rejected the first premise and demonstrated its invalidity, explaining that those who assert it have no evidence for their claim. Something may, in fact, be receptive to a quality while being devoid of both that quality and its opposite, as actually occurs. Those who uphold this principle committed themselves to maintaining that every body has a taste, a colour, a smell, and all the other kinds of accidents that bodies can receive.

The majority of rational thinkers therefore said: “This is a blatant denial of the obvious and an unsupported claim.” The Kullābiyyah committed themselves to it only because of this principle.

As for the second premise—namely, denying the perpetual succession of temporal occurrences—it is rejected by the leading scholars of the Sunnah and hadith who maintain that Allah speaks by His will and power and that His words have no end; by those who maintain that He has always been active, as al-Bukhārī and others state; and by those who say that

---

## Page 2398

movement is inseparable from life, so life cannot exist without any movement at all, as al-Dārimī and others maintain.

Al-Tha‘labī narrated in his Tafsīr, through his chain of transmission, that Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-Sādiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked concerning Allah’s words, “Did you think that We created you in vain?”: “Why did Allah create creation?” He replied:

“Because Allah has always been beneficent, from eternity and for all eternity. Allah therefore willed to bestow His beneficence upon His creation, though He had no need of them. He did not create them to gain any benefit or avert any harm. Rather, He created them, treated them with goodness, and sent messengers to them so that they might distinguish truth from falsehood. Whoever does good, He rewards with Paradise; and whoever disobeys, He recompenses with the Fire.”

Regarding Allah’s words, “And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful,” “And Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise,” and similar expressions, Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “He was so, has always been so, and will always remain so.”

This premise is also rejected by the majority of philosophers. The Jahmiyyah, Mu‘tazilah, Kullābiyyah, and Karrāmiyyah, however, maintain that the perpetual succession of temporal occurrences is impossible. This is one of the major principles underlying discussion of Allah’s speech and His creation. This position is the foundation of the speculative theology introduced into Islam that the early generations and leading scholars condemned.

For the adherents of this speculative theology among the Jahmiyyah, Mu‘tazilah, and their followers thought that Allah’s being the Creator of everything—as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah and agreed upon by the adherents of religious communities, including Muslims, Jews, Christians, and others—meant that He, glorified and exalted be He, had always been inactive

---

## Page 2399

doing nothing and saying nothing whatsoever. Rather, He alone existed, uttering no speech and performing no act. Then He brought into being His speech and the things He made that are separate from Him, and thus brought the world into being. They supposed that this was the meaning of what the messengers taught and the adherents of the religious communities agreed upon—namely, that everything other than Allah is created and that Allah is the Creator of everything. They also supposed that the opposing position was that of those who held that the world, or its matter, is eternal. Consequently, they mentioned only two positions in their works of speculative theology.

The first is the position of Muslims and other religious communities: that the world came into being—which, as they understood it, meant what was stated above.

The second is the position of the Dahriyyah, who say that the world is eternal. In their works on speculative theology and the doctrines of various schools, they came to report that all religious communities—Muslims, Jews, Christians, and others—held that Allah had, from eternity, neither done anything nor spoken anything, and then brought the world into being; whereas the Dahriyyah held that the world is eternal. The view commonly attributed to those who maintain the eternity of the world is that it has no Maker; thus, they deny the Maker, majestic is His glory. Writers on the doctrines of various schools have mentioned that the first philosopher to maintain the eternity of the world was Aristotle, the author of philosophical teachings on logic, natural philosophy, and metaphysics.

Yet Aristotle and his early followers affirm the First Cause in their books. They say that the celestial sphere moves in imitation of it, and that it is a cause of the sphere in this respect: were the one whom the sphere imitates not to exist, the sphere would not move, and its motion

---

## Page 2400

is inseparable from its existence; hence, were its motion to cease, it would perish.

Aristotle did not say that the First Cause originated the celestial spheres. Nor did he say that it necessitates its effects by its very essence, as some later philosophers, such as Ibn Sīnā and his like, maintain. Nor did he say that the celestial sphere is eternal yet contingent in itself. Rather, these philosophers shared the understanding of all other rational people: something contingent is that which can either exist or not exist, and only something brought into being can be of this kind. In their view, the celestial sphere is not contingent; rather, it is eternal and has always existed. The actual implication of their position is that its existence is necessary, without beginning or end.

For this reason, in most early works of speculative theology, the doctrine of the eternity of the world is attributed only to those who deny the Maker. But when philosophers such as Ibn Sīnā and his like put forward the view that the world is eternal and proceeds from an eternal cause that necessitates its effects by its very essence, this became another position among those who upheld the eternity of the world. Through it, they removed the apparent odiousness of their position arising from their denial of a Maker of the world. They also began using the expressions employed by Muslims, saying that the world is made, brought into being, and so forth. What they mean, however, is that it is an eternal, beginningless effect. They do not mean that Allah brought something into being after it had not existed. When they say that Allah is the Creator of everything, this is what they mean.

Later speculative theologians thus began mentioning this position alongside the well-known position of the speculative theologians concerning what it means for the world to have come into being—the position they attribute to the adherents of the religious communities, as explained above. Al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others present the matter in this way.

And this principle, which the Jahmiyyah and the speculative theologians who followed them introduced—namely, the impossibility of

---

## Page 2401

Allah’s acting perpetually—is the very principle upon which they built the foundations of their religion, making it the foundation of the Muslims’ religion. They said:

Bodies are never free of temporally originated events, and whatever is never free of such events is itself temporally originated. Alternatively, whatever does not precede temporally originated events is itself temporally originated, because whatever is neither free of them nor precedes them must exist alongside them or after them. Whatever exists alongside temporally originated events or after them is itself temporally originated.

Many of them offer no proof for this, regarding it as self-evident, since they do not distinguish between events as a class and a particular event. Those among them who recognize the distinction, however, offer a proof by saying:

Events cannot be perpetual; rather, it is impossible for there to be events with no beginning.

Some of them also deny the possibility of events with no end, as do the two leading figures of this speculative theology: Jahm ibn Safwān and Abū al-Hudhayl.

Since the real implication of this position is that Allah, glorified be He, was not capable of acting from eternity, but became capable of acting after having been incapable of it, this was among the things for which Muslims condemned these people. Indeed, it was even counted among al-Ash'arī’s innovations during the unrest in Khurāsān, when curses against the people of innovation were publicly pronounced. The account is well known.

Furthermore, the speculative theologians and their leading figures—such as al-Nazzām, al-'Allāf, and other teachers of the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah, together with their followers from the various other groups—say:

The religion of Islam rests entirely upon this principle, and it cannot be known that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, except through this

principle; for recognizing the Messenger depends upon knowing the One who sent him. It is therefore necessary first to establish knowledge of the Maker and to know what is and is not possible with respect to Him.

Most of them say: A person’s first obligation is to know Allah, and He can only be known through this method.

Many of them say:

This is the method of Abraham, the close friend of Allah, peace be upon him, mentioned in his words:

Were this proof called into question, the proof of his prophethood would necessarily be called into question, and it would no longer be known that he is the Messenger of Allah.

This and similar arguments constitute the rational proof which they say conflicts with revelation and reason. And we say: When revelation and reason conflict, it is impossible to affirm both, to reject both, or to affirm revelation rather than reason, because reason is the foundation of revelation. Thus, to undermine the foundation of the revealed religion would be to undermine that religion itself.

It was because of this method that the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah denied the divine attributes and the vision of Allah, and said:

“The Quran is created.” It was because of this method that the Jahmiyyah maintained that Paradise and Hell would perish, and that al-ʿAllāf maintained that movement within them would cease. Others responded to them:

As for your claim that this method is the foundation for knowing the religion of Islam and the prophethood of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, its falsity is among the self-evident truths of Islam. Everyone acquainted with the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions, and the faith and Quran he brought knows that he never called people through this method. Nor did any of the Companions or those who followed them in righteousness ever speak of it. How, then, can it be the foundation of faith when the one who brought faith and those whose faith was strongest never spoke of it at all, and none of them pursued it?

Those who recognized that this method was an innovation fall into two groups:

One group considered it sound in itself, but held that the early generations turned away from it because its premises were lengthy and obscure, and because those pursuing it risked becoming entangled in doubt and protracted inquiry. This was the position of a number of scholars, including al-Ashʿarī in his Epistle to the Frontier, al-Khattābī, al-Halīmī, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn ʿAqīl, Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī, and others.

The second position is that of those who say: Rather, this method is inherently false, and that is why the early generations condemned it and turned away from it. This was the position of the leading scholars of the early generations, such as Ibn al-Mubārak, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad

---

ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Abū Yūsuf, Mālik ibn Anas, Abd al-Azīz ibn al-Mājishūn, and other scholars of the early generations. yet no such cause exists; therefore, action must be perpetual. They then made a false claim whose invalidity those others failed to demonstrate adequately: that if action is perpetual, the celestial spheres and elements must be eternal.

## Page 2407

It has been explained elsewhere that these people are more deeply steeped in disbelief than the Jews and Christians after the abrogation and alteration of their religions, even if they profess Islam.
